Title: The Impact of Intellectual Property Protection “Distance” on Collaborative Innovation Quality: Evidence From Chinese Listed Firms
Authors: Bojun Hou, Ruirui Zhu, Zhijian Cui, Pengcheng Jin
Affiliations: School of Economics Hefei University of Technology Hefei China; School of Management University of Science and Technology of China Hefei China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Cross‐regional collaboration plays a growing role in firm innovation, yet interregional institutional differences create frictions that undermine the quality of collaborative outcomes. Whether institutional distance in intellectual property protection (IPP) reduces collaborative innovation quality and whether professional intermediaries can alleviate these frictions remain open questions. This study investigates how interregional distance in IPP (DIPP) affects interregional collaborative patent quality (ICPQ) using extensive 2007–2022 collaborative invention patent data from Chinese A‐share listed firms. We find that greater DIPP significantly reduces ICPQ, as divergent IPP regimes erode mutual trust, hinder knowledge sharing, and raise coordination and enforcement costs between partners. Patent agency experience effectively mitigates this adverse effect, suggesting that professional intermediaries help bridge institutional gaps between collaborating regions. These findings hold across a range of robustness tests and an instrumental variable analysis addressing endogeneity. The study contributes to the institutional distance literature by identifying patent agency expertise as a mechanism through which firms can navigate interregional institutional frictions. It also offers practical guidance for firms and policymakers seeking to leverage patent agency services to support high‐quality cross‐regional innovation.

Title: From Apollo to Artemis: NASA’s adaptation to radical transformations in crewed space exploration
Authors: Raja Roy, Saikat Chaudhuri
Affiliations: Innovation and Entrepreneurship, Martin Tuchman School of Management, New Jersey Institute of Technology , Newark, NJ . e-mail: rroy@njit.edu; Department of Management Science and Engineering, School of Engineering, Stanford University . e-mail: saikat.chaudhuri@stanford.edu
Abstract: Abstract We examine NASA’s adaptation during radical transformations in crewed space exploration, from the Apollo program, which aimed at astronauts accessing the lunar surface and returning to Earth, to the Artemis program, focused on establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon and Mars. We find that as NASA’s business model for crewed space exploration evolved from the Apollo program to the Space Shuttle program, and thereafter to the Artemis program, NASA adapted by modularizing its technological systems into a launch module, an access and reentry module, and a presence module. These modules partitioned the systems required for escaping Earth’s gravity, reaching the destination in space and journeying back to Earth, and establishing a sustained human presence on other celestial bodies. In addition, NASA’s adaptation involved transforming its organizational structure to mirror the technological modularization. By highlighting the role of modularization during radical transformations in business models, we provide evidence for the theory of technology, which emphasizes horizontal transfer of functional modules, and offer new insights into the mirroring hypothesis, organizational adaptation, and entrepreneurial opportunity creation.

Title: AI, productivity, and digital capabilities: cross-country evidence from early adoption
Authors: Flavio Calvino, Luca Fontanelli
Affiliations: OECD Directorate for Science, Technology and Innovation , Paris, 75016; University of Brescia , Brescia, 25122, Italy. e-mail: luca.fontanelli@unibs.it
Abstract: Abstract This work analyses the early use of artificial intelligence (AI) in firms across nine countries, prior to the boom in generative AI. Based on harmonized analysis applied to official and representative firm-level surveys, it finds that the early use of AI is prevalent in ICT and Professional Services and more widespread across large—and to some extent across young—firms. Different proxies of digital capabilities—notably ICT skills, high-speed digital infrastructure, and digital maturity—exhibit significant complementarities in adoption. Early AI users are on average more productive than other firms. However, this appears to a considerable extent related to the self-selection of firms with higher digital capabilities into AI use. Strengthening digital capabilities of firms and workers can, therefore, be a relevant lever that managers and policy-makers can use to boost both AI diffusion and productivity.

Title: Governing sustainable co-creation in business–NGO collaborations: Institutional logics and innovation outcomes
Authors: Annabeth Aagaard, Lise Andersen
Abstract: This study examines how governance in business-NGO collaborations conditions co-creation for sustainable innovation under institutional plurality. Drawing on institutional logics theory, we conduct a qualitative cross-case study of five Scandinavian retail firms and their NGO partners. We identify three recurrent governance configurations: separated coexistence, assimilated coexistence, and logic blending. The configurations differ in how partners manage organizational boundaries, allocate decision authority, integrate knowledge, and establish accountability. In the cases studied, separated coexistence was recurrently associated with regulative innovation, where protected organizational distance supported credible monitoring and verification. Assimilated coexistence was recurrently associated with inclusive sustainable business innovation, where NGO knowledge entered bounded parts of firm-led innovation. Logic blending was most evident in social impact innovation, where joint problem framing, shared interpretation of evidence, and relational accountability supported long-term societal outcomes. These relationships represent empirical tendencies rather than necessary, sufficient, or exclusive associations. Different configurations may coexist across activities and may evolve as collaborations mature. The study extends institutional logics research by showing how responses to plurality are operationalized as interorganizational governance arrangements that structure decision rights, knowledge interfaces, boundaries, and accountability. It contributes to sustainable co-creation research by explaining why different innovation tasks call for different combinations of governance practices.

Title: Innovation or commercialization? Evidence from firm-level staggered entry into technology development areas in Türkiye
Authors: Saliha Ergün Tanrıverdi
Abstract: This paper evaluates the causal impact of Technology Development Areas (TDAs) on firm-level innovation and commercialization in Türkiye. Exploiting staggered firm entry into TDAs and rich microdata from the Ministry of Science, Industry and Technology’s 2012 Impact Evaluation Survey, treatment effects are estimated using the cohort-specific Difference-in-Differences framework of Callaway and Sant’Anna ( 2021 ), which is robust to heterogeneous treatment timing. The study examines multiple stages of the innovation process, including project completion, product development, patenting, and domestic and international sales. The results show that entry into a TDA has no statistically significant effect on patenting activity in the short run. In contrast, TDA participation leads to sizable and economically meaningful increases in applied innovation and commercialization outcomes, particularly completed projects, developed and sold products, and turnover. These effects emerge quickly after entry and are largely robust to the inclusion of firm-level controls, with the exception of the international turnover effect, which loses significance once firm age and size are included. The findings suggest that TDAs primarily enhance the efficiency with which existing innovative capabilities are translated into market outcomes, rather than immediately expanding firms’ upstream inventive capacity. Title: How Complementarities Affect Technological Innovation Within Platform‐Based Innovation Ecosystems: The Role of Orchestrators' Platform Capability and Interorganizational Trust
Authors: Fenfen Wei, Nanping Feng, Richard David Evans, Xiaohua Xin, Furong Ruan
Affiliations: School of Management Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications Nanjing China; School of Management Hefei University of Technology Hefei China; Key Laboratory of Process Optimization and Intelligent Decision‐Making in Ministry of Education Hefei China; Faculty of Computer Science Dalhousie University Halifax Nova Scotia Canada; School of Economics and Management Xi'an University of Technology Xi'an China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Complementarities in Platform‐based Innovation Ecosystems (PIEs) are crucial for collaborative technological innovation (TECI), yet how they influence TECI remains underexplored. Therefore, by integrating Resource Dependence Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study empirically examined the relationships between two key complementarities (supermodular and unique) and TECI. With a sample of 203 technology firms, this study demonstrates that: (a) supermodular complementarities are more strongly positively associated with TECI than unique ones; (b) orchestrators' platform capabilities and interorganizational trust significantly moderate these complementarities–TECI links, with moderating effects varying by complementarity type. Theoretically, this study advances literature on complementarities–TECI relationships in PIEs. Managerially, it provides practical insights into effectively managing complementarities for TECI performance.

Title: From AI potential to sustainable value: The AI-SDGs value cycle as an integrative framework for sustainable innovation
Authors: Francesco Paolo Appio, Davide La Torre, Vito Giordano, Francesca Lazzeri, Hatem Masri
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a means of advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet its contribution remains conditional, uneven, and context-dependent. To explain this variation, we organize the evidence through a single integrative lens: the AI-SDGs value cycle. The cycle comprises five interdependent functions - mapping opportunities, mobilizing capabilities, deploying applications, governing legitimacy and accountability, and evaluating sustainable value creation and destruction. It connects evidence across technologies, teams, organizations, sectors, cities, markets, and public institutions without reducing diverse contributions to a catalog of applications. The synthesis shows that sustainable outcomes arise not from technological capability alone, but from its combination with organizational readiness, sectoral fit, responsible governance, stakeholder representation, and attention to cross-goal and lifecycle consequences. Collectively, the papers move research beyond broad claims about AI's potential toward explanations of when, how, for whom, and at what cost AI supports sustainable development. They establish governance as constitutive of sustainable innovation and reveal value creation and destruction as simultaneous possibilities rather than separable outcomes. Drawing these insights together, this editorial synthesizes the 17 accepted articles in the Technovation Special Issue “Artificial Intelligence for the Sustainable Development Goals” and clarifies their collective contribution. It concludes with a focused research agenda organized around the same value cycle and directed toward cumulative, comparative, and impact-oriented inquiry.

Title: Can AI Solve Eco-Economic Challenges? Simulating the Impact of AI Systems on Seasonality Using Agent-Based Modelling
Authors: Sara Dalir
Abstract: Abstract As visitors increasingly rely on AI-enabled apps and recommender systems, AI is becoming an important mediator of tourism choice. Tourism decision-making is cognitively demanding, and visitors rarely evaluate all available destinations, attractions, travel periods, and services equally. Consistent with bounded rationality, they simplify complex choice environments through limited information, heuristics, and platform-mediated evaluation. This creates opportunities for AI systems not only to personalise experiences, but also to influence how attention and demand are distributed across attractions and seasons. This research develops and computationally examines a mechanism-based conceptualisation of how AI-enabled information systems mediate visitor choice and how micro-level decision processes accumulate into tourism-system outcomes. Drawing on digital choice architecture, information filtering, platform ecosystem perspectives, and bounded rationality, the research conceptualises AI as a decision-mediating infrastructure. Using an agent-based model of a tourism platform ecosystem, it compares three visitor-facing AI intervention conditions: predictive nudging, a recommender-system filtering, and fairness-oriented visibility enhancement. The model examines how differences in attention, salience, choice-set formation, evaluation, satisfaction, and subsequent behaviour are associated with system-level outcomes. The findings show that AI-mediated interventions can increase visitor activity and spending, but their effects differ across intervention conditions and do not automatically reduce seasonality. The research contributes to Information Systems and smart-tourism research by showing how AI-enabled decision environments can structure attention, consideration, and visibility, while highlighting the limits of digital interventions when destination outcomes are also shaped by wider structural conditions.

Title: Modelling Consumer Resistance Towards QR Code-Based Product Verification Systems: A Comparative Analysis of Traceability vs. Authentication in India and France
Authors: Subhadeep Mandal, Arpan Kumar Kar, Shivam Gupta
Abstract: Quick Response code-based verification technologies are revolutionizing the food and beverages supply chain by offering product traceability and authentication, enabling consumers to access information about their consumables. These systems function via quick response codes, supporting either blockchain-based distributed traceability (farm-to-fork) or company-managed centralized authentication databases. Although manufacturers adopt Quick Response code-based verification to foster trust, consumer resistance remains prevalent. This study compares India and France across contrasting national uncertainty-avoidance profiles and examines active and passive resistance barriers using innovation resistance theory and status quo bias theory. It focuses on two verification mechanisms—traceability and authentication—designed to combat counterfeiting and misinformation, examining how user and system characteristics contribute to resistance. Based on data from 581 retail shoppers, the study applies fuzzy set Qualitative Comparative Analysis to identify key combinations of functional, psychological, system-related, and individual barriers. The findings offer practical insights for selecting and deploying effective traceability/authentication strategies to mitigate consumer resistance.

Title: AI capability and product innovation intensity: Driving B2B marketing innovation under varying levels of market turbulence
Authors: Nisreen Ameen, Jun-Hwa Cheah, Senmao Xia, Tippayanet Sorosrungruang, Vera Hoelscher, Shlomo Tarba
Abstract: In increasingly volatile markets, firms are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance innovation and maintain a competitive edge. However, many organizations continue to struggle to translate AI investments into meaningful innovation outcomes. This study develops and empirically tests a framework examining how AI capability is transformed into business-to-business (B2B) marketing innovation through organizational agility and product innovation intensity. Drawing on survey data from 239 Chinese firms, the findings reveal that AI capability drives B2B marketing innovation through a theorized sequential relationship, in which organizational agility enables intensified product innovation, which in turn supports market-facing innovation. Furthermore, market turbulence acts as a contingent boundary condition, amplifying the effects of AI capability on product innovation intensity and downstream innovation outcomes, while not significantly affecting its relationship with organizational agility. By conceptualizing AI capability as an enabling capability architecture that activates sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring processes, this research advances dynamic capability theory and provides a more granular explanation of how AI is translated into innovation. It also distinguishes between innovation generation (product innovation intensity) and innovation realization (B2B marketing innovation), offering a process-based account of capability-to-innovation transformation. The study provides actionable insights for managers on developing integrated AI capability, enhancing organizational agility, and strategically intensifying innovation efforts under varying levels of market turbulence.

Title: The paradox of experience: Public procurement and delivery timelines across digital solution types
Authors: Tommaso Giaccardi, Luca Gastaldi, Andrea S. Patrucco
Abstract: Lengthy public procurement processes can slow the delivery of essential public services. While most research on procurement duration has focused on infrastructure and public works, digital solutions now play a central role in how public services are delivered. This study uses survival analysis to examine the time required to award contracts, execute them, and report project delivery, drawing on 40,991 digitalization projects carried out by 7838 Italian municipalities under the Next Generation EU program. We proxy experience in procuring digital solutions with historical procurement expenditure and show that its relationship with project duration varies by solution type. Higher prior activity is associated with faster timelines for standardized connections to centrally managed platforms, but with slower timelines for cloud migration and citizen experience projects, where implementation requires more local configuration. Results for interoperability projects are inconclusive. At the median, interquartile increases in prior activity span about 118 days between citizen experience and digital notice projects, or about 22% of median completion duration. These findings challenge the common assumption that procurement experience necessarily speeds up project delivery. Prior activity may reflect both reusable organizational routines and the installed base created by earlier projects, although our data do not directly measure either mechanism. Historical procurement expenditure on digital solutions should therefore not be treated as a general indicator of readiness. Program managers should consider solution category when assessing readiness and setting or monitoring timelines.

Title: Entrepreneurial dynamism and entrepreneurial ecosystem in emerging economies: the role of infrastructure
Authors: Krishna Chandra Balodi, Paul Kattuman, Christina Theodoraki, Ravi Roshan

Abstract: Abstract Although prior research has extensively examined the relationships between entrepreneurship and economic growth, as well as between infrastructure and development, the influence of infrastructure on entrepreneurial dynamism (ED) in emerging economies remains insufficiently understood. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how both the quantity and quality of infrastructure shape productive entrepreneurship in emerging economies. Grounded in the entrepreneurial ecosystem framework, we employ state-level data for India from 2000 to 2019 to empirically examine these relationships. Using the dynamic-panel system generalized method of moments estimator to address the dynamic nature of infrastructure and ED variables and their potential endogeneity, we find that significant infrastructure-ED relationships emerge when infrastructure quality is higher.

Title: Uncovering collaborative patterns and transition dynamics in R&D projects: a longitudinal analysis of EU Framework Programmes
Authors: Andrea Ancona, Roy Cerqueti, Gianluca Vagnani

Abstract: Abstract Policymakers have increasingly supported collaborative R&D, recognizing its role in enhancing the innovation performance and scientific reputation of organizations. This paper proposes a three-step procedure to examine collaborative patterns and participation dynamics over consecutive research programs by integrating Social Network Analysis and statistical methods. First, participants in R&D projects are ranked based on their centrality in the collaborative network. Second, transition probabilities between classes of centrality across consecutive programs are estimated. Third, the Markovian nature of collaborative patterns, which is controversial across methodological, theoretical, and empirical contributions, is tested. Using data from the first eight European Union Framework Programmes (EU FPs), we analyze the relationship between EU funding mechanisms and the micro-level behaviors of participants. Our findings provide an integrated understanding of co-evolving micro- and macro-level dynamics, reflected in the emergence of core–periphery structures, and emphasize the role of EU-funded projects in strengthening organizations’ popularity. However, these dynamics also highlight the risk of “oligopolistic” behaviors that may limit the European Research Area. Exogenous mechanisms, such as R&D policies and funding, emerge as crucial mechanisms in shaping participation dynamics and organizational positions, emphasizing the need to promote openness and democratization in research funding.

Title: Analyzing firm growth with parametric quantile regression
Authors: Paolo Frumento, Alessandro Sapio
Affiliations: Department of Political Sciences, University of Pisa , via F. Serafini 3, 56126 Pisa , . e-mail: paolo.frumento@unipi.it; Department of Business and Economics, Parthenope University of Naples , via Generale Parisi 13, 80132 Naples , . e-mail: alessandro.sapio@uniparthenope.it
Abstract: Abstract We apply quantile regression coefficient modeling (QRCM) to investigate the firm growth process. QRCM imposes a parametric structure to the conditional quantile function and allows to estimate all quantiles at once by minimizing an integrated loss. To handle the presence of repeated measures, we fit a two-level model in which both the level-1 and level-2 parts of the distribution depend on predictors according to a quantile regression (QR) structure. Compared with standard QR, in which different quantiles are estimated one at a time, QRCM improves statistical efficiency, mitigates quantile crossing, simplifies estimation of extremes, and allows to incorporate identifying assumptions. We investigate growth in a panel of UK manufacturing firms. Our analysis accounts for variance-size scaling and allows to disentangle the location effect of firm size on growth from the scale effect. We propose alternative parametrizations of the QR coefficients: a flexible model based on Legendre polynomials, and a variety of more structured models that rely on known quantile functions, such as the Gaussian, logistic, and asymmetric logistic distributions, that differ in their tail behavior. Our results indicate that fat-tailed models, such as the asymmetric logistic distribution, provide a better fit than the normal distribution. We are able to detect a positive location effect and to obtain efficient estimates of the extreme quantiles.

Title: Circular platform orchestration in B2B markets: shaping competitive dynamics and collective industry benefits
Authors: Dagiliene Lina, Varaniute Viktorija, Kaipainen Jenni, Ritala Paavo, Urbinati Andrea, Aarikka-Stenroos Leena

Abstract: Abstract Circular digital platforms can contribute to addressing the challenges of natural resource overexploitation and material waste accumulation. Circular digital platforms incorporate diverse, complementary, and even competitive actors; therefore, circular platform orchestration is a crucial phenomenon yet unstudied. This study examines the conditions of circular platform orchestration in diverse actor settings leading to collective industry benefits, and changes in competitive dynamics among industry actors. We utilize a multiple-case study on circular digital B2B platforms orchestrated by public and private actors in Finland, Italy, and Lithuania. The findings identify three orchestration conditions of B2B circular platforms: incentives and motivation to participate in the platform, control and operational rules, and homogeneity/heterogeneity of actors. The findings also show that these conditions manifest differently under private versus public orchestrators, with the former more motivated by economic goals and the latter more by public good goals; yet, with industry outcomes being relatively similar. Our study provides implications to the literature of circular economy business and platform orchestration by demonstrating how circular platforms help to ‘raise all boats’ in the industry while reconfiguring some competitive dynamics between primary and secondary markets.

Title: Positioning firms along the capabilities ladder
Authors: Alex Coad, Nanditha Mathew, Emanuele Pugliese

Abstract: Abstract A major challenge for innovation scholars is the measurement of capabilities. We develop and apply a novel methodology for quantifying the capability development of firms, where capabilities are measured in terms of expenditures on specific activities. These activities can be sorted in a hierarchy of increasing difficulty, and firms can be sorted according to their positions on the capabilities ladder. Our nestedness algorithm, inspired by biology and network science, defines an activity as complex if it is performed by only a few firms at the upper rungs of the ladder. We analyze company annual reports of almost 45,000 Indian firms for the time period 2000–2020, and observe significant nestedness. Lower rungs of the capabilities ladder correspond to basic managerial and production activities. Mid-level rungs correspond to internationalization and acquiring absorptive capacity. Higher-level rungs are more related to Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A) and innovation. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) capabilities seem to have become more fundamental lower-level rungs on the capabilities ladder in recent years. There is a close relationship between size and capabilities for small firms, but this weakens for larger firms. Some heterogeneity is observed across industrial sectors and across regions. We find that capability ranking can explain future growth patterns and survival probability of firms, summing up in one number their future potential trajectories.

Title: Product and process innovation in the United States from 1980 to 2015 and over the firm’s life cycle
Authors: Colin Davison
Affiliations: The College of Wooster, Department of Economics, College of Wooster , Morgan Hall 207, E Pine St, Wooster, OH 44691 , . e-mail: cdavison@wooster.edu
Abstract: Abstract This paper uses machine learning techniques to classify patent claims as product or process innovations and documents that the overall process share of innovation in the United States was on a secular decline from 1980 to 2015. The reallocation of patenting activity from the chemical to the computer & communication category explains much of the declining process share from 1980 to 2000. This paper rules out the rise of China as an explanation for the declining process share from 2000 to 2015. Instead, this paper finds evidence that a large contributor to the decline in the process share from 2000 to 2015 is patents in the semiconductor and electrical circuit topics becoming less process focused. This paper finds that the process share is low at the beginning of a firm’s product life cycle, peaks in the middle, before plateauing at an intermediate level at the end of the life cycle. Firm size is positively associated with the process share of innovation. These relationships between life cycle, size, and the process share of innovation are not present for alternative classifications of product and process patents.

Title: Beyond the platform: the consumer platform and enterprise software divide in China and Europe
Authors: J S Tan
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology , 77 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA 02139 , . e-mail: js_tan@mit.edu
Abstract: Abstract Despite an already abundant scholarly literature on digital capitalism, analyses have overlooked enterprise software and SaaS as a distinct business model, focusing overwhelmingly instead on consumer platforms. Using regression analysis on firms founded between 2000 and 2020, this article shows that while China’s digital economy is disproportionately oriented towards the consumer platforms, Europe’s is more heavily weighted toward enterprise software/SaaS. I argue that labor regimes, regulatory environments, and domestic market structures explain this divide. China’s flexible labor regime and permissive regulation are better suited for the platform business model, whereas Europe’s stronger protections support the stable inter-firm relationships enterprise software/SaaS requires. These differences have important distributional consequences: whereas consumer platform firms disrupt legacy industries and capture the benefits of digitization for themselves, enterprise software/SaaS firms diffuse those benefits to other industries by providing them with tools to digitize and compete.

Title: Quality- or/and category-based output control strategies for user-generated content platforms
Authors: Takahiro Inada, Nobuyuki Inamizu
Affiliations: Department of Business Administration, Kyoto University of Advanced Science , Yamanouchi Gotanda cho 18, Ukyo ku, Kyoto shi, Kyoto 615-8577 , . e-mail: inada.takahiro@kuas.ac.jp; Graduate School of Economics, The University of Tokyo , Hongo 7-3-1, Bunkyo ku, Tokyo 113-0033 , . e-mail: inamizu@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp
Abstract: Abstract Digital platforms provide arenas in which autonomous participants produce and consume content, and the design of their governance constitutes a critical source of firm performance. This study focuses on output control strategies in user-generated content platforms and introduces a novel theoretical framework that goes beyond the traditional quality-based approach by incorporating category-based mechanisms. Specifically, we classify output control strategies along two domains—quality and category—and introduce a fourfold typology consisting of open, quality-based, category-based, and dual control strategies. Furthermore, we examine two boundary conditions—user composition and revenue models—and conduct an agent-based simulation to compare the relative effectiveness of each strategy. This study makes two theoretical contributions. First, by incorporating participants’ within-category preferences, we establish the theoretical validity of category-based control and refine the conventional open/closed governance dichotomy. Second, we demonstrate that dual control strategies can simultaneously pursue both participant numbers and utility, offering a new perspective of compatibility that challenges the traditional view of governance strategies as a trade-off between the two. Through these contributions, this research extends the theoretical scope of platform governance studies.

Title: Temporal dynamic effects of public innovation subsidies on firms’ significant innovation outcomes
Authors: Robert van der Have, Matthias Deschryvere

Abstract: Abstract Longitudinal studies examining dynamic effects of research, development, and innovation (RDI) subsidies on firm-level outcomes—particularly their role in promoting significant innovations—remain limited. This has left policymakers at a disadvantage in coordinating complementary innovation policy instruments. Using a literature-based innovation output measure, we address these shortcomings by means of a nationally representative panel study of Finnish enterprises’ significant innovation outcomes observed over 22 years. Relative to confounding factors, we find that the average dynamic effects of RDI grant subsidies on companies’ probability to commercialize a significant innovation are modest but mostly positive, persisting, and dynamically increasing, peaking around five to eight years after first receiving a grant. Robustness tests, including results based on counts of granted patents, generally support the main findings of the study. Based on our empirical insights, we provide an economic interpretation of our results, suggesting that a consistent long-term innovation subsidy policy plays a meaningful role in advancing innovation output.

Title: Varieties of regional innovation systems around the world and catch-up by latecomers
Authors: Jinhee Kim, Keun Lee
Affiliations: The Incheon Institute , Incheon, 22711 , . e-mail: jhkim9170@ii.re.kr; Chung-Ang University and Seoul National University , Seoul , 06974, Republic of Korea; College of Business and Economics, University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, 2092, South Africa; ISSEK, National Research University Higher School of Economics, . e-mail: kenneth@snu.ac.kr
Abstract: Abstract This study represents one of the first attempts to develop a global typology of regional innovation systems (RIS) across both advanced and catching-up economies, identifying distinct pathways for regional technological catch-up. Utilizing United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) patent citation data from 33 regions worldwide over the period 2000–2017, we construct several RIS indicators, including intra-regional, inter-regional, and international knowledge sourcing, alongside domestic ownership of innovation. Through cluster analysis, we identify four primary RIS configurations and examine their relationship with economic performance: Group 1: large and mature RIS, characterized by long-cycle technology specialization and high domestic ownership; Group 2: mixed RIS, featuring long-cycle specialization but low domestic ownership; Group 3: strong catch-up RIS, defined by short-cycle technology specialization and high domestic ownership; Group 4: weak catch-up RIS, involving short-cycle specialization with low domestic ownership. While Groups 3 and 4 consist exclusively of emerging economies specializing in similar short-cycle technology sectors, they exhibit divergent levels of economic performance. Ultimately, the analysis identifies two empirically distinct catch-up trajectories: a “stronger” pathway driven by increasing domestic ownership and the localization of knowledge creation and a “weaker” pathway characterized by persistent dependence on foreign knowledge sources. Our findings suggest that domestic ownership and the emergence of large-scale enterprises are critical drivers of localized knowledge sourcing and sustained catch-up.

Title: The evolution of the nuclear industry in Korea: A dynamic model of sectoral innovation system perspective
Authors: Jongyoun Lim, Sunyang Chung
Affiliations: Department of Technology Management, Konkuk University , 120 Neungdong-ro, Gwangjin-gu, Seoul 05029 , . e-mail: jongyoun.lim@gmail.com; Department of Technology Management, Konkuk University , 120 Neungdong-ro, Gwangjin-gu, Seoul 05029 , . e-mail: e-mail: sychung@konkuk.ac.kr
Abstract: Abstract This article examines the evolution of the Korean nuclear industry from the dynamic sectoral innovation system perspective, which integrates the sectoral innovation system (SIS) perspective and industrial dynamics. We analyze the Korean nuclear sector and conclude that it has developed dynamically in three stages: Imitation, Specialization, and Stabilization. During the Imitation stage, key public innovation actors emerged to absorb imported technologies, although interactive learning among them remained limited. In the Specialization stage, enough actors emerged to facilitate close collaboration and begin accumulating technological capabilities. In the Stabilization stage, Korea implemented a competent nuclear SIS, producing sufficient interactive learning among actors and attaining world-level technological capabilities.

Title: The direction of digital transformation: labor-saving versus time-saving trajectories in industrial dynamics
Authors: Andrea Borsato, Elena Cefis
Affiliations: Department of Economics , University of Bergamo, Via dei Caniana 2, 24127, Bergamo, Italy. e-mail: elena.cefis@unibg.it; andrea.borsato@unibg.it; BETA , University of Strasbourg, 61 Avenue de la Forêt Noire, 67000, Strasbourg, France. e-mail: andrea.borsato@unibg.it; Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies , Piazza Martiri della Liberta 33, 56127 Pisa , . e-mail: elena.cefis@unibg.it
Abstract: Abstract The paper develops a theoretical framework with some skill heterogeneity to investigate the way the direction of process innovation, labor-saving versus time-saving, shapes the evolution of the industrial structure, firm dynamics, and macroeconomic performance in a digitally transforming economy. We find that labor-saving innovations deliver higher capital deepening but engender structural fragility. Conversely, when firms focus on time-saving innovations, the economy grows more slowly but exhibits greater resilience: lower downtime supports higher firm survival, reduces volatility, and sustains a more competitive and inclusive market structure. These dynamics are emphasized when labor shortage constrains production capacity. We also discuss the design of more targeted and effective innovation policies, capable of steering digital transformation in directions that are economically robust and socially inclusive.

Title: Generative AI as Support Infrastructure: A Design Theory of Inclusive Intelligence
Authors: Kaveh Abhari, Hossein Shirazi, Morteza Safaeipour, Reut Segal
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed as support infrastructure, yet its capacity to accommodate heterogeneous and fluctuating user conditions through interactional design remains underdeveloped and unevenly realized. This study asks how GenAI can be designed to sustain usable, appropriately bounded support amid such variability. This question is addressed through an echeloned design science research (DSR) process organized into a four-stage theory-development pipeline, using career support for professionals with ADHD as a critical case in which inclusive design requirements become empirically tractable. The evidence base comprises one naturalistic online subcommunity corpus and four participant samples spanning controlled and ecological evaluation. Across four stages, we specify the problem space, derive empirically grounded design requirements, operationalize them as interaction policies within a configured large language model (LLM), and evaluate the resulting policies through controlled and situated evaluation. These stages culminate in a design theory of inclusive intelligence , instantiated through MATRIX, a set of six interaction-level design principles (momentary regulation, ability amplification, trust and stability, resonant attunement, intentional flourishing, and experiential integration) that govern how usable, contextual, and bounded support is enacted in practice. Inclusive intelligence is thus advanced as a mid-range design theory that specifies how GenAI support is calibrated and bounded as user conditions change, locating value in interactional governance rather than model capability. Its transferability is bounded to episodic, text-mediated support characterized by cognitive and affective variability, where guidance must be structured, paced, and delimited under shifting demand.

Title: How High‐Tech Firms Achieve Organizational Resilience Using Dynamic Capabilities and Different Types of Innovations in VUCA Environments
Authors: Sin‐Pei Ng
Affiliations: School of Management and Marketing Taylor's University Subang Jaya Malaysia
Abstract: ABSTRACT High‐tech firms must achieve organizational resilience (OR) to remain viable in volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) environments. Although specific dynamic capabilities (DCs), particularly integrative and reconfiguring capabilities, allow such firms to integrate and complement resource/capability gaps and align resources to maintain evolutionary fitness and develop different types of innovations to become resilient, how they leverage both to achieve OR in VUCA environments remains unexplored to date. This study uses a multiple‐case study approach to explore how high‐tech firms achieve OR by leveraging integrative and reconfiguring capabilities and different types of innovations in VUCA environments. This study finds that high‐tech firms focus on market dynamics, adaptive management innovations, and efficiency‐driven management and process innovations to become resilient. They develop these innovations using proactive and time‐oriented, support activities‐focused, and technology‐driven reconfiguring capabilities, respectively. Additionally, they use ambidexterity‐focused integrative capability to develop supply chain adaptive product innovations and extended technology leveraging market innovations to become resilient. The deployment of complementarity‐oriented integrative capability is found useful in building existing technology leveraging market innovations that underlie firm resilience. This study contributes to the innovation management literature by offering a granular, comprehensive strategic understanding that incorporates both foundations (DCs) and key drivers (innovations) to achieve OR in VUCA environments. It provides managers with nuanced insights for use in developing overarching R&D and innovation strategies by effectively allocating and renewing resources using feature‐specific integrative and reconfiguring capabilities to develop diversified, distinctive types of innovations that provide firms with resilience to support operational continuity in VUCA environments.

Title: Fixation or exploration? A state-dependent dual decoder approach to attribute-aware session-based recommendations

Title: A Configurational Analysis of Digital Interaction and AI Governance Capabilities for Firm Performance
Authors: Shweta Kumari Choudhary, Prashant Kumar, Arpan Kumar Kar
Abstract: Nowadays, firms face escalating pressures to reconfigure their value propositions through AI-driven Digital Transformation (DT); however, aligning users’ interpretations of digital services with those of managers and service providers remains a significant challenge. This study first investigates the specific equifinal configurations of Digital Interaction Capabilities and AI Governance Capabilities that are sufficient to achieve high firm performance among digital service providers. Drawing on Dynamic Capability Theory (DCT), we subsequently examine the perception divide between users and service providers across distinct configurational pathways of Digital Interaction Capabilities and AI Governance Capabilities that are sufficient for high firm performance. We employ fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to analyze dual-survey data collected from a sample of digital service users and service providers. Our findings reveal that service providers frequently misinterpret user expectations, particularly regarding the significant role of perceived website socialness and AI interoperability in enhancing the effectiveness of digital services.

Title: Artifact-enabled societal outcomes of design science research
Authors: Jeffrey Parsons, Leona Chandra Kruse, Thorsten Schoormann, Jinsoo Park
Abstract: Contemporary societal challenges heighten the importance of designing information systems to contribute to improving societal outcomes. While design science research (DSR) has progressively expanded from business settings to broader societal domains, such as healthcare, environmental sustainability, social inclusion, and public governance, the notion of societal outcome is often confused with output and impact. This essay synthesizes insights from the ten papers in this special issue toward improving societal outcomes. Building on this synthesis, we propose an artifact-enabled societal outcome framework. The framework frames societal outcomes as not being achievable through stakeholder engagement alone, but through a rigorous scientific process that combines curiosity in problem framing, timely intervention, artifact validity, and evidence that artifact outputs translate into societal outcomes.

Title: Network-based decision support for cold-start user prioritization in P2P platforms: The value of entry-community information
Authors: Pantelis Loupos, Moran Cerf
Abstract: Predicting the behavior of newly acquired users is a central challenge for digital platforms because direct behavioral histories are sparse at entry. We examine whether relational information revealed by a user’s first transaction can improve decision support for cold-start prioritization in peer-to-peer (P2P) platforms. Using data on approximately 198,000 Venmo users, we compare models based on attributes of the focal user, the first counterparty, and the counterparty’s pre-existing community. We study two managerially relevant outcomes: near-term inactivity risk and future high-engagement-user identification. At entry, adding relational information increases top-decile lift from 1.11 to 1.20 for inactivity risk and from 1.22 to 1.53 for high-engagement identification. Community information also provides additional value beyond the first counterparty, particularly for identifying future high-engagement users. Decomposing the community signal shows that recent transactional activity is more informative than network structure alone. As an interpretable complement, a selection-adjusted analysis shows that entering through a more cohesive community is associated with a 5.0 to 6.5 percentage-point higher probability of becoming a high-engagement user. These findings show how information embedded in the community revealed by a user’s first transaction can support early prioritization when individual behavioral information is limited.

Title: Artificial intelligence at the intersection of innovation and marketing: A conceptual model and research propositions
Authors: Jaihyun Jeon, K. Sivakumar, Gerard A. Athaide, S.P. Raj
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the theory and practice of innovation and marketing, yet its deployment at their intersection remains only partially understood. Existing literature has not thoroughly examined which AI capabilities (analytical, generative) are more appropriate during different stages of the new product development (NPD) process, how a core marketing factor, customer involvement, conditions the outcomes of these capabilities, or how AI-related risks and governance mechanisms shape NPD performance across stages. This study addresses these gaps by proposing a novel conceptual framework that links the two distinct AI capability types to specific NPD stages, examines how customer involvement moderates the relationship between AI capabilities and NPD outcomes, integrates AI hallucination risk as a formal boundary condition differentiating the failure modes of AI capabilities across stages, and extends the framework to NPD governance mechanisms including gate evaluations, feedback loops, and cross-functional coordination. The paper contributes to research and practice by (1) offering a set of propositions regarding AI’s role at the intersection of innovation and marketing, (2) providing theoretically derived guidance for managers on deploying AI capabilities during NPD while recognizing the marketing imperative of customer involvement, and (3) outlining a future research agenda on AI-enabled innovation which is of crucial importance for the future of business. Collectively, the paper advances a more theoretically rigorous and practically relevant understanding of AI’s transformative role in innovation and marketing.

Title: Understanding Business Model Innovation: Unraveling the Role of Schemas, Entrepreneurial Team Faultlines, and Industry Context
Authors: Yingzhao Xiao, Fuwei Li, Jun Yang, David Ahlstrom
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics Tianjin University Tianjin China; China Centre for Information Industry Development Beijing China; School of Management Zhejiang University Hangzhou China; Lee Shau Kee School of Business and Administration Hong Kong Metropolitan University Kowloon Hong Kong
Abstract: ABSTRACT Business model innovation (BMI) is a key decision faced by entrepreneurial firms. Yet, a firm's entrepreneurial team can hold diverse cognitive views of business models, leading to an incomplete understanding of how entrepreneurial teams can actually leverage these diverse cognitive resources for BMI. Drawing on the cognitive view of BMI, we explore how domain‐specific schemas—a key aspect of managerial cognition gleaned from prior industry experience—may influence BMI. Rather than assuming the influence of schemas is uniform across situations, we conceptualize it as contingent on two salient situated factors—namely, team faultlines and industry competition logic. We posit that while the sharing of schemas in entrepreneurial teams is critical for BMI, whether those teams are able to bring about actual innovation depends on the industry context in which their new venture operates. Empirical analysis of 799 IT‐based firms in China provides general support for our arguments. Our study contributes to the cognitive view of BMI and deepens our understanding of the role of situated context in BMI.

Title: Artificial Intelligence in Innovation Management: Identifying Customer Needs for Ideation Using Text Classification
Authors: Dorian Proksch, Alexander Brem
Affiliations: msg systems ag Ismaning/München Bavaria Germany; Institute of Entrepreneurship and Innovation Science University of Stuttgart Stuttgart Germany; Department of Technology and Innovation University of Southern Denmark Sønderborg Denmark
Abstract: ABSTRACT These days, a wave of artificial intelligence applications is arriving in the way we manage innovation. But where are we now, and how can one use AI practically in innovation management? Against this background, we first extend an earlier literature review in text classification to demonstrate that the field remains scarce. We then address the current research gap by successfully conducting a machine learning project to evaluate ideas using text classification with transformer models. For this, we semi‐automatically extracted customer needs in the field of smart speakers by downloading a Twitter dataset containing 473,301 tweets. We classified 107,738 tweets using a machine learning model, identified 12,641 potential need‐containing tweets, and manually coded the first 1000. Our results can assist innovation managers and researchers in implementing high‐performing machine learning models to support their innovation management tasks in different ways. We documented the design choices for this machine learning project in detail, deriving guidelines for creating text classification projects tailored to the domain of innovation management.

Title: Green Tax Reform and Corporate R&D Manipulation: A Quasi‐Natural Experiment
Authors: Xinyi Li, Huaining Xu, Fenglian Gao, Huijuan Duan
Affiliations: School of Public Policy and Administration Nanchang University Nanchang China; School of Business Yangzhou University Yangzhou China; School of Accounting Nanjing Audit University Nanjing China; School of Business Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology Nanjing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Leveraging the exogenous shock of the implementation of China's Environmental Protection Tax Law, this study empirically examines the impact of green tax reform on corporate R&D manipulation. Using the sample of Chinese listed firms and employing a difference‐in‐differences approach, we find that green tax reform significantly curbs corporate R&D manipulation, specifically by reducing abnormal R&D expenditures. This conclusion remains robust after a series of tests. Mechanism analyses reveal that this effect operates primarily through three channels: the optimization of environmental information disclosure, enhanced supervisory governance by external stakeholders, and the reduction of transaction costs associated with regulatory compliance. Further analysis suggests that by mitigating R&D manipulation, green tax reform ultimately enhances both the quality and efficiency of corporate innovation. Our findings contribute to the growing literature on environmental regulation and corporate innovation by highlighting the governance role of green taxation, and provide important policy implications for designing market‐based environmental instruments to foster genuine and sustainable innovation.

Title: Issue Information
From policy to practice: Translating mission-oriented innovation policy into responsible innovation governance and employee behavioral outcomes
Authors: Min Jae Park
Abstract: Mission-oriented innovation policy (MOIP) has emerged as a prominent approach for addressing grand societal challenges by directing innovation toward clearly defined public missions. Although prior research has advanced understanding of mission design, policy coordination, and ecosystem governance, limited attention has been paid to how mission-oriented policies are translated into organizational practices. Addressing this gap, this study develops and empirically tests a policy-to-practice translation framework that explains how policy directionality becomes embedded within organizations through responsible innovation (RI) governance and subsequently influences employee behavioral outcomes. Drawing on the literatures on RI, organizational governance, and trust, RI is conceptualized as an organizational governance mechanism that translates external policy expectations into structured innovation practices. Innovation trust functions as the behavioral mechanism linking RI governance to sustainability-oriented behavioral intentions, while organizational ESG capability and individual Anthropocene awareness serve as important boundary conditions. The proposed framework is examined using a theory-testing dominant mixed-method design combining hierarchical linear modeling, structural equation modeling, and comparative qualitative case studies. Survey data from 538 employees across 38 Korean firms are complemented by qualitative evidence from mission-priority industries. The findings indicate that perceived organizational alignment with mission-oriented policy directionality is associated with employee behavioral intentions through RI governance and innovation trust. This study advances mission-oriented innovation research by introducing a policy-to-practice translation perspective and offers practical implications for governments and organizations implementing mission-oriented innovation policies.

Title: From threat to reconfiguration: How content creators reshape occupational identity in AI-driven creative practices
Authors: Mingsheng Wang, Yongzhong Yang
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is disrupting creative work and challenging occupational identities, yet limited research has examined how creators experience and respond to these changes. Drawing on Albert Ellis’s ABC model, this study investigates relationships among GenAI adoption, identity threat, job crafting, and identity consequences. Using a two-stage exploratory mixed-method design with digital content creators in China, we combined BERTopic analysis of 2994 open-ended responses with structural equation modelling of matched survey data from 1698 creators. The findings show that GenAI is widely perceived through coexisting beliefs about threat, opportunity, and the unknown, and that these beliefs give rise to differentiated job crafting behaviours, including approach crafting, avoidance crafting, and identity crafting. Notably, identity crafting plays an important role in fostering a responsible creative identity and self-actualization. This study advances theorizing on AI technological innovation and creative labour by showing how job crafting translates GenAI disruption into responsibility-oriented and meaning-centered identity reshaping. It also offers actionable insights for creators, platforms, and creative communities seeking to support collaborative, sustainable, and ethically grounded human–AI co-creation.

Title: Policy-induced environmental technology and innovation: a retrospective

Title: A longitudinal and thematic analysis of entrepreneurial university research (1969–2024)
Authors: Martin Bliemel
Abstract: Abstract This study presents the evolution of the ‘Entrepreneurial University’ concept with the literature dating back to sub-concepts published on in 1969, pre-dating the Bayh-Dole Act in 1980 or Etzkowitz’ (1983) coining of the term. Studying this evolutionary path offers suggestions for future directions of research, considering how universities navigate increasingly diverse, yet complementary, expectations from society, industry, government and their own disciplines. This study identifies 5857 articles via Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar and uses keyword co-occurrence analysis to identify 240 topics and their interrelationships relating to the entrepreneurial university literature. The dataset also reveals journals and topics beyond the realm of R&D management journals, including entrepreneurship education, regional development, public policy and public administration. Longitudinal analysis of the topics indicates how the literature has engaged in perspectives that are increasingly based on complex systems views, including technological, social and environmental systems, accompanied by measurement of associated variables (notably in entrepreneurial self-efficacy, orientation and intentions). Despite the exponential growth of the literature, the growth of topics is plateauing, indicating a maturation of the concept. The literature can be considered to span five approximate eras that organically layer onto each other: (i) technology transfer, (ii) clustering, (iii) innovation systems, (iv) social systems, and (v) human-centered systems. The methodology allows for the 240 topics to be categorized and visualized as a hierarchically topic map, with topics clustering around seven core themes, providing a highly nuanced overview of the core and peripheral concepts relating to the Entrepreneurial University. Overall, this study contributes to a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the Entrepreneurial University concept and the evolution of the underlying literature. These contributions open doors to discuss future directions and extensions, and more critical analysis of which topics are more or less peripheral. For instance, we argue that sustainability and wellbeing are beyond scope of the original definitions, and that there is room for more research to on university administration, leadership and strategy. In the appendices, this study identifies top journals and seminal articles that epitomize each of the seven core themes, thus providing a starting point for scholars or policy makers interested in each of the themes.

Title: Technology export controls and persistent firm innovation: evidence from cross-border technology transfer governance in China
Authors: Jialun Lyu, Jinda Wen, Yongxiang Jiao
Abstract: Technology export controls restrict cross-border technology transfer, but their implications for sustained innovation in the implementing country remain unclear. Drawing on the institution-based view and step-by-step innovation theory, this study examines the relationship between technology export controls and firm innovation persistence. We construct an industry-level exposure measure from the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export and patent data, and analyze nonfinancial A-share firms listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen from 2004 to 2024. The baseline estimates indicate an inverted U-shaped association: greater exposure is associated with higher innovation persistence at lower exposure levels and lower persistence at higher levels. Further analyses identify patient capital and innovation diversification as possible channels and suggest that the association between past and current innovation varies with exposure. The shape of the estimated relationship also differs with industry concentration, technological intensity, and the share of export prohibitions. Instrumental-variable estimates based on presample technological composition yield the same coefficient signs as the baseline model, although their causal interpretation depends on the exclusion restriction. We interpret the findings as conditional associations that offer evidence on the proposed trade-off between technological protection and access to markets and knowledge. The study contributes to research on innovation persistence under restrictions on cross-border technology transfer.

Title: Reimagining work in ageing societies: AI-enabled reskilling and the power of future work identities
Authors: Xiaoting Lyu, Reeti Agarwal, Shuo Fan, Jehan Saleh Lardhi, Irma Potháczky Rácz
Abstract: With an ageing population and fast development of AI, the labour force is drastically changing, which presents a need to understand how older adults experience and respond to technologically evolving work environments. Based on Possible Selves Theory, this research investigates how older adults understand the function of AI-enabled digital reskilling to inform future workforce possible selves and continued participation in employment in later life. Data were collected from 51 older adults via the Prolific Academic platform and were analysed using the Gioia methodology. Findings revealed that older adults view AI-enabled digital reskilling as a significant pathway to help them create their future workforce possible selves, which acts as an important motivation for continued participation in the workforce. Additionally, older adults evaluate their future working identities in terms of their expected ability, the likelihood of success, their skill sets, confidence, labour market opportunities, and age-related constraints. Thus, this study extends Possible Selves Theory by demonstrating how AI-enabled digital reskilling shapes future work identities and supports workforce adaptation in later life. The findings further suggest that organizations, policymakers, and digital platform designers should invest in accessible AI-enabled digital reskilling initiatives that foster workforce participation and promote inclusive ageing in the digital economy.

Title: Corporate innovation propensity: From measurement to impact—A text-based analytical approach
Authors: Lingbing Feng, Tianle Zou, Fengwen Chen, Yineng Guo
Abstract: Innovation propensity (IP) is an important antecedent of firms' innovation activities and innovation outputs. This study develops and validates an approach to measuring corporate innovation propensity using annual report texts, and further examines its predictive role in subsequent innovation behavior and its economic effects. Based on a sample of Chinese A-share high-tech listed firms from 2007 to 2020, this study employs a BERT–BiLSTM–CRF model to identify product and technology terms from the Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) sections of annual reports, and constructs a firm-level measure of innovation propensity accordingly. The results show that innovation propensity can predict firms' R&D investment and knowledge accumulation, while also significantly improving firm performance. Further analysis indicates that innovation propensity also affects firms’ capital market outcomes. This study advances the identification and measurement of innovation propensity from a text-analytics perspective, deepens the understanding of the antecedents of corporate innovation from the perspectives of knowledge management and dynamic capabilities, and provides new empirical evidence for revealing the economic consequences of managerial innovation propensity.

Title: Was I scammed? Understanding consumer scam reporting behavior through cognitive appraisal
Authors: Ruochen Liao, H. Raghav Rao
Abstract: Underreporting has been hampering regulatory efforts due to consumers’ hesitance to report ambiguous unsatisfactory transactions, particularly in online marketplaces or consumer services where deceptive business practices are uncertain or difficult to prove. This study examines how consumers appraise harm, effort, and resolution uncertainty when deciding whether to respond to potential scams. Drawing on Cognitive Appraisal Theory and Consumer Complaint Behavior, we develop and test a dual-pathway model that explains when victims pursue private action (e.g., contacting the seller) or public action (e.g., filing a complaint). Using nationally representative data from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission's 2017 fraud survey, we show that financial loss, perceived effort, outcome uncertainty, and their interactions jointly shape complaint behavior. We find that private action is driven by restitution motives and is amplified in high-loss or online scenarios, where it is perceived as a low-cost first step. Public action, by contrast, is less influenced by financial stakes and more by confidence in evidence, reflecting a justice-seeking mindset. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of consumer behavior after perceived scam experiences by adopting long-standing marketing and consumer behavior theories and offers practical managerial insights by shifting the focus from victim profiling to behavioral process modeling. Our findings highlight the need for system-level interventions such as standardized dispute mechanisms, centralized complaint portals, and structured evidence logs to reduce harm and improve reporting confidence in scam-prone “gray areas.”

Title: [State-of-the-Practice-Survey] Environmental Sustainability in Information Systems Research: Beyond Incrementalism Toward a Transformative Path Forward
Authors: Onook Oh, Dawn Greayer Gregg, Navid Aghakhani
Abstract: This state-of-the-practice-survey paper challenges the Information Systems (IS) research community’s incremental approach to the environmental challenges. We instead propose a transformative path forward grounded in ecological economics literature. Analyzing survey responses from 554 global IS scholars, we identify key barriers that they have experienced, along with alternative pathways they suggest for pursuing ecologically responsible and socially accountable IS research. Our analysis of the data reveals that, while IS scholars recognize the importance of environmental issues, their proposed solutions often represent incremental changes within current growth economic paradigm rather than addressing the scale and urgency of current environmental challenges. Drawing on ecological economics frameworks, particularly Doughnut Economics’ dual focus on ecological ceilings and social foundations, we propose paradigm-shifting changes in research priorities, institutional structures, collaborative practices, and methodological approaches. We contend that, given the urgency of environmental crisis, ecological perspectives should serve as a guiding meta-framework for designing and conducting general IS research. We conclude with several actionable recommendations for researchers, journal editors, and institutional leaders seeking to position the IS community as a meaningful contributor to coping with urgent global environmental crisis.

Title: Collective sensemaking as a mechanism of sustainable entrepreneurial ecosystem emergence under institutional fragility
Authors: Aki Harima, Ruzlin Akter, Fabrice Periac
Abstract: Research on sustainable entrepreneurial ecosystems (SEEs) has increasingly emphasized the role of supportive actors, enabling conditions, and ecosystem components. However, this literature still offers limited insight into how SEEs emerge in contexts marked by grand societal challenges and institutional fragility, where stable institutions and pre-existing alignment cannot be assumed. This study addresses this gap through a longitudinal qualitative case study of Bangladesh, drawing on 39 interviews and secondary materials collected across two phases before and after the 2024 political unrest. The findings show that SEE emergence unfolds through collective sensemaking, as heterogeneous ecosystem actors gradually develop shared understandings of sustainability, impact, and legitimate participation. We identify five interrelated processes through which this occurs: constructing societal problems as challenges for entrepreneurial action, mobilizing support around a shared sustainability orientation, institutionalizing impact meanings and practices, negotiating participation and identity boundaries, and revising shared direction after disruption. Based on these findings, we develop a grounded framework that explains how initially dispersed interpretations become more shared and actionable, enabling coordinated efforts under fragile conditions. The study contributes to SEE research by showing that SEE emergence is an interpretive and relational process through which actors construct shared direction and provisional governability. It further contributes to collective sensemaking research by explaining how interpretation develops into ecosystem-level direction, practices, and boundaries, and to technology-transfer research by showing how the circulation and local uptake of sustainability-related knowledge and practices are interpretively mediated under institutional fragility.

Title: Distributed signal production in entrepreneurial ecosystems: evidence from Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa
Authors: Christian Sarfo, Anastacia Mamabolo, Joseph Owusu, David Sarpong, Wilson Karimi, Bennett Nwanguma
Abstract: Abstract Entrepreneurial ecosystem research has established that ecosystems influence venture development through networks, institutions, and support organizations, yet it offers limited explanation of how ecosystems shape the evaluative processes through which ventures gain access to finance and markets. This limitation is particularly consequential in emerging economies, where institutional conditions make conventional indicators of venture quality difficult to interpret, increasing uncertainty for resource gatekeepers. We address this gap by examining how entrepreneurial ecosystems shape venture credibility when the institutional conditions that normally make entrepreneurial signals legible, enforceable, and consequential are weak. Drawing on an abductive qualitative analysis of 174 semi-structured interviews with entrepreneurs, commercial banks, development finance institutions, corporate buyers, incubator and accelerator leaders, university entrepreneurship programmes, mentors, and public agencies across Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa, we develop a process model of distributed signal production. We show that entrepreneurial ecosystems function as distributed evaluative infrastructures that construct the evidentiary basis through which venture quality becomes credible to resource gatekeepers. Ecosystem actors accomplish this through three mechanisms: institutional signal substitution, structured signal amplification, and signal brokerage and conversion. These mechanisms explain how ecosystems construct, strengthen, and coordinate venture credibility while revealing why credible signals do not always translate into resource access under conditions of institutional weakness. Our findings advance entrepreneurial ecosystem literature by explaining how ecosystems shape evaluative processes rather than simply providing resources, extend signaling theory by demonstrating that signal production is distributed across heterogeneous ecosystem actors, and show how institutional conditions influence the conversion of credible signals into entrepreneurial opportunities.

Title: Radical Product Innovation and Export Behaviour in Small and Medium Enterprises: The Roles of Growth Expectation and Customer Portfolio Breadth
Authors: Gordon Liu, Weixi (Louis) Liu, Wai Wai Ko
Affiliations: Department of Strategy and Marketing, The Open University Business School The Open University Milton Keynes UK; School of Management University of Bath Bath UK; Brunel Business School Brunel University Uxbridge UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT Drawing on the theory of the growth of the firm, this study examines the relationship between radical product innovation and export behaviour in small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs). Utilising data from the UK Longitudinal Small Business Surveys (LSBS) for the period 2015–2017, this study shows that SMEs that engage in radical product innovation develop heightened growth expectations, which in turn drive export behaviour. The findings reveal a nonlinear moderation effect of customer portfolio breadth on the relationship between radical product innovation and growth expectation. This effect is strongest when SMEs target either a single customer group or a highly diversified customer base. The study contributes to the literature by elucidating the mechanisms through which innovation influences SMEs' internationalisation and highlighting customer portfolio composition's vital role. These insights offer valuable theoretical contributions and practical implications for SME managers seeking to leverage innovation for international expansion. This research also emphasises the importance of strategic customer targeting for innovation outcome optimisation.

Title: Between the lines or behind the lens? Examining the content and helpfulness of airline reviews
Authors: Masoud Shayganmehr, Indranil Bose

Title: Pursuing technology sovereignty under dependency: The case of Mistral AI
Authors: Yann Truong
Abstract: This study examines how organizations pursue technological sovereignty while embedded in infrastructures controlled by geopolitical competitors. We address this question through an in-depth longitudinal case study of Mistral AI (2023–2025), Europe's only frontier-scale Large Language Model developer competing with American incumbents. Our analysis draws on two primary data sources collected over the firm's first three years: 16 media interviews with CEO Arthur Mensch and 30 monthly activity reports published by Mistral, triangulated with technical documentation, industry analyses, and European policy documents. We employed an abductive analytical approach, combining iterative open and focused coding of institutional work practices with theoretical dimensioning and process tracing across four temporal phases of the company's evolution. Our findings reveal three interrelated forms of institutional work: selective decoupling of critical dependencies while maintaining beneficial connections, strategic leveraging of embeddedness in some structures to contest dominance in others, and structural reconfiguration creating alternative institutional arrangements. These practices constitute geopolitical embedded agency, a distinctive form of organizational action characterized by material rather than symbolic embeddedness; cross-scalar institutional contradictions; and sovereignty objectives that reshape conventional organizational rationality. Our framework contributes to institutional work theory and emerging technology sovereignty scholarship while extending analytically to other capital-intensive sectors facing geopolitical dependencies.

Title: Metaphor of overreaching: effects of AI agglomeration on innovation
Authors: Yanling Lian, Jie Jian, Chengcheng Xia
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping innovation, yet the spatial dynamics and innovation consequences of its AI agglomeration remain underexplored. We introduce the concept of city-level AI agglomeration and examine its dual effects on city overall and radical innovation. Integrating organizational ecology with economic geography, we propose that AI agglomeration acts through two mechanisms. On the one hand, it generates computing spillover, a positive externality that expands the region’s environmental carrying capacity by sharing critical computing resources, thereby promoting overall innovation. On the other hand, it fosters algorithmic convergence, a negative externality that intensifies structural inertia, thereby constraining radical innovation. Using city-level data from China (2019–2023) and causal forest methods, our empirical analysis supports these hypotheses. Further analyses reveal heterogeneous effects moderated by geographic proximity to provincial capitals, fixed asset investment intensity, and regional innovation ecosystem support. This study advances agglomeration and innovation literature and offers insights for urban innovation policy.

Title: Divide Et Impera: Structuring design science projects
Authors: Michael Werner, Jonas Sveistrup Søgaard
Abstract: Design Science (DS) has attracted growing interest in entrepreneurship and innovation research in recent years. Typically implemented through projects, DS projects are often complex and challenging to manage. This study explores how DS projects can be effectively structured to support several tasks for DS project management particularly regarding the division of research tasks and the allocation of project resources. We present a framework that segments the content of DS projects into small, well-defined, and individually manageable research components. The framework enables researchers to assign resources strategically, assess the balance of research output, schedule and monitor activities systematically, and adapt to changes in scope and objectives during project execution. To illustrate the framework's practical utility, we draw on a case study involving the development of an innovative blockchain-based solution for VAT settlement in Denmark. Additionally, we evaluated the framework's general applicability by comparing it against ten DS projects described in the scientific literature. This is complemented with a discussion of how the framework can be embedded into the DS project management process according to established projects management standards. The evaluation results support our claims about the framework's broader applicability and its potential to improve DS project management.

Title: How team structure shapes technological differentiation: A semantic embedding-based assessment
Authors: Wonchang Hur, Bogang Jun, Jonghyun Kim
Abstract: A firm's research portfolio often faces a tension between reliance on dominant technologies and the pursuit of technological differentiation. This study examines how invention teams generate such differentiation by linking network structure to innovation outcomes. We develop a novel semantic distance measure based on patent text, capturing technological differentiation along a continuous space rather than discrete classification categories. Using this measure, we show that invention teams achieve higher levels of differentiation when they combine strong internal cohesion with diverse external network connections.
