Specifically, cohesive internal ties facilitate knowledge integration, while external ties spanning structural holes expand access to novel knowledge. These findings highlight the importance of balancing cohesion and brokerage in shaping technological differentiation and offer new insights into the organization of inventive activity.

Title: Cyclical carbon productivity and the role of innovation
Authors: Terhi Maczulskij, Paolo Fornaro
Affiliations: ETLA Economic Research; Labour Institute for Economic Research LABORE
Abstract: We examine the cyclicality of carbon productivity and consider innovation as a potential mechanism. We use unique data on greenhouse gas emissions matched with comprehensive administrative data sources for manufacturing firms. To identify causal effects, an input-output approach is applied, where the output of downstream industries serves as an instrument for upstream industries’ output. Our findings reveal that carbon productivity is procyclical. Specifically, 2SLS results show that a one percentage point increase in industrial output leads to a cumulative 20% rise in carbon productivity over two years. While innovation activities are unlikely to be the primary mechanism behind these results, the growth in carbon productivity is attributed to emission reductions and firms having more environmentally conscious top management. Overall, our results support the notion that economic growth can be achieved alongside ecological sustainability.

Title: Trains of thought: High-Speed Rail and innovation in China
Authors: Georgios Tsiachtsiras, Deyun Yin, Ernest Miguelez, Rosina Moreno
Affiliations: University of Bristol; Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen (HITSZ); Nanjing University Suzhou Campus (NJUSZ); University of Bordeaux; University of Barcelona
Abstract: This paper explores the effect of the High-Speed Rail (HSR) on local technological change of Chinese cities. Using exogenous variation arising from the courier’s stations during the Ming dynasty as instrument, as well as a large number of controls and fixed effects, we find evidence that the opening of an HSR station increases cities’ innovation activity. The paper also looks at the effect of the HSR on the technological trajectories of cities. Computing least-cost paths between city-pairs, we obtain that the probability of a city to branch into a new technological field is related to the current portfolio of the cities to which it connects through the HSR network.

Title: Mapping critical raw materials in green technologies
Authors: Francesco de Cunzo, Davide Consoli, François Perruchas, Angelica Sbardella
Affiliations: Enrico Fermi Research Center; INGENIO CSIC-Universitat Politecnica de Valencia; University of Valencia; SOAS University of London
Abstract: This paper provides an exploratory analysis of the relationship between critical raw materials (CRMs) and environmental technologies. Using text mining techniques to parse and analyse patent data, we explore: (i) the dependence of green technologies on CRMs; (ii) the countries that are more reliant on CRMs in their green patent portfolios; and (iii) the connections between major users and suppliers of CRMs. Framed in the context of recent policy debates on the viability of the sustainable transition, our study points to the criticalities of both the evolution of green technology and of the spatial distribution of demand and supply of CRMs.

Title: Regional capabilities and co-invention networks for technological diversification: evidence from Brazil
Authors: Mariane Santos Françoso, Vanessa de Lima Avanci, Nicholas Spyridon Vonortas
Affiliations: São Paulo State University (Unesp); University of Campinas (Unicamp); The George Washington University; University of Campinas
Abstract: The literature on regional technological diversification has emphasised the role of intraregional knowledge endowments while progressively acknowledging the importance of network structures. This study contributes to this discussion by jointly examining how regional technological capabilities and network structures (both interregional and intraregional) shape the emergence of new technological specialisations within the context of a developing country. We conduct an econometric analysis employing patenting and microregional level data from Brazil, and explore non-linear relationships. Our findings suggest that the presence of capabilities applicable to new cognitively proximate technologies, along with network-related factors, foster successful diversification. However, this impact is not uniform, as the positive effects of interregional connections are positive from a certain threshold, while the benefits of internal cohesion appear to be concentrated within a specific range.

Title: Not all apples fall close to the tree: survival of pushed spin-offs from Danish shipyards
Authors: Thomas Roslyng Olesen, Agnieszka Nowinska
Affiliations: Copenhagen Business School; Aalborg University Business School

Title: Too alike to thrive? Personality and functionality similarity in virtual teams
Authors: Jingzhao An, Yanxin Wang, Xi Zhao
Abstract: The proliferation of digital collaboration tools has driven the rapid emergence of virtual teams, highlighting the importance of supporting team composition decision-making under conditions of limited intra-team connections. Prior research mainly lacks an integrative framework to understand how multidimensional similarity among team members affects team effectiveness. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of how personality similarity and functionality similarity affect team effectiveness. Drawing on a cognitive resource perspective, we develop hypotheses about the nuanced effects of personality and functionality similarity. Using a unique dataset from a leading online team-based game, we employ a large language model-based approach to measure team members’ personality traits. Consequently, we find that team member personality similarity negatively affects their satisfaction and future growth. Furthermore, functionality similarity exhibits an inverted U-shaped effect: while moderate functionality similarity enhances these outcomes, excessive similarity leads to diminishing marginal benefits. Our research contributes to the decision support systems literature on team composition and online gaming, providing actionable insights for team leaders and game developers to design team composition strategies that enhance team effectiveness.

Title: Beyond the efficiency trap: Regional AI exposure, AI knowledge, and the asymmetric governance of data-driven value propositions
Authors: Minmin Huang, Rui Yang
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping corporate strategy, yet how regional AI exposure (RAE), the intensity of local industry peers' AI inventive activities, shapes firms' data-driven value propositions (DDVPs) remains unclear. Using panel data on Chinese listed firms from 2013 to 2023, we examine the mechanism linking RAE to DDVPs. We find that higher RAE is associated with greater subsequent AI knowledge generation, which is more strongly related to efficiency-oriented than product-oriented DDVPs, reflecting an efficiency trap. Dynamic capabilities govern this conversion asymmetrically: sensing and seizing capabilities primarily strengthen efficiency-oriented DDVP, whereas reconfiguring capability is particularly important for elevating product-oriented DDVP. These findings extend DDVP research beyond firm internal explanations by incorporating regional AI environments and show how distinct dynamic capability dimensions shape heterogeneous value-creation orientations.

Title: Best Paper Awards – Vol. 71
Authors: Tsan-Ming Choi
Affiliations: School of Management, University of Liverpool

Title: Structure over intensity: decomposing interdisciplinarity as a diagnostic for technology transfer complexity in academic spin-offs
Authors: Tine Van Lommel, Herman Bruyninckx
Abstract: How interdisciplinarity is structured at founding—not how much collaboration is present—is more strongly associated with whether academic spin-offs achieve acquisition-based exits: ventures in which disciplinary contributions are more symmetrically distributed are significantly more likely to achieve acquisition-based exits than ventures with equivalent collaboration intensity but asymmetric knowledge structures. This paper introduces the first venture-level operationalisation of interdisciplinarity anchored at the founding moment of academic spin-offs, designed for direct integration into technology transfer office (TTO) workflows. Where existing measures collapse interdisciplinarity into a single bibliometric scalar, we decompose it into three independently measurable structural dimensions—Variety (V), Disparity (DP), and Balance (B)—and extend Stirling’s diversity framework beyond publication contexts by operationalising each dimension using auditable administrative data: founder disciplines, equity distributions, and organisational footprint. Applied to 58 health-related academic spin-offs from KU Leuven across Biotech, Medtech, and Digital Health clusters, we show that these clusters exhibit systematically distinct knowledge recombination profiles. Configurational analysis reveals that exit-based success is more sensitive to how interdisciplinarity is organised at founding—particularly Balance—than to overall collaboration intensity. Disparity (cognitive distance) emerges as the strongest early signal of knowledge integration complexity, with direct implications for IP alignment, governance design, and partner configuration. These findings reframe interdisciplinarity from a scalar input into a multidimensional governance diagnostic, offering TTOs an auditable, founding-moment tool for portfolio triage and targeted intervention.

Title: How institutional quality configurations shape national innovation: a configurational moderation approach
Authors: Marcelo Pereira Duarte, Fernando Manuel Pereira de Oliveira Carvalho
Abstract: This study analyses how configurations of institutional quality moderate the relationship between countries’ innovation inputs and outputs. Drawing from comparative institutional research on national innovation, we argue that a country’s capacity to translate innovation inputs into outputs is contingent on combinations of institutional dimensions. We expect the rule of law and open markets to act as core conditions anchoring institutional configurations, and government size and regulatory efficiency to play peripheral, supporting roles. Using a two-stage fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis on 125 countries (2012–2022), we identify two equifinal configurations that moderate the innovation input–output relationship: one combining open markets with a large state, the other anchored by the rule of law. The core roles of the rule of law and open markets, and the peripheral role of regulatory efficiency, confirm our theoretical expectations. Government size does not. It emerges as a core condition, indicating that a large state combined with open markets reshapes the input–output relationship in coordinated market economies. Analyzing the absence of the outcome yields configurations that are not the exact opposite of these. This establishes causal asymmetry and characterizes the institutional profile of countries with persistently low innovation outputs. The study advances a more configurational account of institutional quality and identifies the institutional combinations that raise the return on innovation investment.

Title: Self-reinforcing barriers to municipal digital government: A system dynamics perspective
Authors: Fabian Steinert, Philipp Staudt
Abstract: Municipal governments have invested substantially in digital government endeavors, yet progress in public sector digital transformation remains surprisingly slow. Although research has repeatedly identified, categorized and reclassified barriers while also proposing numerous strategies to address them, the same obstacles continue to reappear across ongoing digitalization efforts. This persistence suggests that existing knowledge about barriers and their remedies remains insufficient. To address this gap, this study adopts a systemic perspective to explain why the barriers to municipal digital government persist, even after being repeatedly identified and targeted. We conducted 56 semi-structured interviews with 67 municipal employees and employees of GovTech providers in Germany and analyzed them through an inductive multi-stage coding process. Using system dynamics principles, we reconstruct the shared mental model through which actors perceive, explain and interlink barriers into a causal map. The resulting model reveals a dense web of interdependencies among barriers that form extended causal chains and self-reinforcing feedback loops. This perspective provides a dynamic and system-level explanation of persistence that reconceptualizes barriers not as discrete factors, but as generative mechanisms that sustain digital stagnation through their mutual reinforcement.

Title: Omni-channel integration capability and usage: the role of usefulness, privacy concern, appeal, and integration experience
Authors: Debalina Bera, Yonghoon Choi, Dan J. Kim
Abstract: Despite progress in understanding omni-channel integration (OCI) from a firm-level perspective, user-side mechanisms through which OCI capability sustains OC usage remain underexplored. Two gaps persist: How does OCI capability translate into OC usage for users in semi-structured, cross-channel purchase environments? Which combinations of OCI capability and user factors are sufficient to achieve high OC usage? Drawing on Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Decision Support Systems tradition, this study frames OCI capability as a firm-deployed, decision-enabling IT system whose value is realized through users' cognitive, evaluative and experiential responses. Using a multi-method approach on 495 OC users, PLS-SEM examines linear relationships consistent with S-D Logic's value-creation chain, while fsQCA explores configurational and non-linear associations consistent with S-D Logic's equifinal co-creation premise. Findings yield two contributions: (1) a validated evaluation model explicating how OCI capability translates into OC usage through users' value-in-context - perceptions of usefulness, privacy concerns, OC appeal, and OCI experience - providing a diagnostic framework for evaluating OC system effectiveness; and (2) a configurational decision framework derived from fsQCA offering prescriptive, segment-aware guidance on which capability-perception combinations are sufficient to drive sustained OC usage.

Title: Shared digital leadership in government: a roles and competencies study
Authors: Boniface Ushaka Adie, Mary Tate, Wonhyuk Cho, Elizabeth Valentine
Abstract: Digital leadership capabilities and associated clusters of competencies form a foundation for digital transformation in the public sector. This increasingly depends on leadership contributions and strategy-matching competencies shared across organisational levels and professional roles. Drawing on shared leadership theory, we analysed how public sector employees at different organisational levels contribute to digital leadership. The study uses a qualitative research design with independent sources of evidence: document analysis of job descriptions and semi-structured interviews with digital leadership professionals. We mapped the theory-informed competencies to the Skills Framework for the Information Age (SFIA), an industry-recognised competencies framework. We find that digital leadership competencies and contributions should be understood as a shared leadership construct requiring multiple contributions across multiple levels. We offer an illustrative example of our shared digital leadership conceptualisation in practice, using a horizontal and vertical slice of the roles involved in cyber security risk management as the context.

Title: Mandating business-to-government data sharing for public interest: Coalitions and their policy beliefs in the shaping of the EU Data Act
Authors: Iryna Susha, Louis Knüpling, Philip Leifeld
Abstract: To address complex societal challenges like the climate crisis or pandemics, governments need to make evidence-based decisions based on the best available data. However, data needed to make policy decisions are no longer solely in the domain of the public sector, but increasingly also in the hands of the private sector. As part of its Data Strategy, the European Union (EU) has recently adopted the Data Act, which includes provisions to mandate business-to-government data sharing in situations of exceptional need. Some critics argue that the adopted text of the Data Act has made significant concessions to the interests of the private sector and that the initial text was much more ambitious. In this study, we aim to understand and explain the conflicting narrative framing of the public and private sectors on mandatory B2G data sharing for public interest. To answer our research question, we analyze the public and private narratives found in the public consultation on the Data Act using the method of discourse network analysis (DNA). We established a clear division into two coalitions which partly agreed on the problem, yet widely diverged on the solution. We highlight the difference found in the belief systems of the main coalitions and discuss them through the lens of institutional logics. Our findings showcase that the resulting legislation has aligned more with the policy preferences of the private-sector-dominated coalition favoring a “narrow” data access mandate.

Title: Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Capability: Translating Information Contingencies into Decision Effectiveness and Operational Impact
Authors: Digvijay Singh Bizalwan, Rahul Kumar, Indranil Bose
Abstract: Contemporary healthcare research suggests that information bottlenecks hinder human decision-making abilities, rendering healthcare services inefficient. In this regard, scholarly attention on enhancing decision intelligence capabilities of healthcare service providers to address information contingencies remains minimal. Grounded in Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT), we offer a remedy to eliminate information contingencies by proposing a novel healthcare artificial intelligence capability (HAIC). Based on OIPT, we realize HAIC as a third-order construct, through two critical second-order constructs: information processing (IP) and information decisiveness (ID). In our analysis, we deduce that predictive accuracy and data interoperability within AI systems augment IP capabilities. We also observe that decision support and organizational collaboration reinforce ID. We establish the positive association of HAIC with timely and cost-efficient service delivery, thereby reinforcing operational effectiveness in healthcare. We extend the OIPT literature to develop a multidimensional foundation for HAIC. Furthermore, the study offers AI-enabled configurations to the executives for efficient and effective healthcare provision.

Title: When Does Data-Driven Strategic Decision-Making Enable Firms to Overcome the “Filtering Effect” for Exploration?
Authors: Lulu Sun, Zelong Wei, Paike Xie, Qining Jia
Affiliations: Xi’an Jiaotong University; Lyuliang University

Title: Improving Profitability in Online Healthcare Platforms: Charging Specialists or Patients?
Authors: Rui Wang, Haiqing Song, Yanli Tang
Affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University

Title: From Moral Disengagement to Re-Engagement: Investigating the Dynamic Impact of AI Orientation on Corporate Social Responsibility Performance
Authors: Yuwen Xiang, Jian Mou, Wenqing Wu
Affiliations: Tianjin University; Pusan National University

Title: Technology transfer through inter-firm networks and SMEs’ formal R&D: evidence from Japanese buyer–supplier and ownership linkages
Authors: Akira Yamaguchi, Kenta Ikeuchi, Kyoji Fukao, Hyeog Ug Kwon, YoungGak Kim
Abstract: Inter-firm networks provide SMEs with external technological knowledge, but such access need not increase their own formal R&D. This paper argues that partner R&D may complement SME R&D when external knowledge expands technological opportunities, but may be associated with lower formal R&D when knowledge is accessed through dependent, hierarchical, or ownership-based ties. We interpret this pattern as consistent with a network-governed allocation of innovation tasks , in which large or controlling firms conduct core R&D, design, platform development, and standard-setting, while SMEs focus on implementation, adaptation, and production problem-solving. Using a firm-level panel linking Japan’s Survey of Research and Development to Tokyo Shoko Research data on buyer–supplier and ownership ties for 2011, 2012, and 2014, we analyze 648,299 matched firm-year observations. The results document conditional associations, not causal effects. Partner-R&D exposure exhibits governance-contingent size gradients: parent/investor and several ownership-coupled ties move from negative associations among smaller firms toward less negative or more complementary associations as size increases, whereas independent supplier and customer ties become less complementary or more negative. The ownership-coupled analysis remains exploratory. Because ownership ties are multidimensional governance proxies and inference does not correct for possible network dependence, the findings provide descriptive evidence that exposure to R&D-active partners and network governance are associated with where formal R&D is performed and recorded across connected firms.

Title: CirrhosisCare: a decision support system enabled by complication-aware deep learning to predict one-year mortality among cirrhotic patients
Authors: Hamid Reza Firoozfar, Da Xu, Paul Jen-Hwa Hu, San-Yih Hwang
Abstract: Cirrhosis represents a major cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. Patients in advanced disease stages have few curative options and limited access to liver transplantation due to organ availability constraints. Accurate prognostic estimates thus are important for therapeutic planning and resource allocation optimization. Clinicians usually depend on score-based methods, including models for end-stage liver disease and sodium-adjusted variants. Yet, these methods cannot capture dynamic disease progression and tend to underestimate the risks for certain patient groups. While predictive analytics can provide accurate estimates, most existing methods are not particularly flexible in temporal encodings and often overlook associated complications that are also essential for downstream mortality prediction. To address these limitations, this study develops a complication-aware, multitask, deep learning–based method that integrates patients' (disease) trajectories with both direct and complication-aware routes to estimate their mortality. This method employs a multi-shape time gate to flexibly capture diverse, temporal dynamics, and incorporates an interpretable hypernetwork-based graph neural network that links multiple complication pathways to obtain mortality estimates. It also leverages bidirectional knowledge distillation to achieve robust performance through adaptive exchanges between distinct predictive routes. A sample of 66,383 cirrhotic patients is used to evaluate the proposed method in comparison with 13 prevalent methods. The results reveal its superior performance, as reflected by significant improvements in both F1 scores and AUC values. We apply the proposed method to develop a prototype clinical decision support system, CirrhosisCare, which facilitates physicians' decision-making and patient management. A survey of 17 physicians in the U.S. and Asia clearly and consistently indicates that the system is valuable to their clinical practices, and that they are likely to adopt such a system if it is fully implemented. The proposed method is generalizable and can be flexibly adapted to other chronic diseases featuring patient heterogeneity, complex intervariable relationships, and temporal dynamics, all of which are likely to influence patient risks and outcomes.

Title: Ambidextrous innovation leap and patent abandonment: A resource orchestration perspective
Authors: Shan Chen, Jiangfeng Ye, Bin Hao, Chao Yu, Xin Gu
Abstract: Patent abandonment can be conceived as a deliberate approach to orchestrate and streamline patent assets, which is often shaped by firms' innovation strategies. This study conceptualizes ambidextrous innovation leap as a strategic reconfiguration of innovation trajectories that redeploys and recombines existing knowledge resources across distinct innovation domains. It investigates how these leaps influence patent abandonment decisions. We propose that such transitions can either disrupt or reinforce the coherence of firms’ knowledge bases, thereby affecting the perceived value and retention of current patent holdings. We distinguish between two types of leaps: upward innovation leap, involving a shift from exploitative to exploratory innovation, and downward innovation leap, denoting the reverse transition. Using panel data on 1623 A-share listed firms in Shanghai and Shenzhen from 2003 to 2021, we find that upward innovation leap has a positive effect on patent abandonment, whilst downward innovation leap negatively affects patent abandonment. We also show that network centrality and knowledge integration capability both negatively moderate the relationship between ambidextrous innovation leaps and patent abandonment. By shedding light on these relationships, this study enriches the research on strategic antecedents of patent abandonment from a resource orchestration perspective, and also has important practical implications for firms making patent abandonment decisions during innovation transitions.

Title: Design longevity: Institutional lock-in and the Toyota Crown Comfort taxi
Authors: Steven Chen
Abstract: While product design is a key driver of organizational success, companies increasingly struggle to sustain relevance in markets with ever-shortening product lifecycles. This study investigates how products achieve longevity without frequent redesign. A historical analysis of the Toyota Crown Comfort taxi, which remained in production for approximately 23-years (1995–2018), is used as a case to examine institutional lock-in as a complementary explanation for design longevity. The results identify three interrelated institutional mechanisms operating at the government-, industry-, and consumer-levels that collectively reinforced the vehicle's enduring market position. Building on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual framework demonstrating how institutional ecosystems can sustain dominant product designs over time. The research contributes to the product design, timeless design, and institutional lock-in literatures by demonstrating that long-term institutional relationships may provide an alternative pathway to design longevity beyond continuous redesign and R&D investment.

Title: Impact of supply chain digital transformation orientation alignment on corporate green innovation: An extended resource-based view perspective
Authors: Ao Zhang, Deting Jia
Abstract: This study examines how supply chain digital transformation orientation alignment affects corporate green innovation using matched supplier-customer data from Chinese listed firms. We develop a digital orientation alignment metric and employ two-way fixed effects modeling to establish a positive causal relationship, particularly enhancing green innovation quantity. This conclusion remains robust after a series of robustness and endogeneity tests. Drawing on the extended resource-based view (ERBV), we conceptualize digital transformation orientation alignment as an interorganizational capability and investigate the observable mechanisms through which it promotes green innovation, including the alleviation of financing constraints that support flexible R&D investment, the mitigation of geographical barriers through enhanced information sharing, and the optimization of operational synergies enabled by digital supply chain integration. Heterogeneity analyses further reveal stronger effects among non-state-owned firms, in regions with stricter environmental regulation, and in central and western China. The findings provide empirical evidence on how digital collaboration can be leveraged to achieve sustainable competitive advantages within supply chain ecosystems.

Title: Science-driven or engagement-driven? Shaping commercialisation pathways in public research organisations
Authors: Mabel Sánchez-Barrioluengo, Oscar Llopis, Irene Ramos-Vielba, Pablo D’Este, Alfredo Yegros-Yegros
Affiliations: Alliance Manchester Business School University of Manchester; University of Valencia and Associated Unit with CSIC-INGENIO; University of Gothenburg; Spanish National Research Council; Technical University of Denmark; Universitat Politècnica de València; Leiden University

Title: Between facilitative and hindering roles: situational conditions triggering boundary spanners’ dynamics in knowledge transfer within university–industry collaborations
Authors: Bo Wen, Guoqing Zhao, Matthew Tucker, Fa Wang, Jocelyn Finniear
Abstract: Boundary spanners play a critical role in facilitating knowledge transfer in university–industry collaborations (UIC). However, their intermediary roles are not static and may shift in response to changing project conditions. While prior research has examined facilitative and hindering boundary-spanning roles separately, limited attention has been paid to the dynamic between them, particularly in management-discipline UICs. This study examines a dynamic boundary spanner, Knowledge Transfer Partnership (KTP) associates within UK management-oriented KTP (mKTP) projects, employing qualitative interviews with thirty participants from four stakeholder groups. The findings reveal that unsupportive situational conditions, including insufficient supervisory support and engagement, competing expectations and power asymmetries, and inappropriate treatment by business partners, can shape associates’ perceptions toward self-interest, leading to their shifts from facilitative to hindering roles. Conversely, supportive conditions, such as knowledge and pastoral support and business’s support in their embeddedness and empowerment, encourage a perception of confident and legitimate conduits. This drives their role movements from hindering to facilitative conduits. The study also identifies three novel hindering boundary-spanning roles: project stewards, disempowered conduits and unembedded newcomers. By developing an integrated framework, this paper advances understanding of the dynamic and context-dependent nature of boundary spanners in knowledge transfer within UICs and extends boundary-spanning research beyond its traditional STEM focus.

Title: Path dependence and path breaking in the fourth industrial revolution: digital technological diversification in Chinese firms
Authors: Xiaodan Yu, Dan Luo, Simone Maria Grabner, Qingzhi Zhang
Affiliations: Nottingham University Business School China, University of Nottingham Ningbo China , Ningbo, 315100; School of International Relations and Public Affairs, Fudan University , Shanghai, 200433; Research Group for Regional Development, Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies , Vienna, 1060; School of Public Policy and Management, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences , Beijing, 100049
Abstract: Abstract A constellation of digital technologies is triggering the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR), yet how firms in catching-up economies build mature inventive capabilities in this new paradigm remains underexplored. This study examines this capability-building process through the lens of firm-level digital technological diversification. Using a comprehensive patent dataset of Chinese listed companies (2000–2020), we investigate the interplay between path-dependent capability accumulation and path-breaking learning. Our findings reveal a profound degree of path dependence in 4IR technological diversification within firms, particularly in the creation of enabling technologies that power data-driven value creation. Furthermore, while internal innovation efforts and ownership types have limited impact on altering this path dependence, we identify a critical exception: in application domains, simultaneous engagement with research alliances and public science bases can effectively facilitate path-breaking learning. These findings illuminate the heterogeneous learning regimes that govern firm-level capability accumulation in the 4IR era.

Title: Governance and innovation in higher education: The moderating role of vice-chancellors’ professional characteristics
Authors: Arpine Martirosyan, Keun Huh
Abstract: As universities play an increasingly central role in regional innovation, understanding how internal governance influences academic entrepreneurship is becoming essential. While prior research has emphasized external conditions for spin-off generation, this study shifts the focus inward, examining how board size and diversity are associated with the generation of university spin-offs. Further, this study addresses these effects with the consideration of vice-chancellor's professional characteristics. Based on the analysis of a panel dataset of UK universities through time-lagged models, the findings suggest that while board diversity consistently supports spin-off activity, the relationship between board size and spin-offs generation varies across institutional contexts. When adding the factors of leadership characteristics, the findings provide partially robust evidence that these characteristics may condition the effects of board governance: longer vice-chancellor's tenure may dampen entrepreneurial outcomes, whereas a science-based educational background appears to offer short-term advantages but may limit the benefits of board diversity, with the strength of this moderating effect varying across model specifications. This study adds to the literature on university governance and academic entrepreneurship showing how internal governance and leadership characteristics may condition the effectiveness of governance structures in academic spin-off generation.

Title: From functional connectivity to human-machine empathy: Scene value co-creation driven by GenAI-enabled smart elderly care based on a hybrid agency perspective
Authors: Supeng Zheng, Xiangan Ding, Yue Liu, Haifen Lin, Andrea Appolloni
Abstract: Against the dual pressures of accelerated smart eldercare adoption and rising ethical risk, Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping how value is created in elderly-care scenes. However, extant research has scarcely explored how GenAI—as an agent endowed with generative capabilities—deeply couples with eldercare scenes to reconfigure human-machine hybrid agency, thereby actualizing scene value co-creation. This study conducts an exploratory longitudinal dual-case analysis of iFlytek, an ecosystem orchestrator, and UBTECH, a vertical subordinate enterprise within China's smart eldercare sector. The findings reveal that: (1) Generative AI and eldercare scenes, serving as dual parallel elements, drive the emergence of hybrid agency. (2) Scene value co-creation evolves through three distinct stages: functional connection, precision service, and empathic symbiosis. Correspondingly, hybrid agency transitions from automated agency to augmented agency and ultimately to symbiotic agency, successively actualizing safety value exchange, value-in-use alignment, and embodied value symbiosis within respective scenes. (3) The ecosystem orchestrator adopts a centralized orchestration and cognitive connection path to construct a platform-based hybrid agency, while the subordinate enterprise employs the path of terminal embedding and embodied companionship to construct a vertical hybrid agency. (4) To mitigate the latent risks of value co-destruction during the evolutionary process, enterprises must establish dynamic governance mechanisms spanning from boundary constraints and human calibration to ethical correction. This research extends the theoretical boundaries of digital innovation within the context of an aging society and provides strategic insights for leveraging Tech for Good to address the global challenges of population aging.

Title: The future of work in creativity and innovation: perspectives on on-site versus remote work policies and practices
Authors: Maria P. Roche, Prithwiraj Choudhury, Barbara Larson, Anne L. J. Ter Wal
Affiliations: Harvard University; London School of Economics and Political Science; Northeastern University; Imperial College London

Title: Does financialization threaten productive development?
Authors: Jimena Castillo, Gary Dymski, Annina Kaltenbrunner, Sandra Lancheros
Affiliations: Leeds University Business School , Economics Department, Moorland Rd, Woodhouse, Leeds, LS2 9JT, United Kingdom. e-mail: jimecas3@gmail.com
Abstract: Abstract This paper explores financializaton’s effects on productive development—proxied by the Economic Complexity Index (ECI)—in a panel of 78 countries from 1975 to 2019. Financial globalization affects negatively ECI in Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa region, and South Asia. In Latin America, stock market capitalization also harms economic complexity by incentivizing short-term capital gains at the expense of technological upgrading. In developed economies, liquid liabilities and financial globalization support economic complexity, while private credit is detrimental.

Title: How Alliances Build Innovation Capabilities but Narrow Their Redeployment in Amazonian Community‐Based Enterprises
Authors: Renata Elaje Azevedo da Mota Carmona Chaves, Simone Vasconcelos Ribeiro Galina, Marlon Alves
Affiliations: School of Economics, Business Administration and Accounting at Ribeirão Preto University of São Paulo Ribeirão Preto Brazil; SKEMA Business School Université Côte d'Azur (GREDEG) Suresnes France
Abstract: ABSTRACT Research on strategic alliances often treats supplier capability development as an outcome, but rarely asks which capabilities are built or what they can be used for. We address this through an embedded single‐case study of a lead‐firm‐orchestrated network in the Brazilian Amazon, comprising six community‐based enterprises (CBEs) supplying sociobiodiversity ingredients, drawing on 60 interviews and 43 h of observation. Sponsorship proved systematically imbalanced, concentrating in the capabilities that make these CBEs reliable suppliers and largely absent from those that would allow them to price, negotiate and sell elsewhere. In doing so, capability development converted general‐purpose biodiversity and traditional knowledge into buyer‐specific assets, narrowing redeployability in fact and in how the CBEs perceived their options. Counterintuitively, redeployment required alternative demand rather than additional capability. We name this mechanism developmental lock‐in: the progressive dedication of a supplier's resource base to a supplier through the activity that upgrades it, absent any contractual restriction. The study contributes to work on supplier development, which treats capability as the binding constraint on supplier independence, and to work on asset specificity, which treats specificity as a prior condition rather than a product of the relationship itself.

Title: Do matched and mismatched null hypothesis significance testing of mediators matter? An example of fintech continuance and guidelines for the future
Authors: Wen-Lung Shiau, Chia-Hsing Shih, Israr Qureshi, Ye Yuan, Ching-I Teng
Abstract: Pursuing new directions in information systems (IS) research demands renewed methodological rigor. Based on an analysis of 134 mediation-related papers published between 2000 and 2025 in the Association for Information Systems (AIS) basket of 11 journals, we identified an important issue: a misalignment between mediation hypotheses and the null hypotheses tested, which indicates mismatched null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) that in turn may lead to inconsistent interpretation. NHST is widely used in the empirical sciences as the primary method for interpreting and reporting research findings. In mediation research, mismatches between the hypothesized and testing models are common. To clarify how mismatched NHST affects the results, we conducted an empirical study of fintech continuance intention as an example. We proposed a checklist for conducting accurate mediation analysis that enhances the methodological rigor and epistemic validity of mediation analysis and supports theoretical contributions to the IS literature. The checklist informs future IS researchers by helping them avoid the problem of mismatched NHST and advance theories that support optimal decision-making.

Title: Source of novelty and invention impact: Evidence from biotechnology patents
Authors: Fang Wang, Xinyu Liu, Zhenting Xiao
Abstract: This paper investigates the sources of invention novelty and their relationship to invention impact from an evolutionary perspective on knowledge recombination. Emphasizing the role of scientific knowledge in the inventive process, the study develops a refined analytical framework that categorizes sources of novelty into three types: scientific originality, technological originality, and recombinative creation. Analyzing 73,228 biotechnology patents granted by the USPTO between 2010 and 2021, along with their citations to scientific publications and patents, the study reveals that novelty — derived from original scientific knowledge, original technological knowledge, or recombinant approaches — has heterogeneous implications for invention impact. Specifically, scientific originality and recombinative creation are significantly associated with greater invention impact, whereas technological originality and dual originality in science and technology do not exhibit a significant effect. Furthermore, scientific originality increases invention impact by facilitating the integration of distant technological knowledge and previously disconnected knowledge components. These findings highlight the distinct roles of different novelty sources and elucidate the mechanisms through which new scientific knowledge influences invention impact, particularly in the context of science-intensive sectors.

Title: How digital platform capability builds competitive advantage in platform firms: The mediating role of intrapreneurship and user value co-creation
Authors: Yue Liu, Xiumei Zhu, Shengliang Deng
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between digital platform capability (DPC) and competitive advantage (CA) in platform companies, focusing on the mediating roles of intrapreneurship and user value co-creation. Using a two-wave, time-lagged survey of 236 platform firms, we tested our hypotheses with polynomial regression and response surface analysis. The results indicate that DPC, particularly integration and reconfiguration capabilities, is positively associated with CA. Moreover, both internal and external value co-creation factors, namely intrapreneurship and user value co-creation, significantly mediate this relationship. Our findings also suggest that CA is enhanced when intrapreneurship and user value co-creation are balanced, but declines when their development is uneven. These insights deepen our understanding of how platform companies can align internal and external value co-creation processes to leverage DPC for sustainable competitive advantage.

Title: Balancing human and artificial creativity: A paradox perspective on artistic production in the GenAI era
Authors: Galina Kondrateva, Patricia Baudier, Chantal Ammi
Abstract: The relationship between creativity and artificial intelligence (AI) has attracted widespread attention from the public, corporations, and academia. Advanced AI-based examples of artistic production, such as AI generated music, poetry, and paintings, have started transforming the creative and cultural industries. This study analyzed the componential model of creativity through the lens of the Generative AI (GenAI) artwork produced by artists. A qualitative approach was employed utilizing data collected from interviews with various artists, critics, and technicians who worked with GenAI, thereby helping in identifying the creativity paradoxes in the AI era. The results suggest that the use of GenAI has created dualities in the components of creativity, including tensions between extrinsic and intrinsic motivations, artistic and technical skills, and creations by an artist and those generated by AI. Given that AI will continue to develop, the cultural and creative industries need to find ways to navigate these creativity paradoxes.

Title: Digital Transformation and Green Total Factor Productivity in China
Authors: Junbing Huang, Wanrui He, Yajun Wang, Yimin Lu
Affiliations: School of Economics Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu China; School of Digital Economics and Management Wuxi University Wuxi China; Department of Economics, Business School Nanjing University Nanjing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving sustainable development relies on the continuous improvement of green total factor productivity (GTFP). Although existing studies have documented a positive association between digital transformation and GTFP through technological innovation, the underlying mechanism remains insufficiently understood because technological innovation is often treated as an aggregate channel. Such aggregate treatments are ineffective in clarifying the underlying mechanisms of action within it and carrying out targeted policy. In this paper, we open this black box by dividing the technology innovation caused by digitization into indigenous R&D efficiency improvement and technology spillovers increase. Through a dataset covering China's A‐share listed enterprises over the period 2012–2021, together with the Global Malmquist‐Luenberger index based on a super‐efficiency Slacks‐Based Measure model and econometric analysis, we show that digitization significantly enhances GTFP. More importantly, the increases in both indigenous R&D efficiency and technology spillovers coming from digital transformation are two important channels to promote GTFP. Our study offers insights for emerging economies aiming to achieve green growth through digital reforms.

Title: Factors influencing drug diffusion: a practical guide to the use of medicare part D claims
Authors: Yuchen Wang, Giedre Kvedaraviciene, Phillip Phan
Abstract: Because of the methods by which they are produced, drugs embody technical knowledge and are the subject of technology transfer strategies among biopharmaceutical companies. Additionally, drug diffusion shapes the structure of the biopharmaceutical industry, the sustainability of pharmaceutical markets, and patient outcomes. This article provides a practical guide to using Medicare Part D Prescription Drug Event (PDE) data to model and analyze the factors and dynamics that drive drug diffusion. Medicare accounts for approximately a third of total U.S. prescription drug spending and covers more than 56 million beneficiaries, making it the most representative dataset of the U.S. older adult population and people with disabilities. The PDE’s strengths include national representativeness, detailed transactional data, and the capacity for longitudinal and multilevel analyses. Its limitations include the absence of diagnostic detail, the reporting of list rather than net prices, and limited generalizability to non-Medicare populations. The complementary use of other data sources can mitigate these weaknesses. Hence, we describe linkage strategies that integrate PDE claims with the Medicare Beneficiary Summary File, the Prescriber Characteristics File, outpatient claims, and external data sources, including FDA approval data and U.S. Census indicators. Particular attention is given to handling many-to-many linkages and to constructing analytic datasets that preserve contextual validity. We demonstrate how researchers can evaluate the roles of patient demographics, comorbidities, prescriber attributes, and formulary design in shaping drug diffusion. We argue that Medicare Part D claims data provide a uniquely powerful platform for studying technology transfer and innovation diffusion in an industrial sector that accounts for 20% of the U.S. economy.

Title: Short-run pain, long-term gain? R&D investment and firm growth in Indian pharma
Authors: Rosa Cocozza, Serena Gallo, Amith V. Megaravalli, Vincenzo Verdoliva
Abstract: This paper examines whether R&D investment enhances firm growth and profitability in the Indian pharmaceutical industry, with particular attention to capability thresholds, heterogeneity, and peer spillovers. Using an unbalanced panel of 195 listed pharmaceutical firms from 2012 to 2024, we estimate fixed-effects regressions, propensity score matching, and quantile regressions to assess the impact of R&D intensity and adoption on sales growth and profitability, while accounting for firm heterogeneity and selection bias. Results show that firms with higher R&D investment tend to experience lower short-run growth but stronger long-run growth, consistent with the delayed innovation payoffs. Investment intensity consistently supports growth, whereas profitability and leverage do not mitigate short-run R&D adjustment costs. Peer R&D exposure generates modest spillover benefits, and heterogeneity analysis indicates that fast-growing firms are better able to absorb R&D costs. This study provides novel firm-level evidence on R&D payoffs in the Indian pharmaceutical sector during the post-TRIPS and post-demonetization period, extending prior OECD-based evidence to an emerging-market context.

Title: How technological path of internationalization matters? A dynamic capability perspective
Authors: Zhen Wang
Abstract: Internationalizing technology operations early are widely regarded as important antecedents to superior growth among international new ventures (INVs). Yet, while studies have examined the effects of technological position on INV growth, a dynamic perspective is still missing. Taking a perspective of dynamic capability theory, I shed light on the effect of heterogeneity in technology path on INV growth in terms of a curvilinear relationship. How do dynamic technological path matter for INV growth? To address this question, I introduce and measure for the first time a concept of internationalization technological path heterogeneity to capture the path-specific feature for INVs’ technological capability building, on panel data from 160 INVs. The results shows that technological path heterogeneity play a significant role in driving the growth of INVs.

Title: Facilitating corporate patent transactions: the effect of director networks and the moderating role of technological competition
Authors: Lulu Lin, Huaqi Chai, Xiaodong Geng, Wenbo Jiang
Abstract: Based on resource dependence theory and social network theory, this study examines the impact of two types of director network structures on corporate patent transactions and their boundary conditions using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2007 to 2023. First, we find that the centrality of the director network significantly promotes patent purchases, while structural holes exhibit a U-shaped effect on patent purchases. Second, both network centrality and structural holes positively influence patent sales. Third, we further explore the moderating mechanisms by which director networks affect firms’ patent transactions. Specifically, in terms of patent purchases, technological competition negatively moderates the positive relationship between the centrality of the director network and patent purchases while positively moderating the U-shaped relationship between structural holes and patent purchases. In terms of patent sales, technological competition negatively moderates the positive effects of network centrality on patent sales, yet it cannot moderate the positive effect of structural holes on patent sales. This paper enriches the research on expanding corporate patent trading partners through director networks. The findings provide some references for firms to optimize patent transaction strategies.

Title: Fostering economic growth and convergence: assessing the impact of innovation on county disparities in the United States
Authors: Hannah E. Richards, Spencer A. Yasar
Abstract: This study examines the impact of latent innovation on the growth and convergence of economic outcomes across United States (U.S.) counties from 2005 to 2020. We find that counties with lower initial gross domestic product (GDP) experience increased growth, and this growth accelerates with higher overall levels of innovation, with initial GDP and GDP growth both relative to the frontier of New York County. Additionally, we investigate innovation arising from supplier transactions (process innovation) and supplier transactions (product innovation). Our results are consistent for both process and product innovation, though we find that process innovation has a greater impact on growth and convergence than product innovation. These findings remain robust against endogeneity due to unobserved variables. Our research demonstrates that innovation influences economic development even at the granular level of U.S. counties. This can motivate policymakers to foster a local environment that encourages innovation and, consequently, economic growth.

Title: The impact of technology transfer on industrial upgrading in China: an analysis based on patent data
Authors: Yujiao Xian, Min Hu, Suping Peng, Mei Song
Abstract: As a major technological power, technology transfer (TT) is crucial to China’s industrial upgrading and high-quality economic development. Based on 127,586 patent data from 25 high-innovation economies over 2003–2023, this study develops an integrated framework to analyze the impact of TT on industrial upgrading in China. We first estimate the effectiveness of technology transfer-out (TT-out) and transfer-in (TT-in) in China. TT-out denotes domestic-originated patents exported from Chinese entities to international recipients, while TT-in indicates patent applications originating from foreign entities legally transferred to Chinese recipients. Then, we apply fixed-effect and threshold effect models to elucidate TT-driven mechanisms for China’s industrial technology and structure upgrading. Results indicate that (i) there are cyclical fluctuations in the effectiveness of TT-out and TT-in during 2003–2023, with values ranging from 0.028 to 0.102 and 0.049 to 0.125, respectively. (ii) TT-in and TT-out both significantly drive China’s industrial technology and structure upgrading at 1% significance level. A one-unit increase in TT-out corresponds to a 0.873-unit advancement in technological upgrading and a 0.143-unit gain in structural upgrading, while each unit rise in TT-in drives a 0.684-unit improvement in technological upgrading and a 0.050-unit enhancement in structural upgrading. (iii) Threshold effect models further demonstrate nonlinear relationships between TT and industrial upgrading, moderated by indigenous innovation input, imitative innovation input, and technology absorption capacity.

Title: Research on the impact of policy tool combinations on digital technology R&D alliances in complex network environments
Authors: Neng Shen, Jing Zhang, Yangchun Cao, Lianjun Wu
Abstract: Policy tools serve as critical instruments for promoting the diffusion of digital technology R&D alliances. However, there remains a lack of in-depth analysis regarding the combined effects and dynamic revenue of these policy tools. Based on the complex network evolution game model, this study systematically investigates the comprehensive impact of various policy tool combinations on digital technology R&D alliances, innovatively integrating the rule-based context of the dynamic revenue mechanism. The findings reveal that individual policies can all play positive roles in fostering digital technology R&D alliances. Nevertheless, the combined effects of policy tools vary, leading to heterogeneous outcomes such as enhancement, weakening, or even reversal. Under the dynamic revenue mechanism, factors such as innovation dividend factor, opportunity loss factor and revenue influence cycle exhibit positive promoting effects. Conversely, the scale of the network may exert adverse effects when it becomes excessively large. This research broadens the analytical perspective of digital technology R&D alliances by considering the combination of policy tools and the dynamic revenue mechanism, thereby proposing corresponding strategies that can provide optimization insights for both enterprise alliance strategies and government management mechanisms in the realm of digital technology R&D.

Title: University–industry interaction and firms’ innovation performance: new evidence from the biopharmaceutical industry
Authors: Anna Giunta, Eleonora Pierucci, Davide Vurchio
Abstract: Abstract This study examines the impact of university-industry (U-I) interaction on firms’ innovation performance in the biopharmaceutical industry, focusing on understanding the temporal relationship between co-publishing and innovation. Using a sample of Italian biopharmaceutical firms from 2000 to 2010, we explore whether collaborative research, specifically co-publishing between public and private research entities, influences firms’ likelihood of innovation and the intensity of their innovation activities. Our investigation sheds light on the temporal aspects of the knowledge generation process and its implications for firms’ innovation endeavours. It reveals an “anticipatory effect” of co-publishing on innovation outcomes. Our findings, corroborated by a set of robustness checks, detect that the influence of collaboration on innovation activities precedes the appearance of a joint publication, ruling out the hypothesis of “defensive publication” as a complementary part of a firm’s overall IP protection strategy pursued by biopharmaceutical firms.

Title: The role of traceability technologies in the sustainable evolution of the luxury industry
Authors: Martine Hlady-Rispal, Benjamin Adam, Christina Theodoraki, Vincent Jolivet
Abstract: In the emerging literature on the role of traceability technologies in corporate sustainability, the context of luxury products remains underexplored. This study draws on value theory to examine the role of traceability and its potential to shape the sustainable evolution of the French leather luxury industry across its supply chain (SC). Adopting a qualitative approach combining analysis of luxury brands’ CSR reports with longitudinal interviews, the study examines the complexity of the leather SC and traceability practices across a diverse range of luxury stakeholders. The results indicate that traceability is not inherently linked to sustainability, yet it can address emerging sustainability challenges and support the transformation of a complex luxury industry. Moreover, the scope, benefits and knowledge spillovers identified require extensive collaboration across all levels of the supply chain, which can be difficult to achieve in practice. The findings also underscore the importance of aligning traceability with technological, strategic, and relational dimensions to create value and foster the development of sustainable SCs.

Title: Bridging digital transformation and green innovation in firms: a dual-dimensional analysis of disclosure-behavior alignment
Authors: Yue Yang, Fan Luo
Abstract: Digital transformation (DT) has emerged as a critical catalyst for corporate sustainable development, wherein the alignment between DT disclosure and actual behavior plays a vital role in shaping organizational credibility and determining the effectiveness of its green innovation (GI) outcomes. Utilizing data from China’s A-share listed companies spanning 2010 to 2022, this study investigates how DT disclosure-behavior congruence influences corporate GI. The results reveal that a “high disclosure–high behavior” (HDHB) digital transformation, characterized by strong alignment between rhetorical commitments and concrete actions, substantially enhances the quantity and quality of GI. These positive effects are especially pronounced under conditions of heightened economic policy uncertainty, stringent regional intellectual property protection, and within technology-intensive industries. The mechanism analysis identifies three primary channels through which HDHB digital transformation facilitates GI, namely by enhancing information transparency, improving investment efficiency, and strengthening corporate social responsibility awareness. A quadrant-based analysis further indicates that while both DT disclosure and behavior independently support GI, their alignment in the HDHB configuration delivers the most substantial benefits, whereas other configurations yield more limited or inconsistent effects. This study contributes novel empirical evidence on how strategic alignment between DT disclosure and behavior functions as an effective governance mechanism, enabling firms to better translate digital transformation efforts into sustainable innovation outcomes. It also offers policy insights for promoting standardized corporate disclosure and fostering innovation-driven green development.

Title: The Bell inequality: applying the lessons of compulsory licensing to AI/ML and the Big 5
Authors: Antonio Llopis, Nicholas Vonortas
Abstract: Silicon Valley is viewed as an exemplar of rapid progress and innovation, but the US Government’s role in its origins is often overlooked. In 1956, as a result of anti-competitive behavior, Bell Corporation entered into a consent decree with the Department of Justice which enforced compulsory licensing of all its patents. This licensing led to a dramatic change in the dynamics around the development of the transistor, resulting in an era of growth and innovation that fundamentally altered the world and established the US’s dominance in computing and high-tech industries. Today, the situation with artificial intelligence parallels that of the transistor, with the Big 5 technology companies—Alphabet/Google, Apple, Meta/Facebook, Microsoft and Amazon—playing the role of the Bell System in controlling patents surrounding the technology and engaging in similar anti-competitive behavior. This paper serves as an exploration of major questions surrounding Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML), innovation and the Big 5. In this paper we: explore how AI/ML differs from other general purpose technologies (GPT); discuss why AI/ML, as a nascent GPT needs additional protection; and discuss why applying compulsory licensing of artificial intelligence patents on the Big 5 may be essential for ensuring that the US economy reaps the rewards of the coming technological boom. We draw parallels between Bell’s behavior and that of the Big 5 today, including their anti-competitive behaviors, argue that compulsory licensing of the Big 5’s AI intellectual property can be the appropriate remedy, and examine the risks and benefits of enacting such measures.

Title: Struggling with entrepreneurial ecosystems
Authors: Michael Fritsch
Abstract: Abstract This article discusses the notion of entrepreneurial ecosystems and proposes directions for the further development of the concept. Since the main goal of the concept is to identify factors that determine regional development, the key variable to assess the quality of an EE and the effect of respective policy measures should be a measure of regional performance. It is argued that a broad definition of entrepreneurship should be applied that includes the entire universe of new businesses (‘everyday’ entrepreneurship), and also accounts for incumbent firms. There is good reason to regard EE as a part of the regional innovation system and merge the two concepts. The paper discusses a number of open questions concerning the elements of a system and its dynamic properties. Finally, it outlines several key challenges for the further development of the concept.

Title: The impact of cumulative experience and R&D investment on technological change amid uncertainty in technological learning
Authors: Shiguo Zhou, Yaru Zhang
Abstract: This study constructs a two-factor technology adoption model that integrates uncertainty in technology learning by incorporating learning-by-doing (LBD) for cumulative experience and learning-by-searching (LBS) for research and development (R&D) investment. It uses the model to focus on the impact of uncertainty in the two types of technology learning (LBD and LBS) on the diffusion trend of emerging technologies. The main findings of this study are as follows: (1) Factors such as high learning rates, low initial investment costs, high carbon taxes, low uncertainty in learning rates, high risk tolerance, and high demand may promote the adoption and widespread deployment of emerging energy technologies. (2) The sensitivity of technology diffusion to changes in technology learning rates is highly non-linear, particularly when influenced by the LBD learning effect. This indicates that the tendency toward technology diffusion is affected more by cumulative experience than by R&D investment. (3) Accumulated experience is more sensitive to uncertainty than R&D investment.

Title: The business of supporting open innovation: drivers of value capture of business incubators across German regions
Authors: Adrian Toroslu, Brita Schemmann, Maryse M.H. Chappin, Carolina Castaldi, Andrea M. Herrmann
Abstract: Abstract Business incubators (BIs) play a crucial role in fostering entrepreneurship and regional innovation. However, while considerable attention has been given to their positive impact on tenants, little is known about how BIs capture value from offering their services. Drawing on the open innovation framework and regional innovation systems literature, this research investigates the relationship between internal and external openness of BIs and their ability to capture value, considering the influence of regional knowledge resources on this relationship. We tested our hypotheses on a sample of 109 German BIs, collecting data from a survey of their managers and from regional data sources. Our findings suggest that fostering internal networking among tenants is positively associated with BIs’ value capture, emphasizing the importance of facilitating knowledge exchange within incubator environments. Surprisingly, external openness was not related to BI value capture. Moreover, we identify a negative moderation effect of regional private knowledge levels on the relationship between external openness and BI value capture. These findings bear implications for research and practice alike.

Title: Cluster and local science-industry collaborations: evidence from a place-based innovation policy
Authors: Aurelien Quignon
Abstract: Place-based cluster policies have been widely adopted to foster regional innovation by promoting R&D collaborations. While previous research highlights the behavioral additionality of these policies, evidence regarding their effectiveness in fostering science-industry (S-I) collaborations remains limited. This paper examines the impact of the establishment of the French Competitive Cluster Program in 2005 on S-I collaborations. Leveraging a novel dataset of collaborative patents from 2000 to 2018, the results show that the cluster policy increases S-I collaborations within targeted regions. Additional analyses suggest that the effect is strongest in knowledge-intensive sectors and is associated with higher patent quality. Furthermore, the cluster policy induces a shift in innovative search strategies, with greater reliance on prior knowledge, suggesting a move toward incremental innovation. The findings contribute to the literature on the effectiveness of place-based cluster policies on science-industry collaborations and offer new insights into how to promote new collaborations through direct R&D subsidies and the diffusion of academic research into industrial applications.

Title: Innovation culture, technology transfer & performance: An empirical examination of the U.S. Department of Energy National Laboratories
Authors: C. Brooke Dobni, Jason Stolworthy, Grant Alexander Wilson, Tyler Case, James P. Keating
Abstract: To date, innovation culture and performance research has been conducted with heterogeneous samples of for-profit private or publicly traded firms. Limited research has examined the innovation culture and performance relationship among not-for-profit organizations, much less in government organizations with homogeneous resources and strategies. This study advances innovation culture and performance research, as it examines a mediator, technology transfer, among a sample of the U.S. Department of Energy’s National Laboratories. The results show that innovation culture differed among the National Laboratories and had positive direct and indirect effects, via technology transfer, on performance measured by technology-related key performance indicators. This suggests that, all else being equal (resources and strategies), an innovation culture can be the “difference-maker” in achieving key performance indicators. Additionally, an innovation culture can foster technology transfer that also improves key performance indicators. The research offers important contributions to innovation culture research and managerial implications for practitioners seeking to improve organizational outcomes.

Title: The role of research and other inputs for the development and impacts of standards
Authors: Knut Blind, Luzie Kromer
Abstract: Abstract Research as input into standardisation processes is becoming more important because of its role as a knowledge and technology transfer channel. Furthermore, standards have to become more science-based, particularly if they are part of the regulatory framework, such as in the European Union. Therefore, a conceptual model of standardisation as a channel of technology transfer has been expanded further to consider standards in the regulatory framework. The empirical study aims to identify the demands of industry and other stakeholders for standards as potential research results and other drivers and inputs. A survey among over thirty thousand experts active in the German standardisation body DIN generated almost three thousand responses, mainly from the industry. The responses from the experts reveal that policy initiatives, including regulations and customer requirements, alongside own and collaborative research, are the most relevant sources for standard development. Research input is assessed to be most important for measurement and testing standards, with quality and environmental standards closely followed. The primary benefit of utilizing research as input for standardisation is free access to scientific insights and the capability to stay updated with scientific advancements. Eventually, we correlate the relevance of inputs into standards by assessing various impact dimensions, revealing significant linkages. Finally, we link the empirical findings to the presented model and derive avenues for future theory-building research.

Title: Innovation prizes as a novel approach to university technology transfer: insights from the 2004–2007 DARPA Grand Challenges
Authors: Andrew Hanus, Christopher S. Hayter
Abstract: Abstract Although innovation prizes are increasingly recognized for their ability to catalyze technological advancement, stimulate public engagement, and foster the formation of technical communities, their role in university technology transfer remains underexplored. To address this gap, we examine the 2004–2007 DARPA Grand Challenges (DGCs) as an illustrative case. Based on an eight-year inductive investigation, we find that the DGCs accelerated the dissemination, development, and commercialization of robotics technologies rooted in publicly funded research by attracting diverse participants, fostering novel collaborations, and emphasizing real-world performance over formalized IP protection. In contrast to linear, patent-centric models of technology transfer, the DGCs catalyzed two-way knowledge flows between universities and external actors—including industry professionals, entrepreneurs, and hobbyists—while reinforcing core university missions of research, education, and public engagement, thereby generating broader public value. The competitions also leveraged broader policy and technological trends, such as enabling technologies and supportive prize legislation, illustrating how contextual factors shape when and how prizes complement traditional transfer mechanisms. In doing so, this study underscores the value of innovation prizes as an important complement to linear approaches and advances understanding of alternative pathways for university technology transfer.

Title: Launching lean: insights from early-stage entrepreneurship development programs for scientists
Authors: Christopher S. Hayter, Jonathan Merker, Tennille Eyre, Alan C. O’Connor
Abstract: Abstract University-based technology commercialization is widely recognized as a key driver of economic development, prompting extensive research into support programs—such as venture funds, accelerators, and proof-of-concept centers—designed to support academic entrepreneurship. Yet, many university scientists lack the entrepreneurial skills, experience, and networks required to navigate commercialization pathways effectively. In response, a new generation of government-supported programs has emerged globally, with a primary focus on early-stage entrepreneurial development. This study examines the origins, design, and evolution of such initiatives across eight countries, most of which are modeled on the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Innovation Corps (I-Corps) program but have been adapted to reflect regional contexts and institutional needs. Through cross-case analysis, we demonstrate that these programs constitute a multi-tiered infrastructure that strengthens the translation of academic research into market-ready innovations. These initiatives are increasingly vital to the advancement of entrepreneurial universities and the maturation of national and regional innovation ecosystems. The paper concludes with comparative insights and suggestions for future research. For policymakers and program designers, the findings highlight how program choices can be used as levers to strengthen entrepreneurial capacity, align interventions with the diverse needs of scientists, and improve the integration of customer discovery and related forms of training withing broader ecosystems.

Title: Revealing the impact of technological niche on value co-creation: the moderating role of the open innovation ecosystem structure
Authors: Hongwei Wang, Xuemei Xie
Abstract: Organizations have been endeavoring to establish or integrate into open innovation ecosystems (OIEs) to achieve value co-creation with their components efficiently due to the development of a global value system. However, empirical research on the factors influencing value co-creation within OIEs remains limited. Therefore, this study proposes a conceptual framework for examining the relationship between technological niche and value co-creation within OIEs. Using a dataset of 397 listed biopharmaceutical enterprises from 2012 to 2020, we find that technological niche has a significant positive effect on value co-creation within OIEs. Further, the component interdependence within OIEs exhibits a U-shaped moderation effect on the relationship between the technological niche and value co-creation. In contrast, the component status dispersion demonstrates an inverted U-shaped moderation effect on this relationship. Overall, this research provides a clearer understanding of how OIEs realize value co-creation by analyzing the influencing factors from the technological niche perspective and examining the contingent factors from the ecosystem structure perspective.

Title: Knowledge co-creation in innovation ecosystems and breakthrough innovation: the contradictory roles of capability reconfiguration
Authors: Yi Jin, Bo Liu
Abstract: Firms may benefit from knowledge co-creation in the innovation ecosystem, causing the innovation ecosystem to serve as an efficient way to generate breakthrough innovation. However, the in-and-out ways of knowledge co-creation in the ecosystem have not been fully explored collectively. Drawing on knowledge-based view and dynamic capability theory, we categorize two types of knowledge co-creation between the focal firm and ecosystem partners, namely embedded knowledge co-creation and alliance knowledge co-creation. Thereafter, we link knowledge co-creation and breakthrough innovation of the focal firm and further analyze the mediating role of capability reconfiguration. An empirical examination of 382 surveys from Chinese high-tech firms reveals that both two types of knowledge co-creation can promote breakthrough innovation. Besides, substitutional capability significantly mediates the relationships between knowledge co-creation and breakthrough innovation, while evolutionary capability reconfiguration suppresses the above relationships. Our findings extend the context of knowledge co-creation to innovation ecosystems and contributes to innovation and dynamic capability literature. Our study also expounds on valuable practical implications for managers.

Title: Agglomeration and spillovers: concentration versus dispersion. Evidence from regional innovative startups in Italy
Authors: Gustavo Barboza, Alessandro Braga
Abstract: Abstract Tracking more than 9000 Italian innovative start-ups geocoded at the one-kilometer resolution, we deploy a multilevel space–time model, instrumented with historical road networks, to examine how regional ecosystems shape entrepreneurial concentration. We revisit the three classical Marshallian channels (specialization, competition, and labor pooling), and we test asymmetric, cross-border knowledge spillovers and show that agglomeration can either amplify or dilute technology transfer across neighboring territories. Our results reveal sharp regional–sector asymmetries: some pairs intensify clustering while others next door disperse, exposing hidden dynamics that uniform models overlook. By reframing agglomeration as both conduit and barrier to technology transfer, we demonstrate that firm intensity depends not only on local Marshallian forces but also on the relative stocks of high-skilled human capital that mediates “push” and “pull” spillovers along shared borders. Sector-level decomposition further indicates that manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services respond differently to diversity and specialization, challenging one-size-fits-all prescriptions. Because identical policy levers yield divergent outcomes, the implications of this study suggest that policymakers need to be well aware that agglomeration is industry-sector-specific and conditional on the existing level of industry development already existing in each location.
