Title: Too old for TikTok? Nope! Exploring senior adult viewer’s short-form video platform addiction through attachment theory and socio-technical framework
Authors: Zhenya Robin Tang, Xueyan Dong, Yuxin Tian, Dahui Li
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of short-form video platforms (SVPs) has fundamentally reshaped the digital media ecosystem, engaging users from diverse demographic backgrounds. Contrary to popular belief, older adults are not immune to the allure of SVPs, with a growing number of older users becoming addicted to these platforms. Drawing on attachment theory and socio-technical perspective, this study developed a research model to examine the factors driving SVP addiction among senior adult users. Our results indicate that social factors (lack of entertainment channels) and technical factors (perceived functionality complementarity and perceived recommendation personalization) influence senior adult users’ SVP addiction through emotional attachment with content creators and functional attachment with SVP. The findings of the current study offer implications for theory development in the fields of social media addiction and technology use among older adults as well as practical suggestions for promoting the mental health and well-being of older adults in the digital age.

Title: Government institutions and data custodianship over personal information: Comparing citizen preferences in Hong Kong and South Korea
Authors: Jung Eun Kim, Kwan Nok Chan, Wai Fung Lam, Edward Kei Fung Chan
Abstract: Public administration researchers traditionally approach the use of personal information in public service through the lens of direct user control, but a combination of cognitive constraints and rapid digitization has made privacy-preserving choices exceedingly difficult for citizens to manage independently. Recent research has shifted toward the notion of “data custodianship”, where public institutions serve as custodians of personal information. In a survey experiment conducted in Hong Kong ( n = 1031) and South Korea ( n = 1040), citizens evaluated their trust in various institutions serving as custodians tasked with managing biometric information for facial recognition. The findings suggest that while institutional trust can be influenced by accountability mechanisms, it is also shaped by individuals' experiences with public institutions, as well as their political orientation, social trust, and privacy preferences. Trust in one functional domain of data custodianship—such as data collection—may not carry over to others, like storage or management. Custodianship is only viable as a policy alternative to user control in data-intensive solutions if its design accounts for variation in public trust across societies, individuals, and aspects of data governance.

Title: Digital resilience in delivering public services. A conceptual model
Authors: Katarzyna Sienkiewicz-Małyjurek
Abstract: Digital resilience has gained increasing attention as public organizations face accelerating digital transformation and growing social threats. However, research remains fragmented, providing limited understanding of how digital resilience develops in public service delivery and how its determinants relate to its manifestations. This study addresses this gap by conceptualizing digital resilience from an organizational perspective and examining the relationships between its determinants and manifestations in public service delivery. The analysis draws on 59 semi-structured interviews conducted in Poland, a relevant setting due to its advanced public-sector digital transformation and exposure to multiple contemporary crises. Using thematic analysis and the Gioia methodology, the study identifies three manifestations of digital resilience: continuity and availability of public services, organizational development, and technologization of internal and external processes. It further reveals four determinant groups: social, technological, organizational, and legal. The findings show how these determinants jointly enable and shape the identified manifestations, resulting in different resilience outcomes in public service delivery. Building on these relationships, the study develops a stakeholder-driven conceptual model and proposes a definition of digital resilience. The study contributes to digital governance research by offering conceptual clarity and an integrated framework that explains how digital resilience develops in public service delivery.

Title: Can Larger Language Models Always Perform Better? A Comparison of GPT, FinBERT, and Dictionaries in Evaluating Management Sentiment
Authors: Xu Yang, Peng Liang, Indranil Bose, Nan Hu
Abstract: Management sentiment analysis is a foundational yet domain-intensive task in information systems (IS) research, requiring substantial domain knowledge to be measured reliably. Domain-specific models emphasize specialization by embedding knowledge through extensive pretraining and fine-tuning, whereas general-purpose large language models (LLMs) rely on few-shot learning to achieve broad generalization across tasks. In this study, we investigate the extent to which general-purpose LLMs, without domain specialization, can capture managerial sentiment. We conduct a series of experiments to evaluate the performance of a general-purpose LLM (GPT-3.5) relative to a domain-specific model (FinBERT) and a traditional dictionary-based approach in classifying managerial sentiment from MD&A disclosures. These findings reveal a non-linear pattern of model performance: GPT-3.5 substantially outperforms the dictionary-based approach, while FinBERT achieves slightly higher accuracy than GPT-3.5. These findings show that larger-scale general-purpose LLMs do not uniformly dominate smaller domain-specific models and highlight the importance of model-task alignment in domain-intensive IS contexts.

Title: A review on blockchain-driven e-healthcare service user empowerment
Authors: Anjali Shishodia, Rohit Sharma, Angappa Gunasekaran, Prikshat Verma
Abstract: This paper aims to conduct a hybrid study focusing on blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment and its applications in e-healthcare concepts, using bibliometric, network, thematic, and content analyses. The study considered 778 published articles from 2016 to 2024 and conducted a network analysis of the 49 most-cited articles in the domain of blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment. The results underscore the underlying research areas, which are further clustered into five major principles, namely, data ownership and control, data privacy and security, trust and transparency, incentivization and engagement, and accessibility and equity. The results offer unique insights for theoretical and managerial implications and propose a conceptual framework for future study in this sector.

Title: Mental Health Support for People with Depression Using Artificial Intelligence: The Effects of Appearance and Emotion Anthropomorphism
Authors: Jingjing Tong, Wenjing Chen, David Jingjun Xu
Abstract: Depression is globally prevalent, yet psychiatric shortages restrict care access. Artificial intelligence (AI) doctors may address this shortage, but their adoption is hindered by distrust and privacy concerns. By making AI doctors seem socially present and humanlike, anthropomorphic design may shape users’ psychological responses. Drawing on media equation theory, this study distinguishes between appearance and emotion anthropomorphism and examines their effects on trust, privacy concerns, and adoption intention, with perceived public stigma as a moderator. A 2 × 2 experiment with 319 participants showed that emotion anthropomorphism increased trust and reduced privacy concerns, whereas appearance anthropomorphism had no significant effects. Trust increased adoption intention, whereas privacy concerns reduced it. The two designs showed negative interaction effects: each effect weakened when the other design was high. Emotion anthropomorphism’s effects were stronger under high perceived public stigma. This study advances AI anthropomorphism research and guides AI doctor design.

Title: AI advice and human metacognition
Authors: Leily Soleimanof, Derrick Neufeld
Abstract: Although organizations increasingly rely on artificial intelligence (AI) to support decision making, research consistently finds that decision makers exhibit varied responses to algorithmic advice. While prior research has examined when users are more likely to accept or reject AI advice, little is known about the cognitive factors associated with these responses or the broader psychological consequences of working with AI. Drawing on metacognition theory, this study explores how individuals monitor and revise their judgments when confronted with algorithmic advice in a behavioral experiment with 440 participants. The results indicate that metacognitive estimates of confidence are strongly associated with responses to algorithmic advice. However, individual differences in metacognitive sensitivity shape how consistently they rely on confidence when responding to AI advice. Specifically, when metacognitive sensitivity is low, confidence judgments are based on noisy internal states, which, in turn, lead to inconsistent patterns of advice-taking. We also find that exposure to contradictory AI advice is associated with lower retrospective confidence in individuals' subsequent decisions. This loss of confidence is more pronounced when individuals reject the AI advice, highlighting a hidden psychological cost of advice rejection. These findings contribute to the growing body of information systems (IS) research on algorithmic advice-taking by demonstrating that effective human-AI collaboration requires not only improvements in system design but also fostering users' metacognitive sensitivity.

Title: The impact of generative AI on news believability: A mind perception perspective
Authors: Yang Liu, Junming Zeng, Shan Liu, Lu Han
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into news production, concerns have emerged about its impact on audience trust and news believability. Drawing on mind perception theory, this study investigates how perceived attributes of the news producer's mind, namely, cognitive ability, emotional ability, and intentionality, mediate the relationship between the type of news generator (AI vs. human) and news believability. We adopt a multi-methods approach, combining an empirical analysis of news videos and user comment data from Douyin with two controlled online experiments to uncover the psychological mechanisms. Results reveal an AI trust penalty: AI-generated news is perceived as significantly less believable than human-generated news, primarily because of lower attributions of cognitive and emotional abilities, as well as heightened perceptions of manipulative intent associated with AI news generators. However, this effect varies across evaluative contexts. The AI trust penalty is attenuated in hard-news contexts, compared with soft-news contexts, where audiences evaluate believability through diagnostic content-based cues such as factual accuracy and evidentiary support. It is also attenuated in belief-consistent contexts, where belief alignment activates an automatic acceptance process that reduces scrutiny of the news generator. These findings contribute to research on trust in AI-generated content, mind perception, and news consumption by identifying the specific mental attributes audiences consider when evaluating news and by delineating the boundary conditions under which mind attribution is more or less likely to occur. We conclude by discussing practical implications for AI involvement and disclosure strategies in news production.

Title: Actualized fitness technology affordances: Conceptualization and validation of a measurement scale
Authors: Yafang Li, Michelle Carter, Robert E. Crossler
Abstract: Prior research on fitness technologies has identified numerous affordances that support users’ fitness goals. However, these affordances are often conceptualized as perceived action possibilities and described using inconsistent labels across studies, resulting in fragmented constructs and limited cumulative theorizing. Affordance actualization theory suggests that technological affordances have consequences only when enacted through users’ actions. Yet empirical measures capturing such enactments remain underdeveloped. To address this gap, we developed and validated a measurement scale for actualized fitness technology affordances. Following established scale development procedures, we generated items, refined the scale, and assessed reliability and validity through three rounds of data collection across student, MTurk, and Prolific samples. The resulting four-factor, 18-item scale captured distinct patterns of actualized affordances—self-appraisal, social appraisal, rewarding, and reminding—reflecting recurring, goal-directed actions performed through fitness technologies in practice. We found that the validated instrument extended the explanatory value of affordance actualization theory in fitness technology research and established a foundation for examining how enacted behaviors relate to user experiences, identities, and downstream outcomes across digital health contexts.

Title: Designing away technostress: Digital interface nudges, cognitive effort, and digital mindset in complex decision environments
Authors: Maximilian Valta, Christian Maier, Yannick Hildebrandt
Abstract: Complex digital decision tasks can become obstructive when interface design requires users to interpret, retrieve, and compare dispersed information under ambiguity. Although technostress research recognizes information system (IS) design as a potential mitigation lever, it remains underspecified how concrete interface-level mechanisms shape users’ stress appraisals during interaction without removing objective task complexity. We theorize digital interface nudges, which are choice architecture based interface elements that structure options and guide attention without restricting choice, as a focused IS design lever that can reduce perceived cognitive effort during decision making and in turn lower perceived hindrance technostressors. We test this argument in an online experiment in which participants complete a complex car-booking task under either a default setting digital interface nudge, a salience-framing digital interface nudge, or a control interface. Both digital interface nudges reduce perceived hindrance technostressors relative to the control, and these reductions are stronger for individuals with a higher digital mindset. The study contributes to technostress research by showing how minimal choice architecture based interface interventions can shape how users appraise complexity in structured decision interfaces without removing objective complexity from the task itself. It also extends digital nudging research from behavioral choice outcomes to stress-related perceptual outcomes and identifies digital mindset as an initial user-level scope condition that shapes the effectiveness of interface structuring.

Title: Navigating institutional constraints on university spin-off development in the social sciences and humanities context: a multiple-case study
Authors: Eugenie Delzenne, Johanna Vanderstraeten, Barbara Tan, Tim C. E. Engels
Abstract: University spin-off (USO) creation is typically associated with Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) disciplines. This study shifts the focus to the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH). Drawing on institutional theory, we argue that SSH-based USOs constitute a peculiar object: they conform neither to prevailing modes of knowledge transfer in SSH, nor to the established, STEM-centric commercialization routines of technology transfer offices (TTOs). To explore how this particular institutional context shapes the development of SSH-based USOs, the study relies on a multiple-case study of 14 SSH-based USOs, primarily informed by interviews with SSH academic entrepreneurs and TTO staff members. The results demonstrate that SSH-based USOs face specific institutional constraints hindering their development. Most are normative and cognitive, rooted in disciplinary values and mental models that sustain distinct models of knowledge transfer—that of SSH versus a dominant STEM-based model, enacted respectively by SSH academic entrepreneurs and TTO staff members. Additional regulative constraints arise from formal procedures and resource allocation policies. Nonetheless, our findings also indicate that these constraints are not static. Drawing on the concept of institutional work, our results show that these constraints constitute instead spaces of active boundary work, where SSH academic entrepreneurs and TTO staff members change, redefine, or maintain the boundaries of university knowledge transfer. Importantly, our findings reveal that TTO staff members’ efforts to adapt established practices as they expand into SSH are fraught with internal tensions, as they contend with resource constraints and entrenched disciplinary norms privileging STEM-based models of USO creation.

Title: Who, how, and where: navigating towards a micro-foundations perspective on university technology transfer ecosystems
Authors: Thomas Crispeels, Kevin De Moortel, Marie Gruber, Maribel Guerrero
Abstract: This introductory paper for this special issue links prior knowledge on technology transfer ecosystems with recent critiques on the ecosystem concept as a research tool, examining how university actors navigate their ecosystems by investigating who is involved, how processes are navigated and where this takes place. We put forward that researchers should ‘drill down’ rather than ‘close down’ the ecosystem concept and regard the ambiguity surrounding it as a valuable analytical starting point rather than as a problem to be solved. The five articles in this Special Issue contribute to this conversation and expand our understanding of the micro-foundations of “navigating university ecosystems”. We conclude with a research agenda and several implications for university actors and policymakers.

Title: The effects of university-industry collaboration subsidies on firm performance
Authors: Palangkaraya Alfons, Jensen Paul, Thomson Russell, Webster Elisabeth
Affiliations: Faculty of Business, Law and Entrepreneurship, Swinburne University of Technology , John Street, Hawthorn, Victoria 3122; Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, Faculty of Business and Economics, University of Melbourne , Parkville, Victoria 3010 , . e-mail: pjensen@unimelb.edu.au; Faculty of Business, Law and Entrepreneuship, Swinburne University of Technology , John Street, Hawthorn, Victoria 3122; Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, Faculty of Business and Economics, University of Melbourne , Parkville, Victoria 3010
Abstract: Abstract We quantify how competitive funding programs that promote university-industry (U-I) research partnerships affect firm performance. To do this, we estimate staggered difference-in-differences models using data from more than 5000 funded and non-funded Australian Research Council Linkage Project grant applications from 2002 to 2015. Our results show grant funding led to a 12% increase in employment over a 5-year period with both employment and turnover trending upward relative to untreated firms over our 5-year post-treatment window.

Title: Can Innovations That Are Good for Environment Be Also Good Business? A Case Study on Biodiversity Loss Mitigation
Authors: H. Taimisto, V. Tiitola, G. Pigatto, A. Hirvensalo, T. Laine, T. Korhonen
Affiliations: Industrial Engineering and Management Tampere University Tampere Finland; Sant'anna School of Advanced Studies Institute of Management Pisa Italy; Information and Knowledge Management Tampere University Tampere Finland
Abstract: ABSTRACT The adoption of biodiversity loss mitigation innovations (BLMIs) in business markets depends on customers recognizing their value. Current literature lacks sufficient understanding of the decision processes, through which suppliers and customers make the ecological value of BLMIs visible, credible, and economically actionable. This paper explores decision‐making concerning and development of BLMIs at the supplier‐customer interface, using an interventionist research approach. The paper combines the switching path analysis technique (SPAT) and the Gioia method to analyze interview data on how decisions on BLMIs are currently being made and how these innovations could be developed to accelerate their adoption. Our results suggest that BLMI decisions currently rely on identifying cost‐efficient approaches that sufficiently address the biodiversity‐related concerns, while merely hoping to also capture the more ambiguous but broader ecological value in economic terms. Moreover, our study suggests that in addition to introducing the BLMIs themselves, the measurement of the ecological value and its translation into economic customer value need to be developed to enhance the adoption of BLMIs. The paper contributes to literature on biodiversity innovations and customer value by identifying the core business challenges related to BLMI.

Title: Toward explainable clinical decision support for irregular and incomplete ICU EHRs: An observation-aware multi-level attention model
Authors: Kaibo Zhu, Xuan Wei, Xiuxian Wang, Na Geng
Abstract: Intensive care units (ICUs) are high-acuity environments where patient conditions evolve rapidly and require continuous monitoring. These settings generate rich, high-frequency electronic health records (EHRs), offering critical opportunities for data-driven decision support. However, ICU EHRs are characterized by irregular sampling, widespread missingness, and a heterogeneous structure. These characteristics hinder the development of reliable and interpretable machine learning models—two qualities essential for safe clinical deployment. This study proposes MMAEM (Masked Multi-level Attention Encoding Model), an observation-aware clinical decision support model that integrates static demographic information with dynamic multivariate time series through a hybrid encoder architecture. The approach employs an explicit masking strategy to learn directly from sparse and irregular sequences without imputing unobserved values. Moreover, it incorporates a multi-level attention mechanism, spanning the feature-, timestep-, and trend-level dimensions. This mechanism is designed to provide structured, temporally resolved explanatory signals grounded in observed clinical data and to improve the transparency of model output in irregular ICU time series. Using real-world ICU data, we evaluate the model in an early sepsis prediction case study and show that enhanced transparency can be achieved without compromising predictive performance. By aligning algorithmic innovation with the transparency requirements of clinical practice, this work advances the development of explainable predictive models and supports their practical adoption in ICU decision support systems.

Title: How sharing-platform SMEs innovate their business models in developing economies: A process and ecosystem perspective
Authors: Sara Odat, Omar Al-Tabbaa, Zaheer Khan, George Saridakis
Abstract: Sharing-platform small and medium-sized enterprises (SPSMEs) are a critical player in the sharing economy. However, how they innovate their business models in the developing economies setting is still unclear. This is because most research focuses on large sharing-platform firms in developed economies, often treating their business models as relatively static configurations, while explaining their innovation mainly from the firm's internal perspective. Accordingly, we ask: how SPSMEs, that operate in developing economies, adapt and reconfigure their business models over time while responding to challenging external conditions (including weak institutions, regulatory uncertainty, low digital awareness, fragmented provider networks, and limited ecosystem support). Drawing on multiple-case studies comprising seven SPSMEs in Jordan and the UAE, we develop a 3Ts process model (Triggering, Theming and Transforming) which explains how SPSMEs recognise opportunities, define value logics, and reconfigure their digital activity systems over time. We also show that the SPSMEs business ecosystem consists of two networks (the Digital Activity Network and the Digital Business Network), whose actors enable, constrain and redirect the business model innovation process. The study contributes to research on business model innovation (BMI) and the sharing economy literature by showing that BMI in SPSMEs is not a one-off design outcome. Rather, it is an evolving and context-sensitive process shaped by firm-level adaptation and business ecosystem conditions, particularly in developing economies.

Title: Academic entrepreneurship: uncovering the role of formal and informal logics in the academic entrepreneurial space
Authors: Giulia Giunti, Joanne Duberley
Abstract: Abstract This study integrates the embedded perspective of entrepreneurship with institutional logics theory to theorise AE as an embedded phenomena, sitting at the intersection of individuals within surrounding contexts. Drawing on qualitative data from STEM academics at three research-intensive universities—in the UK (23), Australia (32), and Italy (26)—we develop the concept of the academic entrepreneurial space , as the arena within which AE unfolds, structured by a constellation of four logics: profession, discipline, impact, and resource & culture. We show how each logic shapes individual attitudes and motivations through three socio-cognitive mechanisms—signification, legitimation, and domination—and how the logics interact through four cross-level mechanisms—filtering, resistance, refraction, and compounding. By conceptually defining the logics underpinning AE, foregrounding the mechanisms through which multiple logics shape academics’ attitudes and motivations for AE, and how logics interact, the study contributes understanding on the embedded nature of AE, providing theoretical and practical insight.

Title: The pursuit of industrial sovereignty in the face of increasing knowledge base complexity. The case of the medical device sector
Authors: Darío Vázquez, Verónica Robert, Ignacio Oscar Cretini
Affiliations: EIDAES, UNSAM; UNLAM; CONICET , Edificio Tornavías, Campus Miguelete, Av. 25 de mayo y Francia, San Martín, Buenos Aires, CP 1650 , . e-mail: rvazquez@unsam.edu.ar; CONICET , Edificio Tornavías, Campus Miguelete, Av. 25 de mayo y Francia, San Martín, Buenos Aires, CP 1650 , . e-mail: vrobert@unsam.edu.ar; UNPSJB; EIDAES, UNSAM, Ciudad Universitaria - Km 4 - Ruta Prov. Nº1 , Comodoro Rivadavia, Chubut, CP 9000 , . e-mail: ignaciocretini@gmail.com
Abstract: Abstract The COVID-19 pandemic reignited discussions about the medical device (MD) sector’s role in industrial and economic development. Rapid technological advancements are increasing the complexity of is Knowledge Base (KB), potentially restricting countries’ ability to develop comprehensive capabilities across all fields. This leads to varied specialization patterns and creates tension with healthcare autonomy objectives. Our study examines the MD sector’s KB evolution, comparing trajectories of leading nations (United States, Germany, Japan, and China). The research reveals how traditional manufacturing and engineering foundations have incorporated biotechnology and Fourth Industrial Revolution technologies (AI, robotics, and big data). Distinct national specialization patterns are also shown: The United States maintains the most diversified KB, Japan remains strongly specialized in electronics-related industries, meanwhile mastering manufacturing domains has allowed Germany and China to expand their KB to other fields.

Title: Towards a dynamic conceptualisation of the regional innovation system: the systemic knowledge network continuum
Authors: Adi Weidenfeld, Tom Broekel, Nick Clifton
Affiliations: University of Warsaw; RWTH Aachen University; School of Business and Law; Cardiff Metropolitan University
Abstract: The Regional Innovation Systems (RIS) framework has traditionally explained regional innovation performance through structural conditions and external knowledge linkages. While this perspective has generated influential typologies and policy approaches, it provides more limited insight into how RISs emerge and transform through endogenous regional dynamics. This paper develops a dynamic and network-based perspective that conceptualises RIS development as a continuum from fragmented interaction structures to more integrated and self-reinforcing systems. We argue that RIS evolution depends on the interaction between generative network mechanisms and three systemic dimensions: coherence, a unifying function (UF), and boundedness. These dimensions jointly shape whether regional knowledge networks remain fragmented, become partially integrated, or evolve into more mature RISs. By shifting attention from static structures towards dynamic interaction processes, the framework provides a basis for understanding RIS emergence, transformation, and reversibility, while also pointing towards more adaptive and mechanism-oriented approaches to regional innovation policy.

Title: Elucidating the bifurcated effects of artificial intelligence technostress on customer satisfaction: The role of affective reactions and voluntariness of use
Authors: Siqin Chen, Jiabao Lin, Qinyao Zheng, Xin (Robert) Luo
Abstract: To achieve high customer satisfaction with AI-empowered products, companies need to focus on the undesired effects of AI technostress on customers. However, the current understanding of how AI technostressors affect customer satisfaction remains limited. Drawing on affective events theory, we develop a research model to investigate how AI autonomy and AI privacy invasion affect customer satisfaction through their affective reactions and examine the moderating role of voluntariness of use. Analysis of data from 357 customers who had used AI-empowered products revealed that AI autonomy is positively associated with customers’ positive affect and negatively associated with their negative affect, whereas AI privacy invasion had the opposite effects. Moreover, positive affect was found to be related positively to customer satisfaction, whereas negative affect was associated negatively with satisfaction. The voluntariness of use positively moderated the relationships both between positive affect and customer satisfaction and between negative affect and customer satisfaction. The results also confirmed that positive and negative affect play indirect roles between AI technostressors and customer satisfaction. This study provides valuable insights into the complex interplay among AI autonomy, AI privacy invasion, and customer satisfaction by elucidating the bifurcated effects of AI technostress from an affective reaction perspective. The findings make significant contributions to the technostress literature, further advancing our understanding of the influences of AI technostress from customers’ perspective. Our study also provides practical recommendations for companies to modify and innovate their AI-empowered products and enhance customer satisfaction.

Title: TRACE: Transaction representation learning for large-scale Ethereum phishing detection under limited labels
Authors: Hojun Kang, Sang-Gun Lee
Abstract: Ethereum phishing detection is a decision-support problem: blockchain risk analysts must prioritize suspicious addresses under severe label scarcity and bounded review capacity. We present TRACE, a two-stage decision-support artifact that constructs dense Ethereum address graphs from Etherscan transaction records, pre-trains an edge-aware encoder with graph contrastive learning, and adapts it with validation-based threshold calibration and explanation analysis for reviewable phishing screening. Rather than proposing new learning primitives, the contribution is a domain-grounded configuration whose individual design choices are non-obvious for dense, heavy-tailed transaction graphs and whose benefit grows with graph scale. Across five graphs from 30,000 to 149,930 addresses, six label ratios, eight baselines, and five random seeds, TRACE achieves the best overall mean performance (F1 0.5094; AUC 0.9365). Component ablations, paired significance tests, precision–recall (AUPRC) reporting, and prevalence-sensitivity experiments down to sub-1% phishing rates confirm that each design element contributes and that the advantage is stable under realistic class imbalance. Performance improves with graph scale, reaching F1 0.6720 and AUC 0.9730 on D150k under full labels, and a smaller pre-training graph transfers to a larger target (F1 0.5670). The artifact logic generalizes to other scarce-label, interaction-rich risk-screening settings beyond Ethereum.

Title: Counterfactual patient satisfaction inference under selective observation: A theory-driven machine learning design approach for online consultation services
Authors: Anfei Xia, Jian-Jun Wang, Jingguo Wang
Abstract: Online health communities (OHCs) rely on voluntary postconsultation ratings, yet more than 90% of consultations in our setting went unrated and observed ratings were positively skewed. Grounded in computational design science research and the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), we develop a theory-driven artifact for counterfactual satisfaction inference under selective observation. The artifact combines ELM-based central and peripheral route features, heterogeneous stacking, and support-aware self-training with latent structure detection and reviewer support diagnosis. Using consultations from a Chinese OHC, the artifact achieves strong predictive performance on observed reviewer labels while substantially reducing inference latency relative to RoBERTa and API-based ChatGPT5.4. Ablation and SHAP analyses show that peripheral route cues are more predictive than central route cues. For silent patients, shift diagnostics, support analysis, and LLM-fused proxy validation indicate that the artifact produces less positively skewed counterfactual estimates and improves alignment relative to the main supervised, semi-supervised, and domain-adaptation baselines. A randomized experiment with 275 participants further shows that when satisfaction scores are highly positive and provide limited differentiation, patients place greater decision weight on review volume when selecting doctors. The study contributes a theory-driven design approach that links satisfaction formation, selective feedback observability, counterfactual inference, and downstream reputation-signal use in digital healthcare.

Title: Working with semantic machines: The role of semantic reconciliation in public sector data governance
Authors: Jonny Holmström
Abstract: Local governments are beginning to use artificial intelligence (AI) in internal administrative work, including recruitment. In a decentralized municipality, however, a standardized AI assessment must travel between a technology vendor, central HR specialists, recruiters, and hiring managers responsible for different services. This creates a tension between representational portability and contextual adequacy. Based on a qualitative case study of a large Swedish municipality, we examine an AI interviewing system that translated candidates' open-ended responses into competency indicators and narrative summaries used in early-stage recruitment. We develop a process model of semantic reconciliation comprising five recurrent forms of work: scoping what could be delegated to the system, mapping vendor categories to municipal and occupational vocabularies, refining interpretations when role context was lost, embedding shared interpretations across a distributed organization, and composing AI reports with locally accountable human judgment. The study contributes to research on local-government AI and data governance by showing how semantic machines make evaluative information portable while requiring continuous organizational work to restore context. It also specifies practical arrangements through which municipalities can use common AI tools without allowing standardized outputs to displace role-specific knowledge or human decision authority.

Title: The Complementarity Paradox: Human-AI Collaboration, Overreliance, and Skill Decline in Entrepreneurial Contexts
Authors: Srinivas Subramanya, Satish Krishnan, Nasreen Azad
Abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is beginning to reconfigure how entrepreneurial work is organized. Professionals with a strong individual entrepreneurial orientation are often among the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters, yet this same zeal can set in motion a chain of effects that may ultimately undermine essential skills. Drawing on cognitive offloading theory and skill decay literature, we conceptualize GenAI use as collaboration depth and GenAI dependence as collaboration asymmetry. We theorize a sequential mechanism in which individual entrepreneurial orientation prompts deeper collaboration with GenAI, sustained collaboration tends to cultivate GenAI dependence, and dependence in turn is associated with perceived erosion of professional skills. We further argue that a strong long-term orientation can amplify the conversion of collaboration depth into dependence, since future-focused individuals may reframe routine use as a strategic investment and assign less immediate priority to corrective practice. Survey data from 143 knowledge workers across five countries are broadly consistent with this account and point to what we term a hustle-to-handicap pattern: when entrepreneurial ambition meets GenAI under a long-term outlook, perceived skill erosion appears to emerge through sustained behavior rather than through disposition alone. The study contributes to the emerging information systems conversation on human-AI collaboration by illuminating how entrepreneurial and temporal orientations shape the conditions under which GenAI may shift from augmenting capability toward perceived capability erosion.

Title: The Power of Tourists: Exploring How Tourists’ Textual Inputs Influence AI Response and Interaction Quality
Authors: Yuexin Zhao, Long Lyu, Hongyu Zhang, Yingjie Gao
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the travel industry, yet how tourists’ textual inputs influence interactions with GenAI remains underexplored. This study investigates how tourists’ textual inputs influence AI responses and interaction quality. Using a two-study design, we conducted a quasi-experiment to examine subjective interaction quality and a simulation study to examine objective interaction quality. The results show that information density and syntactic complexity increase informational support, whereas subjectivity decreases it. Information density and subjectivity enhance emotional support, whereas syntactic complexity reduces it. The effects on interaction quality differ across dimensions. Information density and syntactic complexity lower subjective but improve objective quality, whereas subjectivity improves subjective quality but has no significant effect on objective quality. Topic consistency further negatively moderates the effects of syntactic complexity on subjective quality and information density on objective quality. These findings advance human-AI interaction literature and offer practical guidance for improving GenAI support for tourists.

Title: Causes of crowdsourcing in science failures: a multi-level approach
Authors: Regina Lenart, Marta Najda-Janoszka, Jin Chen
Abstract: Crowdsourcing in science is an increasingly popular complementary method of conducting scientific research. However, organizing a crowdsourcing in science initiative is a challenge for scientists, and many such initiatives fail. Nevertheless, the literature on failures of crowdsourcing in science and their causes is still in its infancy, and the results to date are scattered and fragmented. Drawing on a multilevel perspective, we recognize, characterize and offer a structured understanding of the causes of the failure of crowdsourcing in science. We collected data using focus group interviews with 36 scholars representing various scientific fields and disciplines. The results show that the causes of failure are the initiator's insufficient competences, their negative attitude towards crowdsourcing in science, insufficient organisational support, the compulsory nature of crowdsourcing in science, and the crisis of trust in science. In addition, normative pressure and technology connect the interactions within and between levels. On the basis of these findings, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that structures the causes of the failure of crowdsourcing in science, and takes into account interactions within and between levels. The results and the framework serve as the basis for offering implications for researchers, managerial staff of institutions of higher education and decision-makers. We show how important crowdsourcing in science is, and that careful management of such projects is workable.

Title: What makes an effective ideator? The distinct roles of cognition, personality, and experience in early-stage venture ideation
Authors: Thomas Maran, Anna Bachmann, Sascha Kraus, Tobias Fitz, Marco Furtner, Marina Dabić
Abstract: A microfoundational account of organizational innovation capability should explain which individual-level attributes distinguish ideators who are better able to generate, select, and elaborate ideas into investment-worthy business concepts. Yet research remains fragmented because prior studies often examine isolated traits and fail to distinguish among key creative ideation outcomes. Drawing on Trait Activation Theory, we conceptualize venture ideation as a staged, trait-relevant context in which cognitive abilities, personality traits, and creative domain experience are differentially expressed across successive stages. We examine this theorizing using a task-based assessment that separates idea quantity , idea originality , and idea quality . Innovation-exposed experts, including R&D experts, managers, and entrepreneurs (n = 208), generated multiple business ideas for a disruptive technology, selected their most promising idea, and refined it into a product or service concept incorporating core elements of a viable business model. Experienced technology-focused venture capitalists evaluated idea quality by indicating whether these concepts merited investment interest. We quantified semantic distinctiveness using multiple large language models as a semantic proxy for selected-idea originality. Divergent thinking predicted idea quantity, but not investor-evaluated idea quality. In contrast, investment-interest judgments were predicted by ideators’ Openness to Experience, creative domain experience, and convergent thinking ability. Overall, our findings show that early-stage venture ideation is not a unitary creative process. Different attributes help ideators generate many ideas and develop selected ideas into investment-worthy business model concepts, advancing a microfoundational account of organizational innovation capability in technology-based venture creation.

Title: Software upgrade pricing under valuation uncertainty: The role of consumer learning
Authors: Shuxia Peng, Qing Zhang, Bo Li, Pengwen Hou
Abstract: Consumer valuation uncertainty for software products significantly impacts purchase decisions and software industry growth. Whereas existing literature explores various methods to mitigate consumers’ uncertainty, few studies investigate consumer learning from the previous generation of a software product. Specifically, it remains unclear how a baseline version of the software mitigates valuation uncertainty for a subsequent upgraded version, and what its strategic implications are. To fill this gap, we develop a two-period analytical model to examine a software vendor's pricing and upgrade strategies under consumer uncertainty and consumer learning. Through this analysis, our study provides concrete managerial guidance. First, regarding pricing strategy, we reveal that under certain conditions, the software vendor should implement price discrimination by charging a premium to existing consumers for the upgraded version of the software. Second, concerning market education, we demonstrate that increasing the proportion of fully informed consumers may harm the software vendor's profit. Finally, regarding product design, we find that controlling the upgrade level to ensure a moderate degree of similarity between the two versions can achieve a “win-win” outcome, simultaneously maximizing the vendor's profit and enhancing consumer surplus. This study provides software vendors with valuable and actionable strategies for pricing, market education, and versioning upgrades in an uncertain market.

Title: Sounds good and feels better—how anthropomorphism influences artificial intelligence voice assistant use
Authors: Yixiu Yu, Sisheng Liang, Haoqiang Jiang, Rui Sundrup, Andrew N.K. Chen
Abstract: Anthropomorphic design is increasingly embedded into artificial intelligence (AI) voice assistants (AIVAs) to create more emotionally engaging interaction experiences. However, despite widespread adoption, users continue to express significant concern regarding security-related risks, and the mechanisms through which anthropomorphic cues help alleviate this concern remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on dual-appraisal perspectives and affect-as-information theory, this study investigates how anthropomorphism can shape evaluative processing (i.e., perceived enjoyment, perceived security risk, and discontinuance intention) under conditions of technological opacity and uncertainty in AIVA use contexts. We develop a research model in which anthropomorphism functions not only as a generator of affect, but also as a contextual amplifier that strengthens the evaluative influence of affective experience during security-related judgment formation. Survey data from AIVA users were analyzed using structural equation modeling, supplemented by robustness checks and post-hoc analyses. The results show that anthropomorphism increases perceived enjoyment significantly, which in turn reduces both perceived security risk and discontinuance intention. However, anthropomorphism does not reduce perceived security risk directly; rather, the relationship operates primarily through perceived enjoyment, highlighting the central role of affective appraisal. Furthermore, anthropomorphism strengthens the negative relationship between perceived enjoyment and perceived security risk, suggesting that affective experience exerts a stronger evaluative influence under humanlike interaction conditions. Post hoc analyses further reveal nonlinear affective effects, highlight the importance of voice-specific anthropomorphic cues, and suggest that anthropomorphism may also facilitate habitual engagement through affective experience. Based on our findings, theoretical contributions, practical implications, and future research directions are provided.

Title: Understanding individual online social exclusion: Conceptualization, scale development, and validation
Authors: Bryan Iwata Hammer, Andy Luse, Caleb Krieger, Gabriel Bahr, Forough Nasirpouri Shadbad
Abstract: Despite an increase in research on social exclusion, a consistent definition and measure is lacking, especially for online and virtual environments. Additionally, previous measures cannot account for inconsistencies in the literature, such as social exclusion's relationship with trust and social factors. In this research, we present a review of the literature, clarify the conceptualization, and provide a definition. Using a student sample and another more general population, we develop a two-dimensional scale. First, we use focus groups to develop new survey items, then rely on subject-matter experts to assess content validity. After developing measurement items, an exploratory analysis for grouping the items and confirmatory analysis for validating the measure was conducted, followed by group & predictive analyses to further validate the measure. The new scale reliably and validly appraises individual online social exclusion. The scale resolves inconsistencies from the literature, showing it to be more discerning than previous operationalizations.

Title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Digital Platforms: Emerging Transformations, Tensions, and Research Directions
Authors: Yuanzhu Zhan, Ajay Kumar, Thanos Papadopoulos, Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo
Affiliations: University of Birmingham; EMLYON Business School; University of Kent; University of Texas at San Antonio
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming digital platforms. Unlike earlier AI technologies centered on prediction and classification, GenAI's creational capabilities, probabilistic outputs, and iterative learning dynamics reshape how value is created, captured, and governed within platform ecosystems. This editorial synthesizes insights from the Special Issue (SI) on “The Transformative Power of Generative AI for Digital Platforms,” which received 38 submissions and published 6 articles spanning organizational, technological, strategic, behavioral, and societal perspectives. Drawing on the existing literature, the editorial develops a multidimensional framework that organizes the dimensions of GenAI-driven platform transformation: adoption and organizational embedding; creational affordances and innovation mechanisms; strategic and operational reconfiguration; human and behavioral responses; and governance, risk, and legitimacy. We further conceptualize the dimensions as a recursive generativity-governance cycle linking embedding, affordance actualization, platform reconfiguration, stakeholder responses, and governance feedback. The published articles are subsequently mapped onto this framework, highlighting their contributions to both literature and practice. The editorial concludes by outlining theoretical implications, managerial considerations, and directions for future research, offering a comprehensive understanding of GenAI as a socio-technical force reconfiguring platform architectures, decision processes, human-AI interaction, and institutional environments.

Title: Lead investor effects, public–private synergy, and hierarchical governance: how government venture capital drives substantive innovation
Authors: Zhihang Zhou, Luze Xie, Yibo Zuo, Fanghao Chen
Abstract: Amid intensifying global technological competition and China’s commitment to high-level technological self-reliance, government venture capital (GVC) has emerged as a core instrument for state intervention in the venture capital market and the implementation of innovation policies. Using a panel dataset of Chinese firms from 2012 to 2021, we innovatively employ a large language model to facilitate multi-level ultimate ownership tracing for the precise identification of GVC-backed firms. We then employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach to systematically examine the impact of GVC on firm innovation performance and its underlying mechanisms. We document four main findings: (1) GVC significantly increases both the quantity and quality of innovation in portfolio firms, boosting patent applications by approximately 12.3% and patent quality by 4.9%. (2) When serving as the lead investor, GVC significantly enhances both the quantity and quality of firm innovation. (3) Public–private synergy generates significant complementarities between GVC and private venture capital (PVC), where a hybrid investment model outperforms standalone capital investments in stimulating innovation efficiency. (4) The fund hierarchy exhibits a middle-is-best governance pattern. While top-tier parent funds suffer from screening bottlenecks due to information decay, and bottom-tier sub-funds face monitoring challenges due to fragmented authority, intermediary funds achieve superior innovation returns by optimizing the balance between informational advantages and monitoring costs. These findings suggest that GVC, serving as a strategic industrial policy tool, effectively enhances firm-level innovation efficacy through deep public–private synergies and hierarchical optimization, providing critical evidence for refining the national innovation system.

Title: Government-backed public equity investment and technology commercialization: evidence from science and technology firms
Authors: Meng Wang, Qingzheng Wang
Abstract: Governments increasingly use public venture capital to address financing and commercialization gaps in technology-based firms, but non-random recipient selection complicates evaluation. We examine the relationship between government-backed technology equity investment and innovation in 190 science and technology firms in Qingdao, China. Using HC3-robust regressions and propensity-score overlap weighting, we distinguish innovation input, innovation output, and downstream firm performance. Government-backed investment is positively associated with innovation output, whereas its relationships with innovation input and performance are not statistically significant. Results are robust to overlap weighting. Investment intensity is correlated with all three outcomes but is treated as endogenous, and no moderator interaction survives false-discovery-rate adjustment. Survey evidence is consistent with financing, certification, governance, resource-access, and risk-sharing mechanisms, although the cross-sectional design does not permit causal or mediation claims. The study provides a cautious, measurement-explicit assessment of how public equity investment is associated with technology commercialization at the city level.

Title: Elements of university entrepreneurial ecosystems: from nice-to-have to must-have
Authors: Pedro Torres, Pedro Godinho, Edgar Nave
Abstract: University Entrepreneurial Ecosystems (UEE) have become increasingly influential within their respective regional and national entrepreneurial ecosystems, significantly impacting innovation levels in societies, particularly through patenting and University Spin-offs (USO). Against this background, this study takes a novel perspective by identifying the elements of UEE that are necessary to produce high levels of these outcomes, specifically patent grants and USO turnover. Instead of focusing on average effects, our study aims to identify what should be in place in order to attain higher levels of UEE performance. To do so, we resorted to data from Higher Education Business and Community Interaction (HE-BCI) in the United Kingdom (UK) employing Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA). The results showed that the necessity of each UEE element is contingent to the target level of the outcomes to be achieved. The total number of academics, patent stock and income from contract research emerge as important bottlenecks on the way to high levels of UEE performance. The findings expand knowledge about the university-specific characteristics that are bottlenecks for UEE development. Thereby, the study brings about a new perspective that has not only theoretical but also managerial and policy implications, which are developed in the body of the text. The importance of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) size in producing high levels of the aforementioned outcomes suggests HEIs should pursue strategies to increase their scale, if they intend to fulfil the third mission. A possible strategic response could be to negotiate mergers and partnerships.

Title: Institutional signal hierarchies and innovation partner selection: a two-sided matching study of university-industry collaboration in China
Authors: Keyan Shou
Abstract: Innovation in emerging economies increasingly depends on university-industry collaboration, yet how innovation partner selection occurs under institutional constraints remains poorly understood. Drawing on a two-sided matching framework and patent data from Zhejiang (2016–2020), we examine how institutional logic reorders the hierarchy of capability signals, reshaping partner selection in collaboration markets. Our findings reveal that scholars’ publishing capability functions as the dominant innovation signal across the collaboration market. It exhibits a robust complementary relationship with firms’ knowledge base breadth. In contrast, the matching value of patenting capability is contingent on institutional legitimacy: complementary to firms’ knowledge base breadth when scholars are from high-reputation universities, but substitutive in low-reputation contexts. These results indicate that university reputation operates as an institutional gatekeeper, determining whether ambiguous signals such as patents can enter firms’ matching evaluations, thereby reshaping the matching patterns of knowledge complementarity. This study extends two-sided matching research to non-Western institutional contexts and shows how institutional environments govern the interpretation of knowledge signals, contributing to signaling theory and university-industry collaboration research.

Title: A condition is not a mechanism. The category error in industrial policy conditionalities: a comment on Mazzucato and Rodrik’s “Industrial Policy with Conditionalities” (2026)
Authors: Philip Rey
Affiliations: Independent Researcher , Poziomkowa 4, 05-520 Borowina , . email: philiprey.org@protonmail.com
Abstract: Abstract Mazzucato and Rodrik’s taxonomy of industrial-policy conditionalities usefully restores public value to public-private economic strategy. This comment argues, however, that the paper commits a category error: it treats contractual conditions as if they were operational mechanisms. A condition can express an obligation, but it cannot monitor decay, detect gaming, or maintain performance through time. Industrial policy therefore needs trajectory diagnostics, including policy-induced turbulence, recovery dynamics, and Stability Overhead, to convert conditionality into governance.

Title: ECS-VTabNet: An interpretable federated learning approach for imbalanced credit classification
Authors: Zhongyi Wang, Eric W.T. Ngai, Zhang Wen, Yuhang Tian, Sihan Li
Abstract: Credit classification, which aims to characterize user profiles and accurately predict default risks, is critical for financial risk management. Although centralized models trained on directly aggregated multi-source data can achieve strong performance, they often disregard data privacy, class imbalance, and model interpretability. To address these gaps, we propose an example-dependent cost-sensitive vertical TabNet (ECS-VTabNet), a novel framework for privacy-preserving collaborative credit classification. The proposed framework integrates vertical federated learning with an attentive interpretable model (i.e., TabNet) and an example-dependent cost-sensitive (ECS) loss function. Our approach enables multiple institutions to collaboratively build a highly accurate credit scoring model without sharing raw data. The ECS mechanism aligns the model with business objectives by minimizing financial losses, and TabNet's inherent architecture provides transparent feature importance. Experimental results on two public credit datasets show that ECS-VTabNet outperforms existing federated and centralized methods in managing imbalanced data and providing interpretable predictions while avoiding raw data exchange under the honest-but-curious assumption. This work provides a practical solution for financial institutions seeking to build robust, compliant, and collaborative risk assessment models without centralizing sensitive client data.

Title: Technological relatedness in green innovation disruptiveness: the role of entry pace and rhythm
Authors: Shijun Mu, Lutao Ning, Jin Chen
Abstract: Achieving disruptive innovation in new green technology domains (NGTDs) is essential for firms seeking sustainable competitive advantage, addressing climate challenges, and complying with increasingly stringent regulations. Building on research on technological relatedness and entry strategies, this study argues that although entering NGTDs enables firms to pursue technological leadership, the disruptiveness of their subsequent green innovations may be constrained by the technological relatedness between their existing knowledge bases and the new green domains. Moreover, this negative effect is shaped by firms’ NGTD entry patterns. Using patent data from 994 Chinese listed firms from 2008 to 2016 and applying a Heckman selection model, we find that technological relatedness reduces the disruptiveness of green innovation. An irregular entry rhythm exacerbates this negative effect, whereas a faster entry pace mitigates it. These findings advance the literature by integrating the concepts of pace and rhythm of entry into studies of green innovation and by providing evidence from an emerging economy context. The results suggest that firms should balance reliance on existing technological trajectories with exploration of new knowledge bases to enhance disruptive outcomes. This study offers actionable insights for firms and policymakers seeking to accelerate green technological transitions and foster more disruptive, high-impact environmental innovation.

Title: Government support, co-creation, and digital transformation on the road to sustainable innovation
Authors: Ana Colovic, Annalisa Caloffi, Alan Bandeira Pinheiro
Abstract: This study examines whether and how different types of government support (financial, technological, market) impact the three types of co-creation efforts (product, process, and knowledge co-creation) of SMEs and how these, in turn, impact sustainable innovation outcomes. It also investigates whether digital transformation mediates the positive relationship between the three types of co-creation and sustainable innovation. The conceptual model is tested on an original dataset of 188 SMEs in France, collected in 2025. Findings indicate that product co-creation is positively affected by government technological support, and knowledge co-creation by market support. The mediation effect of digital transformation is confirmed for the relationship between product co-creation and sustainable innovation, while process and knowledge co-creation directly lead to sustainable innovation. The implications of the study for research, policy and practice are discussed.

Title: Does knowledge proximity attenuate or amplify the impact of credibility signals on knowledge use? Insights from two natural experiments
Authors: Jan Schilpp, Rajiv Sabherwal, Marcel-René Wepper, Hartmut Hoehle
Abstract: People rely on sources with greater credibility when deciding whether to use knowledge. However, the moderating role of knowledge proximity, that is, the perceiver's proximity to the focal knowledge and its source, remains unclear. Prior literature suggests conflicting possibilities: individuals with high proximity may bypass source credibility, as they can evaluate the knowledge at minimal cost or rely on the credibility signal, as they can properly assess the signal. To investigate this, we exploited two natural experiments involving the addition of Information Systems (IS) journals to the Association for Information Systems (AIS) Senior Scholars’ List of Premier Journals and the Financial Times list. Based on our analyses of over 100,000 citations to 1,882 papers over observation windows of up to 20 years using difference-in-differences analysis, we found that papers in FT-listed journals receive approximately 30% more citations overall, while papers in AIS-listed journals receive approximately 36% more citations from proximate (IS) journals than from distant (non-IS) journals. We conclude that knowledge proximity amplifies the impact of source credibility on knowledge use, specifically when the knowledge, perceiver, and source credibility signals are closely aligned.

Title: A stakeholder perspective-based ranking system for assessing the sustainable performance of decentralized applications (DApps)
Authors: Yifei Shuang, Xi Zhao, Hsing K. Cheng, Jian Li, Hong Mei
Abstract: Decentralized Applications (DApps), as foundational components of the Web 3.0 ecosystem, are reshaping digital interactions through decentralized, transparent, and tokenized architectures. Despite rapid growth in adoption and diversity, the absence of a holistic ranking mechanism hinders stakeholders from navigating this complex landscape effectively. Existing systems reliant on singular popularity metrics fail to capture the multidimensional sustainability and stakeholder-driven value inherent in DApps. To address this critical issue, we propose a novel ranking framework grounded in stakeholder theory, integrating the perspectives of five stakeholder groups—customers, financial stakeholders, business partners, employees, and societal stakeholders—to evaluate the sustainable performance of DApps. Our approach leverages an automated data pipeline processing on-chain Ethereum transactions and off-chain DApps metadata to synthesize multidimensional indicators via a graph-structured TOPSIS methodology that incorporates competitive dynamics among DApps. Empirical validation demonstrates the system's capacity to enhance ranking coverage, differentiation among long-tail DApps, and alignment with long-term value metrics. This work establishes the sustainability-centered DApp ranking system, advancing stakeholder-aware evaluation in decentralized contexts and introducing a network-enhanced multicriteria decision making model for the dynamic DApp ecosystem.

Title: Strengthening e-government's impact on corruption perception: The moderating role of Financial Management Information Systems (FMIS)
Authors: Munsu Kim, Wonik Park
Abstract: Using a lagged cross-sectional design, this study provides a historical cross-national assessment of whether Financial Management Information Systems (FMIS) condition the association between e-government development and perceived corruption. This study conceptualizes FMIS as a catalyst that strengthens the anti-corruption relevance of e-government. The analysis combines consolidated indicators of FMIS maturity and FMIS-related fiscal disclosure capacity finalized in 2017 with 2013–2017 averages of e-government development and control variables and subsequent corruption-perception outcomes for 2018–2023, covering up to 160 countries. Across multiple regression specifications, higher e-Government Development Index (EGDI) scores are associated with lower perceived corruption (CPI). More importantly, both FMIS maturity and fiscal information disclosure capacity significantly strengthen this relationship. These findings remain robust across additional specifications and when using the Control of Corruption Index (CCI) as an alternative dependent variable. Overall, the results suggest that e-government development can be more effective in improving corruption perceptions where FMIS are functionally mature and fiscal information is more broadly disclosed.

Title: Digital platforms and regulatory coordination patterns in China: Network evidence from Nanjing's “181” integrated emergency management system
Authors: Wu Chen, Haibo Zhang
Abstract: Digital platforms are increasingly used to address regulatory fragmentation, yet evidence from actual regulatory behavior remains limited. This study examines how inspection coordination is organized under Nanjing's “181” integrated emergency management platform. Drawing on 37,876 inspection records from August 2023 to January 2025, we construct a 2-mode inspection network linking 719 inspection departments and 7934 regulated entities through 34,053 inspection ties, and estimate Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs). The results show that coordination is organized through three related patterns. Structurally, district-level departments occupy central positions, with the strongest cluster in Yuhuatai District. In terms of coordination coverage, inspection overlap is concentrated around selected regulated entities rather than evenly distributed, a pattern consistent with shared regulatory attention. In terms of coordination responsiveness, departments that identify hazards more often are more likely to form inspection ties. These findings show how platform-generated administrative records reveal the organization of regulatory coordination in a hierarchical administrative system through recorded activities, shared targets, and risk information.

Title: AI ambivalence and digital civic engagement: Dual pathways of hindrance and capability development
Authors: Sudong Kim
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes digital governance, citizens may evaluate AI as both a source of public-service opportunity and a source of governance risk. This study examines how AI ambivalence is associated with digital civic engagement through countervailing direct and capability-related pathways. Drawing on the Challenge–Hindrance Stressor Framework (CHSF), this study conceptualizes AI ambivalence as a psychological state that may be negatively associated with engagement through a direct hindrance path while being positively associated with engagement indirectly through AI-related capability formation. Using data from the 2024 Korean Digital Divide Survey ( N = 12,393), this study tests a serial mediation model with AI literacy and AI self-efficacy as mediators. The results indicate a suppression pattern: AI ambivalence is significantly and negatively associated with digital civic engagement through the direct path, whereas the total indirect association through AI literacy and AI self-efficacy is positive and larger in absolute magnitude than the negative direct association. The serial indirect path through both mediators is significant, consistent with a knowledge-to-efficacy pathway in which AI literacy and AI self-efficacy jointly link ambivalence to engagement. Supplementary analyses suggest that prior AI usage experience may shape the relative balance between these pathways. This study extends CHSF to AI-enabled digital participation and shows that ambivalence can be associated with engagement in opposing directions depending on the outcome considered. For policymakers, the findings suggest that AI literacy programs may partly offset, but not eliminate, the participation-inhibiting pathway of ambivalence.

Title: Differentiation of R&D organisations and inventors’ networks: effects on knowledge generation and transfer
Authors: Tomoyuki Shimbo, Motohiro Nakauchi
Affiliations: Kanto Gakuin University; Aoyama Gakuin University
Abstract: Individual centrality has been shown to affect knowledge generation and transfer. However, previous studies have not considered the differentiation of R&D organisations. In a differentiated R&D organisation, different norms are formed in each unit, which may affect inventors’ learning behaviour. Additionally, whether inventors are subject to unit norms depends on their intra-unit networks rather than on their intra-firm networks. Furthermore, assuming the differentiation of R&D organisations, two channels for knowledge transfer exist within a firm: intra- and inter-units, and the effects of centrality may differ. Therefore, this study examines the effects of centrality in inventors’ intra-unit networks on knowledge generation and transfer within and between units in the same firm. The results showed that inventor networks had different effects, and to promote inter-unit knowledge transfer, each unit should establish core knowledge and share it with other units.
