Title: Understanding Virtual Assistants: A Systematic Review
Authors: Citlalli Selene Avalos-Montiel, José G. Rodríguez-García, Sonia Mendoza
Abstract: Abstract Virtual assistants have their origins in the first efforts to emulate human intelligence through systems capable of passing the Turing test. Over the years, they have evolved significantly, with Siri, introduced in 2011, being the first system explicitly recognized as a virtual assistant. Since then, the development of virtual assistants has spread to various disciplines, with the aim of assisting one or more users in various tasks, using increasingly sophisticated technologies. This article presents a systematic review, in which 34 scientific literature reviews, and surveys published between 2015 and 2025 were identified and analyzed, in order to delimit the concept of virtual assistant, its evolution and current trends, including the impact of technologies such as large-scale language models. The findings reveal a terminological ambiguity, a transition from rule-based and closed-domain implementations to Artificial Intelligence driven assistants, and the emergence of capabilities such as personalization, proactivity, context awareness, and multimodal interaction. The review also synthesizes recurring limitations and challenges reported in the last decade, highlighting patterns across domains and temporal shifts. These insights contribute to a clearer conceptualization and outline promising directions for future research.

Title: Concerto of rhetoric and images: The effect of multimodal aesthetics on customers' booking intentions in P2P accommodation
Authors: Haiwang Liu, Xiaoyun Han, Limin Xiao
Abstract: Despite the importance of aesthetics in peer-to-peer (P2P) accommodation, prior studies have neither integrated rhetoric into the multimodal information framework nor examined the synergistic or antagonistic effects between rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics. To address this gap, this study employs text mining and image detection techniques to operationalize aesthetics as rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics, with the latter further comprising cover image aesthetics and sleep space image aesthetics. Based on aesthetic arousal theory, this study uses secondary data from 20,144 Airbnb listings to construct econometric models and conducts four scenario-based experiments. The results indicate that rhetoric aesthetics has an inverted U-shaped effect on customers' booking intentions, mediated by aesthetic pleasure—that is, rhetoric aesthetics exerts an inverted U-shaped effect on aesthetic pleasure, which in turn positively influences customers' booking intentions. Cover image aesthetics enhances the inverted U-shaped effect of rhetoric aesthetics and its indirect effect, whereas sleep space image aesthetics weakens both. Post-hoc analysis shows a positive direct effect of image aesthetics on customers' booking intentions. Supplementary analysis further indicates that rhetoric aesthetics linearly increases cognitive load, and that positive emotion is lowest at a low level of rhetoric aesthetics but does not differ significantly between medium and high levels. This study advances aesthetics research in P2P accommodation, deepens the understanding of the synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms of multimodal aesthetics, and provides decision support for hosts and platform managers to optimize multimodal aesthetic information to meet customers' aesthetic needs.

Title: Navigating AI-driven technological pressure: How top management team IT readiness and strategic orientation shape data breach risk
Authors: Niaz Mohammed, Chul Woo Yoo
Abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping industry practices and creating new security vulnerabilities, raising questions about the effectiveness of firms' internal risk management capabilities under heightened technological pressure. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory, we investigate how top management team (TMT) IT readiness influences firm-level data breach risk under the external technological pressure of industry AI exposure, and how firm strategic positioning shapes that response. Using a comprehensive firm-year panel dataset, we first confirm, consistent with prior research, that TMT IT readiness is associated with lower data breach risk. Building on this baseline, our central findings show that this effect is not uniform but is conditioned by the firm's technological and strategic context. The breach-reducing effect of TMT IT readiness becomes stronger in industries with higher AI exposure, and this moderating effect is itself contingent on firm strategic positioning. Specifically, the effect is more pronounced among innovation-oriented firms and less consistent among efficiency-oriented firms. These findings advance the data breach literature by identifying the boundary conditions of the well-established link between TMT IT readiness and breach risk, showing that its effectiveness amplifies under higher industry AI exposure and depends on firm strategic positioning. This study also offers practical implications for managers by highlighting the need to tailor security governance to industry-level technological pressures.

Title: A Human-Centric Framework for Fair Job Recommendation Leveraging Generative AI and Data Augmentation
Authors: Jianshan Sun, Jie Shao, Kun Yuan, Dongyang Li
Abstract: Online recruitment platforms play a critical role in enabling job seekers to access employment opportunities. However, many job seekers actively browse and apply for positions but receive little feedback, reflecting a fundamental challenge of unequal information access in digital labor markets, especially for information-disadvantaged users with sparse interaction histories and biased exposure. To address this challenge, this study proposes PA2Rec, a human-centric and generative AI enhanced framework that improves fair job information access through data-level augmentation. PA2Rec integrates a multi-attribute job filtering mechanism to construct high-quality candidate opportunity sets, leverages large language models to generate pseudo-interaction samples that expand users’ accessible opportunity space, and incorporates fairness-aware prompt tuning to mitigate systematic exposure bias. Experiments on the public Zhaopin ( https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/231728/information .) dataset demonstrate PA2Rec significantly improves recommendation accuracy and fairness, especially for information-disadvantaged job seekers. The results highlight the effectiveness of generative AI in augmenting information access and advancing human-centric recommendation systems in online recruitment.

Title: Why do Deepfakes Spread? A Multi-Method Study of Adoption in Utilitarian and Hedonic Deep Synthesis Technologies
Authors: You Wu, Xing Zhang, Yingzhen Feng
Abstract: Deep synthesis technology (DST), exemplified by deepfakes, raises significant ethical and legal concerns, yet users continue to actively engage with such applications even when these concerns are salient. This behavioral pattern presents a theoretical paradox: ethical risk does not uniformly suppress adoption behavior across contexts. Conventional technology adoption models such as UTAUT lack ethical constructs and may therefore prove insufficient for explaining adoption in morally contested technological contexts such as DST. Moreover, prior research has predominantly treated DST as a homogeneous category, overlooking variation across application types and the heterogeneous role of ethical factors in shaping adoption intentions. This study addresses these gaps by examining users’ adoption intentions across heterogeneous DST applications and uncovering underlying mechanisms. Integrating the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) with Hunt-Vitell ethics theory, we conducted a scenario-based survey featuring utilitarian and hedonic DST applications, encompassing function-oriented contexts (e.g., public interest communication and organizational management) and entertainment-oriented contexts (e.g., celebrity impersonation and virtual performance). A multi-method strategy combining comparative analysis and configurational analysis assessed adoption differences and identified equifinal pathways. Results reveal significantly stronger adoption intentions toward utilitarian than hedonic DST. The two adoption contexts exhibit fundamentally distinct configurational logics. Utilitarian DST adoption follows a rational-instrumental logic, with descriptive norms serving as the core condition across all configurations. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and technology self-efficacy also emerge as frequently recurring core conditions across multiple pathways. Hedonic DST adoption, by contrast, is governed by an ethico-normative logic, with ethical acceptability serving as the core condition across all configurations. Injunctive norms, hedonic performance expectancy, and the absence of deepfake concern appear as core conditions across several pathways. These findings demonstrate that ethical risk does not uniformly suppress adoption behavior; rather, its causal role varies systematically across application contexts. This study extends UTAUT into ethically sensitive technological domains and offers differentiated, evidence-based guidance for DST governance and context-sensitive regulatory design.

Title: Unveiling the critical role of ethical leadership in information systems security compliance research: An empirical investigation
Authors: Botong Xue, Merrill Warkentin, Xin (Robert) Luo
Abstract: In the existing discourse on behavioral information systems security, a diverse array of individual and organizational attributes has been investigated regarding the employees’ information security policy (ISP) behavior. However, ethical leadership, a pivotal paradigm profoundly associated with employees’ security behavior, has been starkly overlooked in this domain. The research unveils and examines the role of ethical leadership in influencing employees’ ISP-related behaviors. To test our hypotheses and validate the research model, we conducted a scenario-based online experiment pre-study followed by cross-sectional survey of working professionals. The findings reveal that ethical leadership significantly influences both ISP in-role and extra-role behavior, directly and indirectly, through three mediators: attitude toward security behavior (ATT), subjective norm about information security (SN), and perceived behavioral control over security behavior (BC). This research contributes to the growing streams of information security and ethical leadership literatures and offers actionable managerial suggestions on cultivating ethical leadership to enhance organizational information security performance.

Title: Adoption of ChatGPT for Learning-Related Information Access: A Comparative UTAUT2 Analysis of Turkish and Polish University Students
Authors: Ali İbrahim Can Gözüm, Artur Strzelecki, Ümit Ünsal Kaya, Murat Taşdan
Abstract: Abstract This study examines ChatGPT adoption among higher education students in Türkiye and Poland through an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) framework that also includes personal innovativeness. It compares country-specific adoption patterns across the two samples and offers a cautious contextual interpretation of the observed differences. Survey data were collected from 634 students in Türkiye and 531 students in Poland, and the proposed relationships were examined using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that the extended UTAUT2 framework was empirically useful in both samples, although the relative prominence of specific predictors differed across them. Descriptively, Performance Expectancy (β = 0.258, p < 0.001) and Personal Innovativeness showed larger coefficients in the Polish sample, whereas Effort Expectancy (β = 0.104, p < 0.01) and Social Influence (β = 0.199, p < 0.001) appeared more prominent in the Turkish sample. Price Value showed a statistically significant reversed association with Behavioral Intention in Türkiye (β = -0.187, p < 0.001), whereas the association was positive in Poland (β = 0.094, p < 0.01). Habit emerged as one of the strongest predictors in the model and was positively associated with both Behavioral Intention and Use Behavior in the two samples. Taken together, the findings suggest that ChatGPT adoption in higher education is shaped by a combination of perceived usefulness, ease of use, social and practical support, habitual use, and context-sensitive evaluations of value. The study contributes to the growing literature on generative AI in higher education by showing that the same theoretical framework can reveal different adoption patterns across two national samples, while also highlighting the need for context-sensitive implementation strategies. The findings offer practical implications for higher education institutions, educators, and policy developers seeking to support the responsible and effective use of ChatGPT.

Title: A global analysis of female innovative entrepreneurship and the role of financial development
Authors: Cecilia Alvarez-Vargas, Joan-Lluís Capelleras, Francis J. Greene, Victor Martin-Sanchez
Abstract: Drawing on feminist and institutional perspectives, this study analyses whether women are equally likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship and whether the maturity of debt and equity markets strengthens women's participation. We use data from 71,888 early-stage ventures across 101 countries and show that women are as likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship, once crucial individual and country-level factors are controlled for. Further, we demonstrate that both debt and equity market development positively moderate this relationship. These findings reveal that gender gaps in innovative entrepreneurship reflect structural and institutional conditions rather than intrinsic propensities and highlight the role that financial development plays in supporting female innovative entrepreneurship.

Title: LLM-powered contrastive hierarchical interest learning for cross-platform information recommendation
Authors: Datian Bi, Xue Zhang, Jingyuan Kong, Gongkun Chen
Abstract: With the widespread prevalence of multiplatform usage behaviors, cross-platform heterogeneous data offer new opportunities to alleviate cold-start and sparsity issues in recommender systems; however, they also introduce challenges, such as amplified noise, semantic heterogeneity, and negative transfer. Existing cross-platform recommendation methods often merely share user or item embeddings, thereby creating difficulties in effectively distinguishing commonalities and differences in user interests across platforms; moreover, they lack unified modeling and effective utilization of multilevel interest structures. To address these limitations, this study proposes LCHIL, a large language model (LLM)-powered contrastive hierarchical interest learning framework for cross-platform information recommendation. LCHIL leverages LLMs for cross-platform data augmentation and low-order semantic modeling on heterogeneous graphs to characterize platform-local shallow interests. It then uses a heterogeneous graph attention network to aggregate higher-order interactions and extract platform-global deep interests, while incorporating perplexity-based alignment signals and gated multimodal units to model cross-platform dynamic interests. The framework integrates hierarchical interests into a collaborative contrastive learning process to reduce redundancy and noise in heterogeneous graph information and to mitigate cross-platform transfer bias. Experiments using four real-world cross-platform datasets demonstrate that LCHIL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models on multiple evaluation metrics and exhibits strong effectiveness in alleviating cold-start issues and suppressing noise.

Title: Lost in translation? Academic engagement and academic entrepreneurship in Chinese universities: a review of Chinese literature from 2017 to 2024
Authors: Emil Kristoffer Hyttel Bohmann, Jason Li-Ying
Abstract: This study systematically reviews 390 Chinese-language articles published between 2017 and 2024 to examine how Chinese universities approach academic engagement and academic entrepreneurship—the two core components of the university’s “third mission.” Although Western scholarship has extensively mapped university–industry collaboration, indigenous Chinese developments remain largely “lost in translation” due to linguistic barriers and limited cross-citation. Our review identifies key indigenous concepts—such as the transformation of scientific and technological achievements, coordinated innovation, and mixed intellectual property rights (IPR) ownership—that define China’s unique, centrally driven approach to technology transfer. We find that Chinese literature prioritizes institutional and ecosystem-level dynamics, contrasting with Western emphasis on individual-level motivations and informal networks. By synthesizing these findings into a conceptual model, this study bridges the gap between Chinese and Western research communities. It offers a more inclusive, globally balanced perspective for understanding academic entrepreneurship, highlighting how diverse institutional settings shape the translation of knowledge into economic value and providing a foundation for future comparative research.

Title: Knowledge base renewal and the dynamic selection of R&D Partners: a perspective from innovation appropriation
Authors: Delin Meng, Lan Wang
Abstract: Against the backdrop of continuous knowledge base renewal, why and how firms adjust their collaborative R&D partner relationships has become an important issue for understanding the dynamic evolution of open innovation strategies. Drawing on the theory of innovation appropriation, this study uses joint patent application data from Chinese A-share listed firms from 2003 to 2022 to systematically examine the impact of knowledge base renewal on the characteristics of collaborative R&D partner selection and its underlying mechanisms. The results show that knowledge base renewal significantly reduces the number of collaborative R&D partners, the diversity of partner types, and the geographic distance of collaboration, suggesting that firms actively contract their collaboration boundaries as their knowledge bases evolve. Further analysis indicates that knowledge base renewal strengthens firms’ attention to the protection of innovation returns and drives adjustments in collaborative relationships by reinforcing informal appropriability mechanisms and increasing the diversity of knowledge recombination. Moreover, the negative effects are more pronounced when CEOs have richer functional experience and when firms occupy more prominent structural-hole positions in innovation networks. These effects are also stronger in regions with higher levels of judicial protection for intellectual property rights and more developed socialized service systems. This study demonstrates that collaborative R&D partner relationships are not determined solely by the static characteristics of firms’ knowledge bases but are continuously reconfigured as knowledge bases evolve. By revealing the innovation appropriation logic underlying the dynamic adjustment of firms’ collaboration boundaries, this study offers a new theoretical explanation for the evolution of collaborative strategies in the context of open innovation.

Title: The Lasting Impact of the First Comment in Short Videos
Authors: Xiaochen Ma, Yangyin Lin, Qiang Ye, Hao Xia
Abstract: To examine whether early-stage social signals help explain divergent engagement trajectories beyond video content, this study investigates the lasting impact of the first comment in travel short videos. Utilizing a dataset of 499 matched pairs of cross-posted travel videos and over 400,000 comments from Douyin and Kuaishou, we employ a cross-platform differential modeling approach to reduce content-related confounding and isolate comment-dynamics effects. The findings validate a dual-pathway pattern: (1) a direct sentiment pathway, consistent with emotional contagion, in which the first comment positivity shapes subsequent comment sentiment but attenuates over time; (2) an indirect volume pathway, in which a positive first comment increases early engagement, which in turn predicts higher cumulative comment volume through a persistent herding effect. The study provides a novel lens for understanding commenting dynamics in high-velocity digital ecosystems. For tourism marketers, it suggests differentiated early-stage engagement strategies for short-term sentiment management and longer-term interaction accumulation.

Title: Beyond blind feature injection: An information foraging theory-guided deep learning framework for product recommendation
Authors: Weiyue Li, Ming Gao, Jingmin An, Bowei Chen, Jiafu Tang, Xuhui Wang, Yeming Gong
Abstract: Recommender systems significantly improve the quality and confidence of consumer decisions by alleviating information overload through streamlined retrieval, playing a vital role in e-commerce platforms. However, most recommender systems underutilize contextual information and fail to explicitly model users’ cognitive processes, leading to biased preference learning. Drawing on information foraging theory, this study adopts the design science research methodology to develop Tiresias, a framework that aligns with users’ cognitive processes by mimicking how proximal cues and foraging costs are assessed for each product. Proximal cues such as product category and affinitive relationships, and foraging costs such as behavior type, dwell time, and foraging progression, are identified and encoded as learnable features. To model the product-foraging journey, Typhon is designed as a Kolmogorov–Arnold network-enhanced differential transformer with a non-invasive feature injection mechanism. A multi-task learning objective that combines next-product prediction with auxiliary cue and cost prediction refines contextualized preference representations. Experiments on datasets show that Tiresias achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming baselines by up to 5.44%. Finally, post-hoc analysis reveals learned representation patterns consistent with dynamic preference evolution throughout the user’s product foraging journey. Methodologically, the study demonstrates how information foraging theory can guide feature selection, feature learning, and objective design. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for developing cognitive process-aware recommender systems that better support consumer decision-making.

Title: Go your own way: Managerial engagement with regional innovation ecosystems for Industry 4.0 transformation in Belgian SMEs
Authors: Anastassiya Zabudkina, Olivier Lisein, François Pichault
Abstract: While Industry 4.0 (I4.0) has led to the proliferation of policy-driven innovation ecosystems aimed at supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in their digital transformation, limited attention has been paid to how managers engage with these environments in practice. This study examines how SMEs’ managers interpret, evaluate, and mobilise external support within I4.0 Regional Innovation Ecosystems (I4.0 RIE). Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with managers of industrial SMEs in Belgium, we adopt a sense-making perspective to analyse engagement as an interpretive process. The findings show that managers approach these ecosystems as overlapping support mechanisms, which they evaluate in terms of accessibility and usability and enact through selective, adaptive, and sometimes reversible patterns of access and use. These findings suggest that engagement with I4.0 RIE is not driven by the availability of support alone, but by how managers interpret and position it in relation to their firms’ needs and constraints. By foregrounding these dynamics, the study offers a processual view of how SMEs engage with innovation ecosystems under digital transformation.

Title: Knowledge polycentricity and technological diversification: evidence from U.S. Metropolitan Statistical Areas
Authors: Yibo Qiao, Yingcheng Li, Yangyi Wu
Affiliations: Nanjing University; Southeast University; Wuhan University
Abstract: Existing literature on regional technological diversification has primarily viewed regions as points, while little attention has been paid to their inner spatial configurations. To address this gap, this paper investigates the impact of knowledge polycentricity on regional technological diversification. Using the USPTO patent data (1976–2020), we conduct econometric analyses on 354 U.S. Metropolitan Statistical Areas and 558 four-digit CPC technology domains. Integrating the attribute-function polycentricity framework from knowledge polycentricity literature and relatedness-complexity diversification framework from Evolutionary Economic Geography studies, we find that attribute polycentricity leads to unrelated and less complex diversification, whereas functional polycentricity triggers related and more complex diversification. The primary results still hold under instrumental variable estimation and a series of robustness checks. We contribute to Evolutionary Economic Geography literature by incorporating intra-urban knowledge polycentricity into the study of technological diversification.

Title: A new framework for industrial policy: the case of semiconductors in Japan and the United States
Authors: Yukihiro Sato, Viktória Döme, Mateus Labrunie, Carlos López-Gómez, Eoin O’Sullivan
Abstract: Abstract Interest in industrial policy has intensified in recent years, calling for renewed conceptual understanding and more robust analytical tools. However, existing industrial policy frameworks remain insufficient to capture the complexity and dynamics of contemporary industrial systems and policies. To address this gap, this study proposes a novel industrial policy analysis framework comprising four analytically distinct yet interrelated dimensions: drivers shaping policy, value-chain segments, product types, and policy instrument mixes. The framework was developed through theory synthesis by integrating key dimensions identified in prior industrial policy research and was subsequently adapted to the semiconductor sector through policy document analysis of 108 policy interventions and 22 in-depth interviews. The sector was selected due to heightened policy salience arising from geopolitical tensions and supply-chain vulnerabilities. The analytical utility of the framework is demonstrated through two empirical case studies comparing (1) Japan’s semiconductor policies pre- and post-COVID-19, and (2) Japan–U.S. semiconductor policies. The first case study reveals a marked strategic reorientation in Japan’s semiconductor policy after COVID-19, characterised by clearer policy direction, expanded interventions and larger budgets, and a broader R&D scope. The second case study identifies a strategic convergence in policy instrument choices, with both countries prioritising industrial grants to support the manufacturing segment of advanced logic chips as a core competitive domain. This study demonstrates that the proposed framework can serve as a robust analytical tool not only for systematic comparison but also for identification of opportunities and threats within national industrial systems, thereby enabling more strategic industrial policy design.

Title: “Rich-get-richer”? Platform attention and earnings inequality using Patreon earnings data
Authors: Ilan Strauss, Jangho Yang, Mariana Mazzucato
Affiliations: The Bartlett Faculty of the Built Environment, University College London , 22 Gordon Street, London WC1H 0QB , . e-mail: ilan@aidisclosures.org; Office of the DSI/NRF South African Research Chair in Industrial Development, University of Johannesburg, Auckland Park Kingsway Campus , PO Box 524, Auckland Park 2006, Johannesburg; Department of Management Sciences, Faculty of Engineering, University of Waterloo , 200 University Avenue West, Waterloo, ON N2L 3G1; Institute for New Economic Thinking at the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford , Oxford OX1 3UQ; Oxford Martin Programme on Technological and Economic Change (OMPTEC) , Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, 34 Broad Street, Oxford OX1 3BD; UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose, The Bartlett Faculty of the Built Environment, University College London , 11 Montague Street, London WC1B 5BP
Abstract: Abstract Patreon allows content creators to monetize additional content from loyal fans. Because it offers minimal native distribution, Patreon earnings largely reflect creators’ popularity on their primary external platforms (Instagram, Twitch, YouTube, Twitter/X, Facebook, or “Patreon-only”), making them a useful proxy for platform-level algorithmic attention dynamics. Fitting power-law tails to Patreon earnings by primary platform affiliation, we find three key results. First, platforms exhibit “rich-get-richer” earnings dynamics (Barabási and Albert, 1999 Science, 286, 509–512), reflected in a Pareto exponent $\alpha \approx 2$, which is closer to concentrated capital income than labor income. Second, platforms with more concentrated earnings (lower $\alpha$) have lower mean and median earnings, and thus an eroded creator “middle class.” Third, across most platforms, $\alpha$ values decline and converge over time (based on three cross-sections: 2018, 2021, and 2024), meaning earnings become increasingly concentrated among top creators—consistent with algorithmic recommendations rising in importance. Algorithmic attention allocation is a plausible driver of these patterns, though platform-specific conversion rates and audience willingness to pay may be just as important.

Title: “Will a robo-advisor help my grandpa?”: Exploring pathways to better integrate the elderly in the era of artificial intelligence
Authors: Roxana R. Iordache, Fernando A.F. Ferreira, Neuza C.M.Q.F. Ferreira, Marina Dabić, João J.M. Ferreira
Abstract: The global aging population, particularly the increasing number of individuals over 65 in Europe, presents both significant challenges and unique opportunities. This demographic shift has sparked the rise of the Silver Economy ( i.e. , a sector focused on the production, consumption and trade of goods and services aimed at improving the lives of the elderly), increasingly driven by technological solutions such as artificial intelligence (AI). Among these technologies, robo-advisors (RAs) hold promise in enhancing the quality of life, autonomy and social inclusion for older adults. However, while the potential of AI to integrate the elderly into society is widely acknowledged, there remain substantial gaps in understanding how best to deploy such technologies. Existing literature reveals critical limitations in methodologies and a lack of comprehensive models to guide the integration of AI into the lives of the elderly. This study addresses these gaps by adopting a constructivist approach and proposing a decision-support system to guide authorities in crafting effective policies and initiatives. The system is developed with input from field experts through participatory methods, specifically the Nominal Group Technique (NGT) and the DEcision MAking Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL), within a neutrosophic framework. By doing so, the study provides a more nuanced understanding of the barriers and opportunities in using RAs for the elderly, offering both theoretical advancements and practical recommendations to improve their integration into the AI-driven future of the Silver Economy.

Title: The Dark Side of Artificial Autonomy: Formation and Coping of Relationship-related Technostress between Humans and AI
Authors: Fengjiao Zhang, Zhao Pan, Qian Hu, Yaobin Lu
Abstract: Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies offer autonomy features that enable artificial intelligence agents (AI agents) to help users complete daily tasks, facilitating the establishment of human–AI relationships. Since users need to balance their relationship development needs for autonomy and relatedness, artificial autonomy may induce relationship-related technostress during the development stage of human–AI relationships, a phenomenon often ignored by prior studies. In the current study, we aimed to explore how the autonomy features of AI agents shape users’ technostress perceptions from the perspective of human–AI relationships and their subsequent coping responses. The results of a two-wave panel survey indicated that there are nonlinear relationships between artificial autonomy and relationship-related technostress. In detail, artificial autonomy has an inverted U-shaped relationship with intrusiveness and a U-shaped relationship with overdependence. For the intrusiveness stressor, individuals are more willing to escape from stressful situations by seeking emotional and physical distance from the stressor (emotional venting and distance from AI) or controlling the invasive technology conditions by engaging in delegation (control over delegation). For the overdependence stressor, individuals prefer to continuously maintain a close relationship with AI agents while reducing stressful experiences, adopting approach coping strategies to modify their attitudes (parasocial relationship) and behaviors (control over delegation) or avoiding emotional disturbance (emotional venting). This study provides new theoretical insights into the impact of artificial autonomy on individuals and enhances the understanding of technostress in the human–AI interaction context. The findings also offer insightful suggestions for practitioners in designing AI agents to better satisfy users’ needs.

Title: Business models for digital innovation intermediaries: evidence from the digital innovation hubs initiative
Authors: Federica Rossi, Ana Colovic, Simona Ciappei, Andrea Bonomi Savignon
Affiliations: Università di Modena e Reggio Emilia, Dipartimento di Economia ``Marco Biagi'' , Via Jacopo Berengario, 51, 41121 Modena , . e-mail: federica.rossi@unimore.it; NEOMA Business School , 1 Rue du Maréchal Juin, 76130 Mont-Saint-Aignan , . e-mail: ana.colovic@neoma-bs.fr; Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Architettura, Ingegneria delle Costruzioni e Ambiente Costruito , Edificio 15 Campus Bonardi, Via Giuseppe Ponzio 31, 20133 Milano , . e-mail: Simona.ciappei@polimi.it; University of Rome `Tor Vergata', Dipartimento di Management e Diritto , Via Columbia 2, 00133 Roma , . e-mail: bonomi.savignon@economia.uniroma2.it
Abstract: Abstract Innovation intermediaries are increasingly mobilized in policy programs to support the adoption and diffusion of digital technologies. Yet we still have a limited understanding of how different types of organizations enact this role and which business models they adopt. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 20 (European) Digital Innovation Hubs in Italy, Spain, France, Germany, and the UK, we investigate how intermediaries create and deliver value in policy-driven digital transition initiatives. We identify four recurrent business model configurations that combine technology/sector, or territorial focus (value proposition) with centralized or decentralized governance (value delivery), each associated with specific organizational forms such as Research and Technology Organizations (RTOs), business associations, territorial development organizations, and technology and knowledge transfer networks. The study clarifies how organizational characteristics shape the enactment of digital intermediation and offers guidance for the design and targeting of future policy initiatives.

Title: Demand-oriented policy tools and industrial convergence: evidence from cross-regional government procurement in China
Authors: Jun Liu, Chang Cao, Wei Wu
Affiliations: College of Urban and Environmental Sciences, Peking University , No. 100 Zhongguancun North Street, Haidian District, Beijing 100871; Institute of Quantitative & Technological Economics, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences , No. 5 Jianguomennei Avenue, Beijing 100732; School of Public Finance and Taxation, Capital University of Economics and Business , No. 121 Zhangjialukou, Huaxiang, Fengtai District, Beijing 100070 , . e-mail: qinwu18@126.com
Abstract: Abstract Demand-side government procurement policies play a crucial role in promoting industrial modernization and high-quality development, and they profoundly shape the evolution of regional industrial structures. Using city-pair panel data from 2015 to 2022, this paper examines the impact of cross-regional government procurement on the similarity of industrial structures between cities. The results show that cross-regional procurement significantly increases industrial structure similarity, reflecting a form of “desired convergence” driven by coordinated interactions. This effect operates through three main channels: facilitating cross-regional investment expansion, strengthening innovation and R&D collaboration, and reinforcing policy support for resource complementarity. Heterogeneity analysis further reveals that the effect is more pronounced in non-cluster cities, in cities with similar resource endowments, and when suppliers are predominantly located in southern regions. An extended analysis of broader economic and social outcomes shows that cross-regional procurement helps narrow intercity disparities in the share of technology-intensive firms, employment absorption capacity, corporate social responsibility, and overall firm performance, thereby fostering mutually beneficial outcomes across cities. However, in procurement-originating cities, the improvement in firms’ operating performance under such policies remains relatively limited.

Title: Simple and complex identities in high dimensional organizational worlds: dimensional reduction and the emergence of organizational agglomeration
Authors: Christina Fang, Ji-hyun Kim, Joseph Porac
Affiliations: Department of Management and Organizations, Stern School of Business New York University , 40 West 4th Street, New York, New York 10012 , . e-mail: chf3@stern.nyu.edu; Division of Management, School of Business, Yonsei University , 50 Yonsei-ro, Seodaemun-gu Seoul, 03722; Department of Management and Organizations, New York University , 40 West 4th Street, New York, New York, 10012
Abstract: Abstract Organizational clusters are central to how industries evolve, but their origins remain poorly understood. Existing research explains how spatial agglomerations of similar organizations are recognized and labeled and how they influence behavior, yet it rarely addresses how similarity becomes tractable in the first place within high-dimensional organizational worlds. We develop a Schelling agent-based model that formalizes two mechanisms of dimensional reduction: attribute privileging, in which actors selectively foreground a small subset of identity-relevant features, and correlated attribute environments, representing material and technological worlds exhibiting coherent bundles of capabilities. Across four experiments, we show that spatial agglomeration is unlikely without substantial cognitive or environmental compression, that narrowly privileged attributes can stabilize proto-clusters, and that correlated attributes generate robust and durable agglomerations even without focal attention. Together, these results illuminate how the “places and spaces of organizing” become visible long before formal categories or institutions solidify.

Title: The low-value trap: Sustaining multi-actor collaboration across problem spaces in emerging technology commercialization
Authors: Ferran Giones, Daniel Laufs, Carsten Schultz
Abstract: Despite the potential applications of bio-marine technologies, many promising innovations remain confined to the laboratory, missing potential high-value applications and damaging the overall perception of the emerging technology. Prior research has highlighted the positive impact of multi-actor collaborations on technology development, particularly to bridge the gap between the lab and the market. However, we know little about the mechanisms that sustain productive multi-actor collaboration in emerging technology commercialization and why they prove insufficient as actors move from low-to high-value applications. We study the case of an emerging technology – the utilization and application of fucoidan, a bio-marine extract – to explore how collaboration is sustained among actors as they face the increasing complexity of the technology commercialization for high-value applications. By building on patents and publications and analyzing in-depth interviews, we identify three key mechanisms that support effective collaboration: anchoring a shared vision, coordinating across knowledge boundaries, and structuring an operational framework. We show how these mechanisms need to be recalibrated, not simply scaled, when actors transition across problem spaces from low to high-value applications, and why the failure to do so produces a low-value trap for the emerging technology.

Title: Do industrial robots improve firm productivity in China? The role of management practices
Authors: Dezhuang Hu, Tang Li
Abstract: Whether industrial robot adoption improves firm productivity remains an open question, with mixed evidence echoing the broader productivity paradox associated with information and communication technologies. This paper examines whether firm-level management quality can help resolve this ambiguity. Using novel firm-level data from the China Employer–Employee Survey, which uniquely combines direct measures of robot capital and management practices, we show that robot adoption is associated with significantly higher total factor productivity. This finding is robust to alternative measures of robot use and productivity, as well as to instrumental variable strategies exploiting exogenous robot-policy shocks and firm-level robot exposure. A difference-in-differences design further supports a causal interpretation. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that these productivity gains are strongly moderated by management quality. In particular, monitoring, target-setting, and managerial incentive practices act as key complements, whereas non-manager incentives do not play a significant moderating role. Further analysis shows that the gap in productivity gains from robot adoption between small and large firms narrows at higher levels of management quality, suggesting that managerial capability is a key constraint on small firms’ returns to industrial robots. These findings help reconcile the mixed evidence on robot productivity and underscore the importance of management improvement programs as a complement to automation policy.
